knowledge: The origin of the author's sales methodology and subsequent large-scale research (quantitative survey of about 24,000 people and sales support for over 40,000 people at top domestic and international companies) was the frustration of losing deals (失注の悔しさ).
At age 25, the author entered corporate sales (法人営業) without any boss or senior colleagues to teach sales, so they had to self-learn through trial and error while trying to produce results daily.

The author's competitive personality meant that losing a major competition caused such shock that they could not recover for a week, and sometimes even became physically ill and were bedridden for 3 days.

Over 20 years ago, the author was selling corporate training to HR departments and participated in a competition for new-employee training at a large IT vendor that was planning a major overhaul of its existing program.

Despite repeatedly visiting the client, making multiple proposals and revisions based on feedback, and believing they had submitted the best possible proposal, the author received an email one week after the presentation informing them they had not been selected.
Immediately after receiving the rejection email, the author called the client and went to meet them the same day, determined to learn exactly why they lost and what had been wrong with the proposal.

The author approached the post-loss meeting with an intense determination (an 'aura' of 'I will not leave until you tell me everything'), which allowed them to discover 'the customer's hidden side' (お客様の裏側) that only becomes visible after losing.
Losing a deal for the first time revealed insights about the customer's true decision-making process that were not apparent during the proposal stage.

In a competitive B2B vendor evaluation, a customer used a detailed Excel scoring sheet with 24 judgment criteria (axes) on the vertical axis and 8 vendor names on the horizontal axis; each criterion was scored out of 5 points for a maximum total of 120 points.
The author's proposal failed to rank in the top 3, revealing that the customer applied far more granular evaluation criteria than was typical or visible in other similar sales situations.
A large score gap existed between the 1st-place vendor and all others, with the leader pulling far ahead rather than a close contest among top contenders.

The winning vendor had no prior official track record with the customer but had long served as an informal 'discussion partner' (ディスカッションパートナー) on talent development, making frequent visits to the company.

That vendor had proactively built relationships not only with the HR department (the official window) but also with field department heads who would actually receive the new-employee training and with the management-planning staff who controlled the training budget.

These relationships were established well before the customer formally recognized the need to renew training or began issuing inquiries to vendors—i.e., during the earliest stages of issue recognition.

By contrast, the author had spoken only with the single HR contact person and had begun activity only after receiving a formal request for proposal, entering the process at the late 'vendor-comparison' stage after the customer had already completed issue recognition, information gathering, and requirements definition.

Key sales insight: late-stage engagement limited to the official gatekeeper places a vendor at a severe disadvantage; early, multi-stakeholder relationship-building (HR + end users + budget holders) before an RFP even exists can create an insurmountable lead.

In B2B/corporate sales (法人営業), a proposal is rarely evaluated solely by the primary contact person (窓口担当者). Multiple internal stakeholders exist, each bringing different judgment criteria based on their departmental roles and priorities.

Judgment criteria can proliferate as more stakeholders become involved. Example: field department heads demanded that new-hire training programs make recruits immediately productive, while corporate planning/budget staff required quantitative demonstration of cost-effectiveness (費用対効果). This process produced 24 distinct evaluation criteria unknown to the salesperson.

The winning vendor systematically gathered voices from all relevant stakeholders in advance and constructed a proposal that scored highly against every one of the 24 criteria. Success came from mapping the customer's complete internal decision-making landscape rather than iterating only with the contact person.

Iterating a proposal exclusively on feedback from the window contact addresses only a small fragment of the actual evaluation process. The salesperson who lost the deal realized that 'no matter how diligently you craft a proposal, it will never be rewarded if you remain ignorant of what is happening behind the scenes at the customer.'

A core sales methodology is to understand the customer's 'worldview' (世界観) before designing any solution. This means requesting and reviewing the actual internal documents and discussion materials the customer uses when debating the project internally.

Different stakeholders view the same project through completely different lenses. In a subsequent new-hire training RFP at a major IT firm, the HR contact focused on program content and instructor quality, while other parties held entirely different evaluation perspectives that had to be surfaced early.

Practical tactic: during pre-design discussions, explicitly ask to see the materials the customer is already circulating internally. This reveals hidden stakeholders and their conflicting criteria before the formal proposal is written.

In B2B proposal situations (e.g., corporate training programs), multiple internal stakeholders typically have divergent priorities even for the same project: the primary contact may focus on program 'content', the HR director on measurable outcomes such as reduced new-hire turnover, the receiving business-unit director on immediately usable practical skills, the corporate-planning budget owner on numerically demonstrable ROI, and the administrative/operations team on logistical smoothness (venue booking, participant management).

A practical discovery method is to ask the initial contact two explicit questions: 'Which people inside the company will participate in the review/decision process?' and 'What specifically does each of those people care about?' Then, whenever possible, obtain direct conversations with those stakeholders rather than relying solely on the intermediary.

A single proposal document can be engineered to satisfy all parties by explicitly embedding tailored answers: turnover-reduction logic for HR, evidence-based curriculum design for line managers, cost-benefit framing for finance, and operational-support structure for administration.

Engagement timing is a decisive variable. Instead of waiting for a formal RFP, initiate contact while the customer is still only at the 'problem-recognition' stage; even after being told 'we will contact you once requirements are fixed,' continue offering low-commitment information-exchange meetings. By the time formal requirements are written, an internal perception that 'this vendor already understands us' has already formed.

A useful mental model for proposal construction is to imagine a multi-stakeholder review meeting that will apply objective, fair scoring criteria and will scrutinize not only quality/content but also exhaustive risk-mitigation measures. After mapping every stakeholder and every process step, the goal is to produce a proposal that is '減点しようのない' (impossible to deduct points from).

The described approach converted a previously lost opportunity into a won contract, illustrating that systematic stakeholder-and-process mapping plus early-stage relationship building can outweigh a purely content-focused proposal.

The key to raising close/win rates in sales is thoroughly understanding the customer's hidden worldview, background, and 'backside' world that is invisible to salespeople, rather than relying only on visible sales activities.

Personal sales success and winning patterns often fail to transfer to a growing team because telling members to 'understand the customer's worldview' is too abstract; they cannot act on it and the team remains dependent on one person's intuition and experience.
To scale from individual wins to team wins, a highly reproducible system and common language are required so that the leader does not have to be involved in every deal.
A practical method is to create a 'Winning Pattern Construction Sheet' (勝ちパターン構築シート) in Excel and mandate its use in all strategy meetings so discussions stay structured.
Effective frameworks work backwards from how the customer's actual decision-making process occurs and are designed to be usable even by new graduates.
The starting point for systematizing sales was the realization that the customer's purchasing process must be structurally unpacked and turned into a shared, team-wide winning pattern.
Most sales teams spend excessive time on KPI management and proposal improvements while remaining weak at grasping the invisible 'customer's world' behind the scenes.
The widely taught B2B principle of 'just meet the decision-maker' is insufficient by itself; deeper insight into the customer's hidden context is needed.

Even when following the golden rule of meeting the decision-maker (kessaisha) and making every effort to win orders, sales often fail for two main reasons: inability to get a meeting with the decision-maker, or being rejected after internal company discussions even after meeting them.

A quantitative survey of 2,676 people with purchasing experience found that the final decision-maker holds the most substantial influence over a deal in only 16.7% of cases; conversely, in 83.3% of cases, someone other than the final decision-maker exerts the real influence.

Actual influence can come from various parties depending on the nature of the deal, such as the end-user department whose daily use of the service becomes the deciding factor, or administrative departments (e.g., accounting or legal) that hold effective veto power.

Formal decision-making authority (kessai-ken) must be distinguished from actual/substantial influence; the invisible power dynamics that salespeople cannot see constitute both the difficulty and the interest of B2B/corporate sales.
The book analyzes these invisible dynamics stage by stage throughout the purchasing process.
Prior research in the author's books 'Mubai Eigyo' and 'Mubai Eigyo Team Strategy' (Nikkei BP) surveyed 929 people to analyze how the 'gap' (zure) between salespeople and customers affects results.

A larger-scale survey for 'Eigyo no Kagaku' (Kanki Publishing) involved 10,076 salespeople plus 10,303 customers (total 20,379 people) and revealed that 74.4% of customers had already made their decision before even looking at a quotation/estimate, with the majority being swayed primarily by the speed of the salesperson's response.

Corporate purchasing decisions are frequently finalized before estimates are even reviewed, making it essential to understand the hidden mechanisms of organizational buying behavior and internal decision-making processes.
Response speed from vendors is critically important because of how and when decisions actually get made inside customer organizations.

Detailed analysis of over 100,000 customer complaints revealed that root causes were not product defects or service quality issues, but rather unoptimized and poorly defined business processes across different departments.
Unexpected facts that emerge from granular data analysis can become the foundation for high-impact strategies.
Most people tend to make biased or incorrect decisions; simply correcting these misconceptions with data can produce measurable improvements in outcomes.

The book is based on surveys totaling 24,000 people (prior research covering 21,308 individuals plus a new survey of 2,676 people with purchasing experience) that map who is involved, what processes they follow, and how they think when making B2B buying decisions.
Winning patterns for corporate sales should be reorganized and systematized according to the customer's purchasing process rather than the salesperson's proposal process.
The inherent difficulty of B2B sales is conceptualized as a 'maze' that can be navigated by aligning sales activities with the customer's actual buying journey.
The book is structured in three parts to convert the complexity of corporate (B2B) purchasing into systematic logic and concrete actions.
Part 1 is a preparatory section that explains the overall picture of corporate purchasing processes and stakeholders so that salespeople do not panic when they become lost in the 'maze'.
Part 2 is the basic 'defensive strategy' edition that teaches how to escape once lost inside the purchasing maze.
Part 3 is the applied 'offensive strategy' edition that teaches how to proactively approach customers by accurately identifying which stage of the purchasing process they are currently in.
Core goal of the book: make the existence and power dynamics of 'invisible stakeholders' behind the customer visible.
Another core goal: structurally grasp each deal's unique purchasing process so that a salesperson can independently decide 'what to do next'.
Ultimate goal: replace reliance on individual intuition or experience with team-shareable winning patterns, thereby raising the entire organization's sales capability.
Key principle: 'If you cannot see what is happening behind the customer, even the most excellent product or proposal will never bear fruit.'
Complementary principle: 'Winning patterns built on a thorough understanding of the customer's hidden side are rock-solid.'

In B2B/corporate sales (法人営業), salespeople commonly fall into '4 mazes' (4つの迷路); escaping them requires clarifying what is actually happening on the customer side rather than focusing only on the seller's activities.
The standard sales process and the customer's purchasing process are completely different phenomena and must not be treated as the same sequence.
The customer's purchasing process consists of 5 distinct stages; a salesperson must accurately identify which stage the customer currently occupies.
Purchasing decisions on the customer side involve 6 types of stakeholders (関係者); each has a different role and set of priorities.
Effective sales actions depend on correctly diagnosing the role and decision criteria of the specific person sitting in front of the salesperson.

The preparatory section of the material therefore focuses on three foundational frameworks that every corporate salesperson must master: the 4 mazes, the 5-stage purchasing process, and the 6 types of decision-making stakeholders.

Customers frequently select vendors based on response speed rather than proposal quality when multiple options are comparable: A large manufacturer's HR contact received similar proposals from three training companies but chose the fastest-responding vendor because they delivered requested additional materials the next day.

Internal corporate buying processes involve layered approvals and sudden escalations that create hidden urgency: The HR contact needed manager approval followed by an executive meeting; a previously uninterested executive suddenly requested materials for the next week's meeting, prompting the manager to demand an immediate update.

Salespeople typically lack visibility into the customer's internal world and decision mechanics, which include competing daily tasks, unexpected executive requests, and the need for the internal champion to quickly assemble materials for higher-level presentations.

Fast vendor responses enable the customer's internal advocate to meet sudden internal deadlines and successfully champion the deal, turning response time into a decisive competitive advantage even when content quality is equal.
Key concept introduced: Sales fall into '4 mazes' (4つの迷路) precisely because they cannot see the customer's side of the world and therefore do not understand how actual purchase decisions are made.

Customers juggle multiple daily tasks and often delay purchasing considerations; sudden pressure from superiors ('How did that matter go?') creates internal communication urgency that vendors must anticipate.

A vendor who delivered requested materials immediately enabled the customer to proceed with internal discussions right away, while two competitors who took two extra days were dropped mid-process even if their proposals were comparable.
Selection frequently hinges less on proposal quality and more on alignment with the customer's internal business flow and the need to respond promptly to bosses.
A large IT firm's planning director stated: 'To be honest, we had already decided which company to engage before even looking at the estimates.'

During an organizational-reform initiative still in the information-gathering stage (no internal consensus yet on whether to invest), five vendors were invited for discussions; the eventual winner was chosen on the strength of those early conversations rather than formal quotes or detailed proposals.

Customers may request only 'simple materials' while they are still deciding whether an investment is warranted at all; vendors who treat this stage as mere information collection miss the hidden decision-making that is already occurring.

In B2B vendor selection, especially at large enterprises, the preferred partner is often chosen based on early-stage engagement quality rather than formal proposals or pricing; the winning vendor made discussions feel collaborative ('hot') from the information-gathering phase and articulated challenges the client had not yet verbalized, leading the planning manager to decide 'I want to work with this company' before even seeing the quote.

A real example from a corporate planning department: five vendors were asked to submit materials; four responded with only basic service-introduction decks, while the selected firm treated the RFI stage as a joint problem-solving session, organizing unspoken issues and creating a sense of partnership that locked in the decision prior to price comparison.

Obtaining multiple quotes is frequently an internal 'ritual' or procedural formality in large organizations; even when one vendor is already the clear favorite, presenting a single candidate to the management committee invites the objection 'Did you really evaluate alternatives?', so additional bids are collected solely to satisfy governance optics.

Unsuccessful salespeople typically experience a characteristic post-proposal pattern: sparse replies, delayed emails, no access to decision-makers, and non-committal answers to status inquiries ('We're still considering'). This silence often signals that the client has already mentally selected another vendor and is merely completing the comparison paperwork.

The gap between the client's internal reality and the salesperson's external view is large: the buyer may have already decided yet still request quotes for compliance reasons, while the losing seller interprets the lack of engagement as 'the deal is stalling' and reports poorly to their own manager.

In B2B (corporate) sales, a common failure mode is losing deals because the salesperson cannot see or understand the customer's internal world of stakeholders and situations, leading them into one of '4 mazes' (4つの迷路).

A 'maze' in corporate sales is defined as a situation where the salesperson does not know which stakeholders exist on the customer side or what the current internal situation is, preventing them from taking clear, targeted actions while time simply passes.

Salespeople who lose deals often follow their own internal sales process, feel they have 'done everything they should,' yet get no results; because they cannot diagnose why they lost, they repeat the same pattern on the next deal.

This differs from visible, concrete bottlenecks that can be addressed with specific skills: for example, if a customer evades budget questions after granting a proposal opportunity, the salesperson can improve questioning techniques to uncover the budget; if the customer states the proposal is inferior to a competitor on specific points, the salesperson must revise the proposal logic to reverse the situation.

The author previously covered tactics for such visible bottlenecks and competitive responses in earlier books ('無敗営業' and '営業の科学'), which focused on sales skills; the current book instead addresses the harder-to-grasp 'mazes' that arise specifically because of the large number of purchasing stakeholders in B2B sales.

Corporate sales contains four distinct mazes; when a deal is blocked by an unseen wall and cannot progress, the salesperson is typically lost in one of these four mazes, and the book will provide concrete actions for escaping them.

Corporate sales professionals commonly fall into four 'labyrinths' or pitfalls: (1) unable to meet the key person, (2) unable to make contact, (3) consideration/progress stalls, and (4) budget does not increase.

The first labyrinth is 'unable to meet the key person': After a positive reaction from the contact person, the salesperson waits indefinitely for an appointment with the decision-maker/key person, remaining in a 'waiting' state without knowing if internal consideration is even occurring.

Example of the first labyrinth: A contact person says 'I'll talk to my superiors about this,' but weekly follow-ups yield the same response of 'I haven't been able to talk to them yet,' leaving the salesperson feeling they have no choice but to wait.
A core problem in this labyrinth is the lack of visibility into why the contact person cannot escalate the discussion to the key person.

Possible reasons a contact person fails to involve the key person include insufficient 'materials' or talking points to make a compelling internal case, or the key person being fully occupied with other priorities and lacking bandwidth for new topics.

Because the customer's internal world is invisible to the salesperson, they fall into '4 mazes' (4つの迷路). This page covers the second and third of these mazes in a sales context (Chapter 1, Preparation section).

Second maze: the 'contact does not connect' maze (「連絡がつながらない」迷路). After a smooth, positive sales conversation, emails suddenly go unanswered. Salespeople become unsure of the right timing and type of follow-up.
A common trap for salespeople in this maze is binary thinking: either send repeated reminder emails or simply wait for a reply. The customer's actual situation is more complex.

Customer-side complexities include: an unexpected higher-priority internal project arising that postpones the salesperson's matter; or the contact person having consulted their boss and received a poor reaction, making them reluctant to reply.

Example from the book's opening episode: The salesperson who was not selected sent additional materials and received no reply. In the meantime, the customer internally discussed and decided direction based on another company's materials—the entire movement was invisible to the salesperson.

Third maze: the 'consideration does not progress' maze (「検討が進まない」迷路). Contact remains possible, but the speed of '検討' (consideration/review) is slow for unknown reasons. This prevents timely re-proposals and leaves the deal in limbo as time passes.

The phrase 'we'll consider it' (「検討します」) can hide three different realities: (1) they are genuinely considering it carefully, (2) they are politely declining, or (3) they want to consider it but do not know how to proceed with the internal consideration process.
From the salesperson's side it is completely invisible who internally holds the 'ball' at the customer company and why that ball has stopped moving.

The fourth maze in corporate (B2B) sales is the 'budget does not increase' situation: even when the client's company size suggests they can comfortably afford the proposed amount, they claim 'no budget.' This also covers cases where the proposal content is agreed upon but budget approval (決裁) is not granted.

Behind the phrase 'no budget' lie various hidden internal circumstances. These include: an actual lack of budget allocation; budget existing but assigned low priority for this particular project; internal disagreements within the client's company about how to use the budget; or a stalled approval process. 'No budget' is merely a one-word summary of the client's internal situation.

Salespeople who get lost in these four mazes fail to see two important facts: (1) the sales process and the purchasing (buying) process are different, and (2) many stakeholders exist behind the scenes who are invisible to the salesperson.

Without these two facts, salespeople feel frustrated that they are 'doing everything correctly but somehow it is not working.' Conversely, acquiring the two perspectives of 'purchasing process' and 'stakeholders' is the first step to escaping the mazes.
The fundamental reason most salespeople cannot adopt these two perspectives is that they have never personally experienced a corporate purchasing process themselves.

A corporate purchasing process consists of using company budget to buy something, coordinating with internal stakeholders, passing internal approvals (稟議), comparing vendors, and deciding on the supplier. Sales work accumulates only 'selling-side' experience, so few salespeople understand how the purchasing process actually proceeds, who is involved, and who makes which judgments.

Salespeople without purchasing-side experience naturally struggle to feel the reality of the customer's internal world, making it extremely difficult to imagine events inside the customer's company such as the internal power dynamics behind requesting quotes from three companies or the complex circumstances behind the phrase 'we'll consider it.'

Even when the sales side cannot understand why a deal was lost, the ordering/purchasing side's perspective often reveals clear, specific reasons; the two episodes introduced at the chapter start became visible only because they were heard directly from the ordering side.

The author's foundational knowledge of this 'hidden world' comes from personal experience as a company manager who has received and evaluated quotes, confirming that contexts invisible to the sales side definitely exist on the purchasing side.

The book systematically and concretely explains the customer's purchasing process and the structure of involved stakeholders using abundant data so that even salespeople without purchasing experience can understand it.

Reliving the world that is invisible from the seller's perspective through the book is presented as a major first step toward escaping the four mazes that arise from not being able to see the customer's world.
The typical sales process consists of four stages: (1) approach, (2) hearing/needs analysis, (3) proposal/presentation of the product or service together with a quote, and (4) closing.

From the sales side the process appears linear and controllable: Approach → Hearing → Presentation → Closing, with the quote issued during the presentation stage and the decision requested at closing (illustrated as Figure 1-2, 'the world visible from sales').
多くの営業担当者はアプローチ→ヒアリング→プレゼン→見積もり→クロージングという自社視点のプロセスで「次に何をすべきか」を考えているが、これはあくまで営業側から見た世界であり、顧客企業内部ではまったく別の購買プロセスが動いている。
企業の購買行動プロセスは5段階に分けられる：1.課題認識、2.情報収集、3.要件定義、4.ベンダー比較、5.発注決定。
第1段階「課題認識」：業務上の課題・問題が発生したり改善の必要性が認識されたりして「何かの購買が必要かもしれない」と想起されるまでの段階。例：「最近、業務のミスが増えてきた」「このままでは来期の目標達成が難しい」といった問題意識から「何か手を打たなければ」と感じ始めるところからスタートする。
第2段階「情報収集」：課題認識後、いきなり本格検討に入らず簡単なリサーチが行われる。「世の中にはどんな製品・サービスがあるのだろう」「同業他社はどうしているのだろう」と選択肢を探る段階。まだ「買おう」と決めておらず、「どんな選択肢があるかざっと見てみたい」という温度感。
第3段階「要件定義」：予算、機能、導入期間、運用体制などの要件が徐々に言語化され、ベンダーからの提案を受けるための準備段階に入る。社内で「こういう条件で選びましょう」という基準が初めて形になっていく。
第4段階「ベンダー比較」：複数のベンダーから提案や見積もりを受け取り比較検討が行われる。正式な見積もりが揃うまでの検討期間がこの段階。
第5段階「発注決定」：発注する会社を選び契約を締結する。ベンダーからの見積もりが揃ったあと社内検討期間が長期化するケースがあり、それはこのプロセスにおける議論が紛糾したり停滞したりする場合である。

The purchasing process can be divided into 5 stages: 1) Issue recognition (課題認識) - A specific business issue is recognized and the thought that 'some kind of purchase might be necessary' arises. 2) Information gathering (情報収集) - Before full-scale consideration, simple research begins and it becomes clear 'what kinds of products/services might exist'. 3) Requirements definition (要件定義) - Requirements such as budget, functions, implementation period, and operational structure are put into words. 4) Vendor comparison (ベンダー比較) - Proposals are received from vendors from whom detailed estimates are desired, and formal estimates from each company are gathered. 5) Order decision (発注決定) - The company to place the order with is selected and the contract is signed.

The actual purchasing process does not always proceed through these 5 stages in the same way. Cases can start from vendor sales pitches or from customer inquiries. They can proceed top-down or bottom-up from the field. Internal meeting bodies may lead the consideration, or it may start from a specific individual's (like an executive's) awareness of a problem. Decision-making can happen in a short period or consideration can continue over a long period. Thus, even though the same 5 stages are passed through, the way they progress differs greatly depending on the case.

The most important and most easily overlooked difference between the sales process and the purchasing process is the discrepancy in recognition of 'the timing when the decision is made' (「発注が決まるタイミング」の認識がズレている).

Many salespeople position the timing of making a proposal or the closing scene where decision-makers are present as the 'critical moment' (勝負どころ). They put effort into presentation preparation, polish their closing talk, and put all their energy into the final push.
However, there is a fatal pitfall: The customer's 'decision in their heart' (心の意思決定) happens much earlier than salespeople assume.

In B2B sales, the customer's actual decision-making often occurs much earlier than the formal stages of the salesperson's process, frequently during information gathering or requirements definition rather than at the final closing or official approval meeting.

Customers may decide on a vendor as soon as they receive an estimate in the information-collection stage, thinking 'I'll go with this company already.' Others form a conviction during requirements-definition discussions that 'this vendor is a good match' or 'I want to work with this company.'
A concrete example: the planning director of a major IT company stated that the vendor had already been chosen internally before any estimates were even reviewed.

By the time the official order-decision meeting with approvers takes place, all internal groundwork may already be complete and the preferred vendor already decided unofficially inside the customer's organization.
The moment of decision is governed by the customer's own internal context and timeline, not by the linear sales process visible to the salesperson; that moment is often surprisingly early.
Once a customer's mind is already made up, subsequent sales effort—no matter how intense—risks being completely wasted.
Salespeople typically perceive a sequential process (approach → hearing → presentation → closing) and expect the decision and estimate submission to occur at the closing stage.

Customers follow their own sequence (issue recognition → information gathering → requirements definition → vendor comparison → order decision). An estimate may be requested early, the real decision may already have been made, and later formal stages can become mere rituals.
The two worlds therefore do not always align: the sales process flow does not necessarily coincide with the customer's actual decision-making flow.

Losing salespeople often remain trapped in this mismatch, planning to compete at the estimate-and-closing stage while the customer has already built trust with another vendor long before materials even arrived.
In B2B (corporate) sales, one of the most deep-rooted problems is the mismatch in perception regarding the 'timing when the decision is made' between the salesperson and the customer.
A key concept introduced to resolve this timing mismatch is obtaining the 'Matsutai' (松たい明まつ), which will illuminate the path forward (detailed later in the chapter).
Decision-making stakeholders on the customer side often operate in 'invisible places' that salespeople cannot see, influencing the purchasing process behind the scenes.

A common and dangerous misconception in sales is that securing the decision-maker's agreement alone will close the deal, such as believing 'presenting to the president guarantees a win' or 'executive approval is sufficient.'
Relying on this misconception can be fatal, especially when selling to large enterprises, as it ignores the full complexity of the buying process.

In corporate purchasing practice, there are six distinct stakeholder roles: 1) Field users (現場の利用者) who participate in discussions from the perspective of actually using the product/service; 2) Internal promoters (社内推進者) who propose and lead the introduction of the product/service; 3) Ordering personnel (発注担当者) who handle vendor coordination and negotiations; 4) Budget supervisors (予算の監督者) who manage expenditures and investments based on financial conditions; 5) Influencers to the decision-maker (決裁者への影響者) who advise the final decision-maker; 6) Final decision-maker (最終決裁者) who oversees the business at the management level and makes the ultimate judgment.
These six stakeholder types interact in various ways to drive the purchasing process, often in combinations that are not immediately visible to the salesperson.
B2B purchasing processes can start from multiple distinct triggers, each creating a different decision-making flow and set of stakeholders that sales must match in timing and approach.

Vendor-initiated case: The process begins when a vendor approaches the customer. The purchasing/order staff first evaluates whether an order looks viable, then the matter moves to their supervisor and through internal meetings before a conclusion. The initial contact person often controls whether sales ever meets the final decision-maker.

Field-problem-initiated case: Discussion originates inside an operational department; field users gather information and become the primary contact with vendors. These users typically have strong enthusiasm for the product or service but almost never hold budget authority.

Budget-planning-initiated case: A management directive starts the process. An internal champion collects information, socializes it with the field, then escalates it to a management meeting for final approval. Because the origin is a high-level policy, alignment between field and management is required and the cycle tends to be lengthy.

Influencer-initiated case: A specific individual (external expert, trusted advisor to the decision-maker, or the executive themselves after attending a seminar) creates the need, after which information gathering begins.

A one-size-fits-all sales motion that always targets the final decision-maker first will frequently miss the customer’s actual decision cadence, producing delayed responses or actions that fail to meet expectations and resulting in lost deals.

Concrete mismatch example: When a deal originates from field-level pain, an early request by sales to meet the final approver can make field users feel the internal consensus is not yet ready, causing them to distance themselves from the vendor.
In B2B/corporate sales, the person holding 'substantial influence' over vendor selection is highly case-by-case and frequently is not the official final decision-maker.
A survey of 2,676 people with company-budget purchasing experience found that only 16.7% said the final decision-maker has the substantial influence on choosing a vendor.
This means that in 83.3% of purchases, someone other than the official final approver exerts the real influence.

Distribution of substantial influence: internal promoter/champion 21.1%, influencer to the decision-maker 16.5%, purchasing/order officer 16.2%, field/end users 14.7%, budget supervisor 11.4%, final decision-maker 16.7%, other roles 3.4%.
Even when official approval authority belongs to the final decision-maker, actual influence is widely dispersed across six organizational roles.

A key sales pitfall: when a deal originates top-down (from an influencer to the decision-maker), spending most time only with field users can leave the salesperson unable to respond to executive pressure to accelerate, allowing competitors to win.
The survey was an internet panel study conducted in June 2025 by TORiX Corporation among people who had made purchases using company budgets.

In new-customer sales meetings, typically only 1–2 people from the customer side participate initially, but numerous unseen stakeholders who never appear in the meeting still exert deep influence on the decision through internal discussions.

Hidden influencers communicate among themselves (in internal meetings, document comments, hallway conversations) without the salesperson ever seeing those exchanges; the salesperson therefore cannot assume that a positive reaction from the visible contact person means the deal is progressing.

Concrete internal-resistance example: the visible contact says “good proposal,” yet the administration manager later objects “there is no precedent, we should be cautious,” another department head says “if it affects our department we need more study,” and a presidential aide argues that a different investment should be prioritized. None of these conversations are visible to the salesperson.

Operating without the premise that “invisible people influence the decision” produces a high probability that the deal will stall or be lost even when every visible process step appears to be going smoothly.
Informal, unofficial interactions (meeting remarks, comments written on circulated documents, corridor talk) frequently determine the actual direction of a purchase.

Selling only to the person sitting in front of you causes a misalignment of “who, at which stage, and what action is required,” so a salesperson can feel strong momentum yet still lose the final selection.
Purchasing initiative inside the customer organization is highly dispersed rather than concentrated in a single identifiable key person.
Survey result: when asked who has substantial influence over vendor selection, respondents in every role (including themselves) claim “I myself” at rates of roughly 30–50 percent.
Among final decision-makers, only 46.4 percent regard themselves as the true key person; 11.0 percent of them believe the actual field users hold the substantial influence.
Because influence cannot be pinned on one individual, sales activity must map and engage the entire hidden decision network rather than relying on a single champion.

In B2B sales, even final decision-makers (最終決裁者) themselves report that 53.6% feel 'the entity influencing the decision is someone other than myself.' Assuming a deal is secured merely because one met the president or obtained the decision-maker's OK is therefore premature.

Among non-final-decision-maker roles, 30-40% still claim they themselves possess the substantial influence over supplier selection; this indicates that multiple key persons (キーパーソン) typically exist for any single deal.

Agreement from the final decision-maker who holds formal authority is a necessary condition for winning an order, yet it is not sufficient: opposition from other stakeholders frequently causes deals to stall, and obtaining those stakeholders' buy-in is often a high hurdle even to gain access to the final decision-maker.

A survey of 2,676 respondents (broken down by role: field users n=474, internal promoters n=432, purchasing staff n=443, budget supervisors n=432, influencers on decision-makers n=460, final decision-makers n=435) shows that 30 % to just under 50 % of each group selected their own role as having the 'substantial' influence on supplier choice, confirming widespread self-perception of being the key person.

The chapter frames these findings as one of the 'four mazes' (4つの迷路) salespeople fall into when they cannot see the customer's internal world, underscoring the need to map the full multi-stakeholder landscape rather than relying on a single contact.

In B2B sales, a critical insight salespeople must grasp is that key persons (キーパーソン) are distributed across the organization and exist in an ambiguous, fluid state rather than being a single fixed individual.
Many individuals involved in the purchasing decision are people the salesperson has never met, making it essential to look beyond the immediate contact.
The purchasing process consists of 5 stages; even in the very first stage of 'problem recognition' (課題認識), multiple roles already show a certain level of involvement or higher.

Problem recognition (課題認識) is defined as the period that begins when a business issue arises or when internal/external communications occur, and ends when the necessity of introducing or ordering a product or service is recognized.

A survey of 2,676 respondents measured the degree of involvement of six stakeholder roles during the problem-recognition stage on a 5-point scale (not involved at all / little involvement / neither / some involvement / greatly involved) plus an option indicating the respondent lacked information about that role.

The six roles examined are: field users (現場の利用者), internal promoters (社内推進者), ordering personnel (発注担当者), budget supervisors (予算の監督者), influencers on the decision-maker (決裁者への影響者), and the final decision-maker (最終決裁者).

It is an undeniable fact that people occupying many different positions are already involved from the earliest stage of purchasing; assuming that simply securing the person immediately in front of you is sufficient during problem recognition is a mistake because many others are already moving behind the scenes.

In B2B (corporate) sales, two critical facts cause salespeople to get lost in 'mazes': (1) the sales process and the customer's purchasing process are fundamentally different, and (2) many stakeholders exist on the customer side but remain invisible to the salesperson.
These unseen dynamics lead to common problems such as being unable to meet key persons or losing contact with the customer.
To navigate the 'dark maze' of B2B sales, salespeople must light a 'torch' consisting of three elements that provide visibility into the customer's hidden world.

Element 1 of the torch: Accurately identify which of the five stages of the customer's purchasing process they are currently in (e.g., problem recognition, information gathering, requirements definition, or vendor comparison). The appropriate sales action differs completely by stage.

Example of stage-specific action: Presenting a quote to a customer still in the problem-recognition stage will not advance the deal; continuing leisurely information provision once the customer has reached vendor comparison risks being overtaken by competitors.

Element 2 of the torch: Precisely determine which of the six possible roles the currently contacted person occupies (e.g., end-user/field user, purchasing officer, or internal champion/promoter). The person's needs, concerns, and anxieties change according to their role.

Element 3 of the torch: Using the insights from the current purchasing-process stage and the contacted person's role, map a clear path that will lead the customer organization to decide to place the order with your company.
Salespeople must proactively share timely information with multiple unseen stakeholders so that those stakeholders can continue advancing internal discussions from their respective viewpoints.
To advance a sales opportunity, it is crucial to have a clear outlook on what next action to take with the current counterpart in order to move their purchasing consideration forward.

Being able to verbalize key elements (such as the current stage and stakeholders) is like lighting a torch in a dark maze: it makes it clear why a deal is not progressing and what should be done next.

The sales process can be visualized as navigating a dark maze from an entrance toward a goal (winning the deal, customer success, or achieving targets). Understanding the structure of the maze (the buying process and involved parties) reveals how to reach the goal.
The next chapter will deepen understanding of the '5-stage purchasing process' and the '6 types of stakeholders'.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior is the combination of a 5-stage process and 6 types of stakeholders.
The customer's 5-stage purchasing process consists of: Problem Recognition (課題認識), Information Gathering (情報収集), Requirements Definition (要件定義), Vendor Comparison (ベンダー比較), and Order Decision (発注決定).
The vendor is not necessarily decided at the final Order Decision stage; the actual decision point can occur earlier.
A survey of purchasers asked which of the 5 stages most influences vendor decision-making; responses were distributed across multiple stages rather than concentrated in one.
Only 11.3% of respondents identified the Order Decision stage as most decisive, showing that few people believe the vendor choice is finalized at the last moment.
Requirements Definition was cited as the most influential stage by 26.0% of respondents.
Information Gathering was cited by 22.3% and Problem Recognition by 18.5%, indicating that upstream stages also exert substantial influence on the final vendor choice.

In B2B vendor selection and procurement processes, 66.8% of cases are substantially decided by the requirements definition stage (the three upstream stages of issue recognition + information gathering + requirements definition combined). This means more than two-thirds of deals are effectively settled before any proposal is even submitted.

Survey data (n=2,676) on the stage with the greatest actual influence on selecting the vendor: issue recognition (課題認識) 18.5%, information gathering (情報収集) 22.3%, requirements definition (要件定義) 26.0%, vendor comparison 21.2%, order/purchase decision 11.3%, other 0.6%.

Customer decision-making typically occurs much earlier than salespeople assume. The formal 'order decision' or contract agreement stage is frequently just a ceremonial confirmation of a judgment that has already been made.

If a salesperson is in a disadvantaged position during the upstream stages, it is extremely difficult to reverse the situation in the later (downstream) stages. Conversely, establishing a strong position early in the customer's process creates a significant advantage even during final contract negotiations.

A critical practice for salespeople is to continuously diagnose and understand 'what stage of the customer's decision process are we currently in?' to avoid getting lost in the 'maze' of unresponsive or inaccessible stakeholders.
The key to understanding customer purchasing behavior consists of a 5-stage purchasing process and 6 types of stakeholders.

A primary cause of sales problems is failure to grasp the customer's specific purchasing process; customers experience different worries and needs at each stage, which changes what they want from salespeople.
Effective selling requires identifying the customer's current purchasing stage and providing stage-appropriate value.
BANT information consists of Budget, Authority, Needs, and Timeframe; asking only about consideration schedule (Timeframe) is insufficient to determine the exact purchasing phase.

This chapter explains, for each of the 5 purchasing stages and based on survey data from 2,676 people: (1) questions to confirm the current stage, (2) typical worries and needs at that stage, and (3) sales actions that are appreciated and raise order probability.
Stage 1 is 'Problem Recognition' (課題認識): the period until a specific business issue is recognized and the customer begins to think that some form of purchase may be necessary.

Confirmation question for Problem Recognition stage: 'Is the premise of this discussion that you are still exploring what the issue is, or are you already at the stage of starting to move specifically toward solving the issue?' (former answer indicates Problem Recognition).

Diagnostic questions to determine if a prospect is in the '課題認識' (problem recognition / issue awareness) stage: (1) Is there already internal company agreement to proceed with considering this issue? (No → 課題認識 stage); (2) Are they still discussing internally whether they even need to outsource at all? (Yes → 課題認識 stage); (3) Are management and frontline staff aligned on the priority of this issue? (No → 課題認識 stage).
Survey of 2,676 people with purchasing experience identified two distinct categories of concerns specifically in the problem-recognition stage.

The dominant (first) category of concerns is that the consideration process itself cannot even get started properly—before any discussion of 'how to recognize the issue.' Concrete examples include: misalignment between executives and field staff on priority ranking, lack of available time because higher-priority work exists, and fear that spending time on consideration will increase the burden on other employees.

The secondary category of concerns is 'judgment difficulty'—i.e., inability to think clearly about the issue itself. Examples include: inability to judge from urgency/importance whether an order is truly needed, vague root causes that block solution exploration, and insufficient knowledge or experience.

Core finding: The bigger obstacle at the problem-recognition stage is the absence of time and organizational slack to initiate any consideration process at all, rather than the intellectual difficulty of analyzing the problem.

Customer reality in the 課題認識 stage: buyers themselves want to decide 'Do we really need to place an order?' and 'Should we tackle this right now?' but they lack the bandwidth to perform that thinking.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior (購買行動) is the '5-stage process' (5段階のプロセス) and the '6 types of stakeholders' (6種類の関係者).

Definition of the '課題認識' (problem/issue recognition) stage: the period until necessity is recognized that 'some product or service introduction or order might be needed,' triggered by arising business issues or communications from inside or outside the company.
Survey of 2,676 people on worries during the 課題認識 process (respondents ranked top 1-3 concerns; 'other' and 'no worries' excluded).

Highest-ranked worries include: misalignment of priority recognition between management (経営層) and field/on-site staff; inability to allocate time/effort due to higher-priority tasks; burden placed on field staff or other employees during consideration; difficulty judging whether an order is truly necessary from urgency/importance perspectives; vague problem cause making appropriate solutions hard to identify; personal lack of knowledge/experience for defining the issue; inability to obtain understanding from decision-makers; unclear responsibility/who should handle it; unknown how other companies are addressing it; past failed introductions acting as a bottleneck causing stagnation.
Worries fall into two categories: those that prevent even proper consideration from starting (そもそも検討がまともにできない悩み) and those that hinder thinking effectively about the issue itself (課題についてうまく考えられない悩み).

At the 課題認識 stage, salespeople commonly make the mistake of contacting repeatedly without a purpose or using fear-based approaches that incite crisis ('it will be bad if not dealt with now'). Customer research shows such pushy, urgency-inciting tactics rank among the least effective.

In the '課題認識' (problem recognition) stage of the sales/buying process, collaborative work ('共に深める共同作業') with the customer is highly effective and valued, while pushy or pressuring tactics rank lowest in increasing order probability.

A survey of 2,676 respondents identified preferred salesperson actions in the problem recognition stage (ranked 1st-3rd place, excluding 'other' or 'don't know' responses): quick responses to inquiries/questions (19.5% 1st place), gradually deepening understanding of the customer's company while approaching, assisting with on-site hearings and information analysis, providing information useful for verbalizing issues, continuous information provision instead of immediate selling, contacting at the right timing, frequent contact even without specific business, and applying 'healthy pressure' that inaction now would be problematic.

The lowest-ranked action is 'push and incite' behavior such as applying pressure with statements like 'if you don't deal with this now it will be bad,' because customers already recognize the urgency but feel frustrated they cannot proceed with consideration; external pressure from salespeople tends to worsen their impression of the salesperson.

High-impact actions that raise order probability are those involving joint collaborative work: providing fast responses to customer inquiries, approaching while stepwise deepening understanding of the company, helping with necessary analysis or hearing work, and supplying information that aids in articulating/verbalizing the customer's issues.

Customers at this stage experience 'もどかしさ' (frustration) of wanting to advance consideration but being unable to; they already know they should act sooner, so being hurried from the outside is counterproductive.

Example of an effective collaborative response: When a customer says 'we cannot yet enter full-scale consideration,' propose a short 15-minute online meeting to share two case studies from industries similar to the customer's.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior is the combination of a 5-stage process and 6 types of stakeholders.
Presenting small steps (e.g., 'I'll just introduce you a little') makes customers more likely to feel they can spare the time.
A separate analysis comparing top-down versus bottom-up cases found that the power of quick response is especially large in bottom-up cases.

Bottom-up cases require the field person in charge to originate the proposal and move the organization internally; a quick sales response therefore functions as psychological support that the customer has an ally.
The information-collection stage begins after issue recognition and consists of light research until the customer can see what kinds of products or services might exist.

Diagnostic questions that confirm the information-collection stage include: 'Are you still looking broadly at options rather than evaluating specific vendors?'; 'Are you about to start talking with several other companies besides us?'; 'Do you already have even a rough cost image, or not yet?'; and 'Do you already have the information you need to consult upward internally?' (No answers indicate the information-collection stage).
A survey of 2,676 people showed that, in the information-collection stage, customers particularly value knowledge of specifications and prices.

In the information collection (情報収集) stage of B2B purchasing—defined as the phase after deciding to order/introduce a product or service but before full-scale consideration, when buyers start simple research on available products/services—buyers commonly face a dual challenge: they cannot obtain information well, and even when they collect it they cannot properly select or filter it.

The most prominent buyer pain points in information collection are: (1) desired information (specific specs, prices, etc.) is hard to obtain; (2) insufficient time can be secured for information gathering; and (3) there is too much information, making it impossible to judge reliability or accuracy, so one no longer knows what is correct. This is described as drowning in a sea of information.

Survey data (n=2,676, excluding 'other' and 'no particular worries') ranked the top information-collection worries by 1st/2nd/3rd place votes, with the leading items being: wanted information (specs/prices) hard to obtain; insufficient time for collection; information volume too large to judge reliability/accuracy; internal members lack knowledge/experience so consideration does not proceed well; priority points for consideration are vague so it is unclear what information to collect; internal disagreements cause information collection to stall; information collection becomes an end in itself and later steps never begin; information is scattered because multiple people collect it; collected information is full of jargon and hard to understand; persistent sales follow-up after exhibitions or document requests.

Sales behaviors welcomed by buyers at the information-collection stage (same as at the earlier problem-recognition stage) are led by speed of response; next are jointly thinking through cost-effectiveness simulations and explaining service content, specifications, and customization options.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior consists of a 5-stage process and 6 types of stakeholders.

In the 'information collection' stage of the buying process, a survey of 2,676 people found that the most valued salesperson action (increasing order probability) is providing a fast response to customer inquiries and questions (highest first-place ranking at 10.8%).

Other top-ranked salesperson actions during information collection that raise the chance of an order include: jointly developing a cost-effectiveness simulation, giving detailed explanations of service content/specifications/customization options, and providing quotes quickly.
Even at the early information-gathering stage, discussing money and providing estimates/quotes is highly effective and should not be deferred.

For customized products, salespeople commonly wait until after a formal hearing or discussion to issue quotes, due to concerns that requirements are not yet fixed or that an early estimate might later change significantly; however, this approach conflicts with buyer preferences at the information stage.

Additional valued actions in information collection include introducing case studies/success stories, providing objective comparisons versus competitors, explaining support systems, offering free trials/demos/prototypes, giving details on delivery/lead times, sharing unique insights, suggesting selection criteria, explaining industry trends/future outlook, and continuously providing seminars or useful information.

Salespeople often hesitate to discuss pricing early, fearing it will erode customer trust, but from the customer's viewpoint the complete absence of cost information itself constitutes a major risk because internal stakeholders cannot escalate or approve anything without a budget range.

Because the information-gathering stage frequently locks in the eventual decision direction, introducing money talk at that point should be framed as a decision-enabling action rather than a sales tactic; a rough estimate prefaced with “this is only an approximation” is typically welcomed by the buyer.

When a prospect says “today is just information collection,” the salesperson should intensify rather than relax effort, using the meeting to secure genuine understanding of estimates, customization options and cost-effectiveness, since 22.3 % of buyers (more than one in five) report that the information-gathering process exerts the strongest influence on their final vendor choice.

The “requirements-definition” stage begins once internal discussion of the gathered information produces articulated requirements covering budget, functionality, implementation timeline and operating model; salespeople should confirm they have entered this stage with targeted diagnostic questions.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior is the '5-stage process' and '6 types of stakeholders'.

Diagnostic questions can identify if a customer is in the 'Requirements Definition' (要件定義) stage of the purchasing process: (1) If necessary functions and conditions are currently being summarized internally (Yes → Requirements Definition); (2) If there is no written document specifying desired requirements (No → Requirements Definition); (3) If there is no internal agreement yet on budget sense or introduction timing (No → Requirements Definition); (4) If there are specific challenges in solidifying requirements, such as lack of time or uncertainty about how far to decide (then Requirements Definition).
A survey of 2,676 people found that the most common concern during the requirements definition stage is being too busy with other work to take time to think carefully about it.
The biggest bottleneck in the requirements definition stage is the customer's busyness; additional issues include insufficient knowledge/experience and lack of confidence in making judgments.
The requirements definition stage is particularly burdensome for customers within the overall purchasing process, as it requires concretizing 'what the company needs and what conditions must be met.'
Requirements definition is a heavy internal task involving discussion and consensus-building that often must be performed in the gaps between daily work.

Requirements definition (要件定義) is the process following information gathering, in which internal company conditions are reviewed until requirements such as budget, necessary functions, implementation period, and operational structure are put into words.

A survey of 2,676 respondents identified the single largest worry in the requirements-definition stage as lack of time: people are too busy with other work to think the requirements through carefully (18.4 % ranked this first).

Additional ranked concerns include insufficient knowledge or experience among internal members, uncertainty about how far definition must go to be considered complete, overly strong influence of particular individuals that biases the requirements, absence of a reliable discussion partner, fragmented internal opinions that stall debate, and reluctance to consult vendors for fear of being sold to.

Customers in this phase value sales behaviors that reduce their time burden: rapid response, proactive supply of information that can serve as decision material before consideration deepens, and efficient, customer-aligned communication that minimizes rework.

Although sales people commonly assume that offering free demos/trials or organizing information will help internal consensus-building, the dominant customer pain is busyness; therefore the most effective trust-building actions are those that directly alleviate that busyness rather than adding more activities.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior consists of a 5-stage process and 6 types of stakeholders; mastering this provides a significant advantage in sales activities.
In the 'requirements definition' (要件定義) stage, the speed and accuracy of communication are critically important for advancing the customer's evaluation.

Survey of 2,676 respondents identified top salesperson actions that raise order probability during requirements definition (ranked by 1st/2nd/3rd place selections, excluding 'other' and 'don't know'): fastest response to inquiries (16.7% 1st), providing judgment-material information before the customer's consideration deepens (12.7% 1st), and conducting efficient communication in a customer-friendly format (11.6% 1st).

Other valued actions include actively joining discussions until consideration deepens, proposing free demos/trials, organizing information and opinions to support internal consensus-building, and jointly holding strategy meetings to move the customer's internal organization.

Common but lower-ranked actions include waiting without approaching until consideration deepens or pushing for a decision by saying prolonged consideration is pointless; these are 'ありがちだが最上位ではない' (common yet not top-tier).

Effective 'communication design to reduce rework' (手戻りを減らすコミュニケーション設計) includes: sharing the meeting agenda (e.g., 'today's three points') in advance; sending confirmation items and next steps by email on the same day after the meeting; and proactively creating comparison tables or issue-organization materials that the customer can use for internal review.

Actions that make the customer's internal consideration work easier are especially powerful in the requirements-definition stage; many customers highly value communication productivity, so designing waste-free, customer-convenient communication flows is essential.

In sales during the requirements definition phase, an often-overlooked but effective action is proactively providing judgment materials rather than merely organizing and implementing exactly what the customer states after careful hearing.

Instead of stopping at 'we will organize what you said,' it is beneficial to take the initiative by suggesting additional viewpoints such as 'from a requirements perspective, you should also consider this aspect.'

Example: If a customer is comparing options solely on functional aspects, suggest adding post-implementation support structure as a judgment criterion, noting that this can help prevent future troubles.
This proactive presentation of decision axes is a key point to keep in mind when aiming for a higher level of sales performance.

The vendor comparison stage occurs after requirements definition is complete, when detailed estimates are requested from selected vendors and continues until all formal estimates from each company have been collected.

To check if a customer is in the vendor comparison stage, ask: 'Are you currently in the situation of hearing various talks about proposals and estimates from each company?' A yes answer indicates this stage.

Another confirmation question: 'In the comparison consideration, are there any points you are particularly concerned about or points where you are hesitating in your judgment?' Specific answers indicate the vendor comparison stage.
A further question: 'Have you already decided to some extent on the criteria for comparing the proposals?' If they are currently thinking it through, it indicates the vendor comparison stage.
The key to understanding purchasing (buying) behavior is the combination of a 5-stage process and 6 types of stakeholders/involved parties.

A practical diagnostic question to determine if a customer is in the 'vendor comparison' stage: 'Honestly, at this current stage, has there been a proposal that stands out as a head above the rest?' (If the answer is No, they are in the vendor comparison stage).

In a survey of 2,676 people, the biggest customer pain point during the vendor comparison stage is that the vendor's presented price is significantly higher than the budget. Presenting a high amount while ignoring the customer's situation and temperature/sense of urgency is the factor most likely to cause dissatisfaction.
Figure 2-9 insight: In the vendor comparison process, customers tend to struggle with 'misaligned vendors' (ズレたベンダー).

Survey findings on ranked customer worries (1st–3rd place) in the vendor comparison process (excluding 'other' and 'no particular worries'): top issues include vendor-proposed price far exceeding budget, slow responses to questions/requests, and proposal content being misaligned with the customer's requests and needs.
The customer's top 3 worries in vendor comparison all originate from 'ズレ' (gaps/misalignments), such as price misalignment, response-speed misalignment, and content/needs misalignment.

Additional ranked customer concerns in vendor comparison include: uncertainty about how flexibly the vendor will accommodate, low quality of presentations/proposal materials, inability to understand the vendor's proposal, low skill of the sales representative, high burden of responding to vendor requests, lack of felt enthusiasm from the salesperson, excessive contact from the salesperson, and lack of trust in the salesperson's personality.
In the vendor comparison stage of the customer journey, the leading sources of dissatisfaction are slow responses and mismatches between customer needs/requests and the vendor's proposals.
The top three concerns during vendor comparison can be summarized as price mismatches plus problems stemming from gaps in communication and expectation alignment.
This stage is particularly sensitive to competitor actions because customers enter a comparative evaluation mode, lining up multiple options side by side.
Relative evaluation dominates: a competitor's faster response makes one's own slowness stand out more sharply, and a competitor's better-fitting proposal makes one's own misalignment more obvious.
Customer sentiment can shift dramatically at this stage purely because of how one vendor stacks up against others rather than because of absolute performance.

An apparently gentlemanly sales posture of 'doing nothing' (e.g., remaining silent after submitting a proposal because the customer said they would review internally) is actually rated lowest by customers.
Even when a customer explicitly says 'we will consider this internally, please wait,' salespeople who refrain from follow-up contact receive a poor evaluation.

When customers are asked what they most appreciate from salespeople in the vendor-comparison stage, 'response' ranks highest; however, when response is split into speed versus substance, the richness and relevance of the content outranks raw speed.

Additional highly valued sales behaviors at this stage include delivering finely customized proposals, remaining flexible enough to revise estimates and proposals as many times as requested, and providing rough-order-of-magnitude estimates as quickly as possible.
In B2B purchasing, the vendor comparison stage is a critical part of the 5-stage buying process; sales success here depends on understanding buyer preferences rather than passive waiting.

Survey of 2,676 buyers (Figure 2-10) ranked desired salesperson actions during vendor comparison (1st–3rd place votes, excluding 'other' and 'don't know'): top items include providing substantial, content-rich answers to buyer questions; rapid responses to inquiries; finely customized proposals tailored to the buyer's company; unlimited flexible revisions of estimates/proposals; and very early rough-order-of-magnitude estimates.

Mid-tier valued actions: unique proposals that leverage the vendor's distinctive strengths; simultaneous presentation of multiple estimate patterns (e.g., good-better-best / 松竹梅); advice on actions the buyer themselves must take to raise ROI; concrete demos/trials showing usage; and comparison tables of features/price/support across vendors.
Lowest-ranked (explicitly called NG) is 'waiting sales'—doing nothing and waiting for the buyer to initiate contact. Pushing discounts solely to lower price also ranks poorly.

Core empirical finding: late estimate presentation is a clear disadvantage in the comparison stage. The winning tactic is to deliver a quick initial (even imperfect) estimate and then iterate through multiple refinement cycles.

Common salesperson misconception contradicted by data: many sellers believe an imperfect first quote damages trust. Buyers actually prefer speed of first response plus willingness to revise over a single 'perfect' proposal.
Practical sales methodology implied: compete on cycle time of the estimate–feedback–revision loop rather than on one-shot completeness or on passive availability.

The '発注決定' (order decision) stage of the customer purchasing process covers the period from when estimates/quotes from various vendors have been collected until a vendor is selected and a contract is signed.

Confirmation questions to determine if a customer is in the 発注決定 stage: '各社からの見積もりが揃って、あとは最終的なご判断をされる段階でしょうか？' (If Yes, then this stage); 'ご決定にあたって、さらにクリアにしておきたい懸念点やご不安はありますか？' (If none in particular, then this stage); '最終的なご決定までに、あとどのようなステップが残っていらっしゃいますか？' (If only internal discussion remains, then this stage); '契約条件や価格面で、確認しておかれたいポイントはございますか？' (If end-stage confirmation items arise, then this stage).

A survey of 2,676 people found that in the 発注決定 stage, the content of customer '悩み' (worries/concerns) is considerably more varied and scattered than in other stages; there is no single decisive worry that can be identified, and issues differ by company (各社各様).

Specific examples of dispersed customer concerns in the 発注決定 stage include: having a preferred vendor but being unable to fully dispel associated risks or concerns; wanting to increase an insufficient budget but lacking the authority to do so; difficulty negotiating contract terms or pricing; large differences of opinion within the internal review team; inability to clearly understand differences among vendor proposals; judgment criteria remaining undefined; and key persons being too busy.
The key to understanding purchasing (buying) behavior is the combination of a 5-stage process and 6 types of stakeholders.
In the 'order decision' (発注決定) stage of B2B purchasing, the core customer pain is 'cannot decide cleanly / cannot settle on one option' (すっきり決めきれない).

Survey of 2,676 people shows that worries in the final order-decision phase are multi-directional rather than converging on a single issue. Leading concerns include: preferred vendor still has unresolved risks/concerns; insufficient budget and no authority to increase it; difficulty negotiating contract terms or price; large opinion differences inside the evaluation team; vendor proposals look too similar; unclear judgment criteria; key decision-makers are too busy; a stakeholder whose opinion remains vague stalls progress; confusion about how to involve internal stakeholders or structure the review; and no proposal that actually meets the company's requirements.
The order-decision stage is therefore a phase in which 'the deciding factor does not converge to one,' causing concerns to spread across many dimensions until the very end.

A decision-maker (決裁者) should be understood not as 'the person who decides' but as 'the person who cannot decide and is still worrying.' This view is corroborated by the survey data showing persistent multi-issue indecision even at the final stage.

What customers most want from vendors at this stage is (1) speed of response and (2) flexibility of handling, followed by (3) proactive additional information (e.g., spontaneously offering concession points for final negotiation or supplying decision-support material without being asked).

In the 'order decision' (発注決定) process of B2B sales, the single most important action a salesperson can take to increase the chance of winning the deal is increasing the number of communication 'rallies'—specifically, responding quickly to the customer's inquiries and questions.

The second-most important action is spontaneously providing additional information that can serve as a decisive factor in the customer's internal decision-making, without waiting for the customer to request it.

A survey of 2,676 buyers asked them to rank (1st–3rd) the sales actions that would raise the probability of placing an order; the top-ranked items were fast responses and unsolicited decisive information, far ahead of discounting, waiting passively, or pushing for a decision.

Effective closing is not 'Is there anything else we can do for you?' (a reactive, order-taking question). Instead, the salesperson should proactively offer unrequested options: 'You haven't asked for this, but here is another alternative that might help.'

The underlying principle is 'offer even when not requested.' The salesperson must anticipate unspoken concerns (e.g., 'Will we actually be able to use this after we buy it?') and supply supporting information or alternatives on their own initiative.

Other lower-ranked but still useful actions include unlimited flexibility in re-quoting, revealing the vendor's concession points in advance, joining internal stakeholder meetings to help explain/persuade, and synthesizing scattered opinions into a single document.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior is the 5-stage process combined with 6 types of stakeholders.

In the order-decision (発注決定) phase, the differentiating factor is whether the salesperson can proactively present options and next-step proposals before being asked (e.g., post-implementation support plans or approaches that lower adoption hurdles).

Open-ended questions such as “Is there anything we can do?” are not inherently wrong, but salespeople who identify unspoken issues and take the risk of making concrete, forward-looking proposals tend to win more often at this stage.
Offering discounts is one possible tactic but ranked only in the middle of importance according to the survey responses.

Judgment criteria evolve across the purchasing process. When the 5-stage process is grouped into early / mid / late stages, cost-effectiveness (費用対効果) remains the highest-scoring factor at every stage; customers are not simply seeking the cheapest option but evaluating whether the value received matches the price paid.

Fit of product/service quality to the buyer’s own company is very high in the early and mid stages but declines in the late stage, because quality verification has usually already been completed by then.
Relative price versus competitors (“is it cheaper than alternatives?”) starts lower and steadily increases in importance as the process moves from early to late stages.

In B2B purchasing decisions, cost-effectiveness (費用対効果) is consistently the single most important factor across all consideration stages (early, mid, and late), based on a survey of 2,676 people. It scored 17.6% (early), 16.0% (mid), and 16.1% (late).

Buyer evaluation criteria shift by consideration stage. 'Whether the offering accurately captures our company's issues' is especially weighted in the early stage (10.8% early vs. 8.2% mid and 6.5% late), consistent with the issue-recognition phase of the buying journey.
The quality of the first contact is decisive: if the buyer feels 'this salesperson understands our issues,' it strongly influences whether they continue considering the vendor later.

Support/after-sales service and reliable/fast delivery rise in importance only in the late stage (support: 4.9% → 8.8%; delivery: 4.9% → 8.1%), once the buyer has essentially decided to purchase and is now focused on implementation risk and schedule.
Price being lower than competitors also gains weight later (8.9% early → 12.9% late), while 'quality/performance that fits our company' declines (15.8% early → 9.9% late).
Other late-stage concerns that increase include becoming a partner that helps create a better future for the company and reducing internal explanation burden.
Key insight: early-stage conversations should emphasize issue diagnosis and fit; late-stage conversations should emphasize implementation safety, support, and delivery certainty.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior is the '5-stage process' and the '6 types of stakeholders'.

In B2B sales, the person you interact with at the window is not the only customer; there are various stakeholders behind them with different roles, each evaluating proposals based on different criteria.
The same proposal can be perceived positively by some people in the organization and negatively by others, which is typical in corporate sales.
B2B sales often gets lost when salespeople don't understand the various people involved and what they are thinking.
Knowing who judges based on what criteria, based on data, is crucial for improving the accuracy of proposals.
