People tend to understand stakeholders in a customer's organization by their job titles like 'President', 'Director', or 'Manager', but this is insufficient.

The 6 types of stakeholders and their judgment criteria are: 1. Field users: Participate in discussions from the perspective of using the product/service. 2. Internal promoters: Propose and lead the introduction of the product/service. 3. Ordering personnel: Handle coordination and negotiations with vendors. 4. Budget supervisors: Manage expenditures and investments based on financial situation. 5. Influencers on decision-makers: In a position to advise decision-makers. 6. Final decision-makers: Oversee the business at the management level and make the final judgment.

Assessing a person's impact on organizational decision-making is difficult when relying only on job titles, because the same title (e.g., '部長'/manager) can correspond to very different actual functions—one person may control budgets while another drives on-site adoption.

People without high formal rank can still exert strong internal influence; therefore analysis should be organized by functional '役割' (roles) rather than titles in order to reveal structures that sales teams commonly overlook.

Six distinct stakeholder roles are identified; a single individual frequently occupies more than one role simultaneously (example: the same person acting as both '社内推進者' / internal champion and '発注担当者' / purchasing officer).
A survey of 2,676 respondents was constructed so that every one of the six roles is adequately sampled, allowing differences among roles to be compared.

Role ① 現場の利用者 (on-site / end users) are the people who will actually operate the product or service; they evaluate offerings primarily on 'usable?' and 'fits our daily work?' and typically want solutions that are '早く、安く' (fast and inexpensive).
Operational problems or improvement needs frequently originate with end users, so they often enter the buying process at an early stage and possess important, experience-based opinions.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior (購買行動) is the combination of a 5-stage process and 6 types of stakeholders (関係者).
Field users / end users (現場の利用者) show a somewhat stronger tendency than other stakeholders to prioritize low prices when evaluating solutions.
Field users typically evaluate from the perspective of 'burden on their own department' rather than 'budget rationality' or overall company investment return (ROI).
They focus more on 'whether it can be easily introduced for the department' than on 'what investment effect it has for the entire company'.
Reliable and fast delivery (確実に早く納品してくれるか) scores relatively high for field users (around 8.6–8.9% across all consideration stages) and is a key point from the user/operator standpoint.
In simple terms, field users have a strong 'fast and cheap' (早く、安く) orientation.
When salespeople engage field users, they should discuss not only company-wide investment return but also how easy/convenient the introduction will be for the users' department.

Survey data (n=474 field users from a 2,676-person study) shows cost-effectiveness as the top early-stage concern (16.7%), while 'price cheaper than competitors' rises from 9.5% (early) to 15.0% (late stage).
Product/service quality that fits the company itself starts high (14.6% early) but declines later (8.2% late); support/after-service importance increases in the late stage (to 12.0%).
Factors such as brand image, sales-rep attitude, internal explanation burden, and becoming a long-term partner score consistently low for field users (generally under 4%).
In B2B proposals, specifically communicate how quickly on-site users can start using the product or service to help them form a concrete usage image.
The core of an effective proposal is whether field users can visualize actually using the solution in their daily work.

Example approach for field users: First ask 'Which part of the current work takes the most effort?' then explain 'If that process is replaced by ○○, you will no longer need to do △△ work,' showing burden reduction in the users' own terminology.
Communicate delivery/implementation speed early and concretely, e.g., 'Shortest ○ weeks, standard ○ months as a guideline,' because vagueness on this point stops internal information flow.
If the 'time-to-use' picture remains unclear, field users tell internal promoters only that 'we still don't know if it can actually be used on site,' causing the entire evaluation to stall.
Give field users ready-to-use talking points so they can internally declare 'this can be used'; that endorsement is the key to turning them into allies.
Internal promoters (社内推進者) are the people who champion a product or service inside the buying organization and try to move the project forward.
They typically possess a clear problem consciousness ('I want to introduce this' / 'I want to solve this issue') and actively collect information and perform internal coordination.
Salespeople often interact most frequently with the internal promoter and therefore perceive them as the key internal driver, yet the promoter usually lacks final decision-making power.
When an internal promoter says 'This is a good proposal, let's proceed,' it means they want to advance internal consideration, not that they are ready to place an order.
The internal promoter is only the starting point; subsequent hurdles include supervisor approval, budget-department confirmation, and other internal gates.

Internal promoters place unusually high weight on whether the salesperson has correctly grasped the company's issues; they strongly evaluate 'Does this proposal genuinely address our specific problems?'
The key to understanding B2B purchasing behavior (購買行動) is the 5-stage process combined with the 6 types of stakeholders involved.

Internal promoters (社内推進者) who champion product adoption inside their company place particular emphasis on 'issue grasping' (課題把握), especially whether a vendor accurately understands the company's problems.

Survey of 432 internal promoters (from a larger 2,676-person study) shows that in the early consideration stage (issue recognition and information gathering), the top-valued factors are: being convinced of cost-effectiveness (16.9%), product/service quality and performance fitting the company (15.0%), and the vendor accurately capturing the company's issues (12.0%).

Cost-effectiveness remains consistently important across all stages of consideration: 16.9% early, 13.7% mid-stage (requirements definition to vendor comparison), and 16.0% late-stage (vendor comparison to order decision).
Price being cheaper than competitors grows in importance over time (5.6% early → 9.3% mid → 10.9% late), while product fit to the company declines (15.0% early → 11.1% mid → 10.0% late).

Internal promoters hold a strong problem-awareness mindset and are actively trying to drive internal change; therefore the feeling that 'this salesperson correctly understands our issues' resonates most strongly with them in the early stage.

An effective early-stage sales tactic is to first ask 'What is the issue your company currently most wants to solve?' and then respond with a structural hypothesis such as 'That may be because of this underlying structure...'.

Proposals that miss the mark on the company's actual issues cause the internal promoter to conclude 'this vendor does not understand our problems,' resulting in the vendor being dropped from the candidate list.

In the early stages of a purchase consideration, internal promoters (社内推進者) tend to be relatively indifferent to price. Conversations with them may give the impression that budget is not an issue, but once budget supervisors or final decision-makers become involved, price discussions ('how much is it?') can suddenly emerge. Salespeople must remain cautious about this shift.

Do not assume safety just because the internal promoter is unconcerned about cost. Proactively share a rough cost estimate early, for example by saying: 'Sharing a rough sense of the costs first might make internal discussions smoother—what do you think?' This preparation helps prevent later surprises.

The purchasing officer (発注担当者) handles practical vendor communications, including obtaining quotes, negotiating terms, and managing contract procedures. They often hold overlapping roles (e.g., also being an end-user or internal promoter), but the analysis here focuses on the purchasing-officer function specifically.

Purchasing officers have more dispersed judgment criteria than other stakeholder roles. They typically do not have one strongly dominant priority; instead they care about 'quite a few' different points, which makes their decision-making harder to pinpoint.
In the early consideration stage, purchasing officers show a comparatively stronger concern for 'performance satisfaction' than other roles.

Purchasing officers generally exhibit weaker personal judgment biases. Because they act as the overall window person and often consolidate opinions from multiple internal stakeholders, they tend to operate with a balancing mindset of wanting to select something that satisfies everyone.
The key to understanding purchasing (buying) behavior is the '5-stage process' and the '6 types of stakeholders'.
Figure 2-17 illustrates that orderers (purchasing managers) have dispersed judgment criteria/axes across different stages of the buying process.

A survey of 443 orderers asked what elements they prioritize from considering product introduction to actual order decision, broken into early stage (problem recognition and information gathering), mid stage (requirements definition to vendor comparison), and late stage (vendor comparison to order decision).

Early-stage priorities (n=443 orderers): product/service quality and performance fitting the company (16.3%), cost-effectiveness/convincing ROI (14.2%), price cheaper than competitors (12.9%), accurately grasping the company's issues (9.9%), rich track record providing security (9.0%), quality/performance superior to other vendors (10.2%).

Mid-stage priorities: cost-effectiveness (14.4%), product fit to company (13.8%), price cheaper than others (11.3%), quality superior to other vendors (10.4%), accurately grasping issues (8.8%), flexible customization (7.9%).

Late-stage priorities: price cheaper than others (14.4%), cost-effectiveness (14.2%), support and after-service being substantial (8.1%), quality/performance superior (7.9%), flexible customization (7.7%), fast and reliable delivery (7.2%), product fit to company (9.3%).

Support/after-service importance increases from early (2.9%) to late stage (8.1%); internal man-hours for introduction also rises (2.7% to 5.4%); salesperson response and internal explanation burden remain low throughout.
Brand image trustworthiness stays very low (2.0-3.2%); being a partner for a better future declines from 5.0% early to 3.6% late.
Data source: survey of 2,676 people.

When a salesperson asks an orderer 'What is the most important judgment criterion for your company?' they often receive no clear answer; instead ask 'Who in the company has particularly strong opinions?' or 'Whose judgment will have a large influence on the final decision?' to identify hidden true decision-makers.

There is often a person with actual intent/will behind the visible orderer who is invisible to sales; just because a quote request arrives does not mean an order is imminent—it may only be for internal budget planning reference.

Requested estimates or quotes in B2B sales may serve only as internal budget planning (information gathering) rather than indicating active vendor selection; they can also be for competitive comparison (相見積もり).

To accurately gauge the buyer's current position in the purchasing process and reduce the risk of misjudgment, salespeople should casually confirm the purpose of an estimate request with a question such as: “今回のお見積もりは、社内のご予算計画用（＝情報収集）でしょうか、それとも具体的なベンダー選定の段階（＝ベンダー比較）でしょうか？”

予算の監督者 (budget supervisors) are stakeholders from finance, management departments, or corporate planning who check the validity of expenditures and investments; they concentrate their judgment on 費用対効果 (cost-effectiveness) while also seeking initial reassurance or peace of mind.

Survey of 432 budget supervisors (from a larger 2,676-person study) shows their top priorities shift across buying stages: early (課題認識・情報収集) they most value being convinced of cost-effectiveness (19.0%), fit of product/service to their company (13.2%), and accurate understanding of their challenges (11.1%); mid-stage (要件定義～ベンダー比較) cost-effectiveness remains high (16.2%) along with company-specific fit (14.6%); late-stage (ベンダー比較～発注決定) cost-effectiveness (16.4%) and relative price (14.1%) dominate, with faster delivery also rising (10.0%).

Budget supervisors consistently prioritize cost-effectiveness across all stages more than other factors such as brand image, sales-rep rapport, or customization flexibility; they also value proven track record and quality/performance fit especially in earlier phases, reflecting a need for both economic justification and reduced risk.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior is the '5-stage process' and the '6 types of stakeholders'.

Budget supervisors (予算の監督者) frequently exert influence in situations such as 'the budget is not increasing' or 'there is no precedent, so we should be cautious.' They are usually difficult to meet directly and are often viewed by salespeople as making negotiations harder. Because they are responsible for protecting company funds, they tend to adopt a conservative stance.
Compared with other roles, budget supervisors' decision criteria concentrate heavily on cost-effectiveness (費用対効果). This follows naturally from their function.

Budget supervisors place a higher premium on proven results (実績) than other stakeholders. Being distant from day-to-day operations, they constantly feel the anxiety of 'I don't really understand this, but is it truly safe?'

They remain continually aware of the risk that an approved investment might fail. Even when front-line staff insist a product is excellent, the supervisor still worries 'is it really all right?' Consequently, objective evidence—adoption records at other companies and cases from similar industries—serves as crucial reassurance.

What matters most to the budget supervisor is material that lets them judge whether the investment is appropriate. Clearly demonstrating return on investment or presenting results from past similar projects makes it easier for them to conclude there are grounds for approval.

When dealing with budget supervisors, functional claims such as 'our product is superior in this respect' are less effective than quantified evidence of results and cost-effectiveness: e.g., 'At similarly sized Company A, XX effect appeared within X months after introduction' or 'payback period is estimated at X months.'

Do not treat the budget supervisor as an obstacle ('wall'). The decisive question is whether you can turn them into an ally who will help the proposal pass. Asking 'When you explain this investment internally, what materials would make the discussion easier?' allows you to prepare in advance the information they need for internal approval.

Influencers on the decision-maker (決裁者への影響者) are people who offer opinions or advice to the final approver. In the early stage they place particular weight on 'degree of match with our own company' (自社とのマッチ度).

The role of 'influencer on the decision maker' (決裁者への影響者) is characterized as a presence that is difficult to surface publicly, yet frequently exerts substantial influence on actual decision-making processes in B2B purchasing.

Typical individuals filling this influencer role include a trusted right-hand person of the executive team, the head of the corporate planning department, or a long-term external consultant with established relationships.
This influencer is the person the final decision-maker consults by asking questions such as 'What does that person say?' before proceeding.

Survey of 460 'influencers on decision makers' (from a total of 2,676 respondents) on factors most emphasized across buying stages: early (issue recognition/information gathering), mid (requirements definition to vendor comparison), and late (vendor comparison to order decision).

In the early consideration stage, the highest priority for these influencers is whether product/service quality and performance match the company's needs (20.7%), followed by whether cost-effectiveness is convincing (18.7%) and whether the vendor accurately captures the company's issues (12.4%).

Cost-effectiveness remains consistently important across all stages at approximately 18.5–18.7%, while the importance of quality/performance matching the company drops from 20.7% early to 12.2% in mid and late stages.
Price competitiveness (cheaper than other vendors) increases modestly from 7.6% in early stage to 11.1% in late stage; support/after-sales service also rises from 4.1% early to 9.3% late.
Even when the final decision-maker shows a positive reaction, a single comment from the influencer such as 'it might not fit us' can alter the entire direction of the deal.
Identifying the existence of these influencers is inherently difficult due to their low visibility, yet they remain critical to monitor because of their outsized impact on outcomes.
The key to understanding purchasing behavior (buying actions) is the combination of a 5-stage process and 6 types of stakeholders/involved parties.
Always maintain the question: 'In this deal's decision-making, is there any person with influence who does not appear on the surface?'

The role of 'influencer to the decision-maker' is characterized by strongly focusing on performance/fit alignment in the early consideration stage. They prioritize 'will this function/work given our company's situation?' over general product quality or market reputation.

Whether an influencer to the decision-maker internally states 'I think this fits us' significantly determines the direction of the deal. Salespeople must therefore be aware of and address this judgment criterion.

Effective tactics include proposing solutions tailored to the customer's industry characteristics and current organizational situation, and offering customized value propositions such as 'For your company, this particular usage would be most effective.'

Influencers to the decision-maker often do not appear in customer conversations, so salespeople must proactively identify their existence by asking questions without hesitation, such as 'Is there anyone else who might influence the final judgment in this consideration?' or 'Is there someone whose opinion the president would check when making a decision?'

The final decision-maker typically refers to executives or those in a position to render the ultimate judgment. They are generally regarded as the most important party, and there exist decisions that only they can make.

A core message is that 'authority to decide' must be distinguished from 'influence on the decision.' Even a final decision-maker with formal authority frequently bases their judgment on opinions and information from other roles rather than deciding in isolation.
Survey results (from Chapter 1) show that the proportion of cases in which the final decision-maker is reported to have substantial influence is only 16.7%.
The final decision-maker is essentially the person who 'puts the stamp last,' but their actual judgment is heavily swayed by information and opinions rising from other internal stakeholders.

Final decision-makers (最終決裁者) prioritize cost-effectiveness (費用対効果に納得できるか) over low price throughout the B2B consideration process, based on a survey of 435 such approvers (from a larger 2,676-person study).

Survey percentages for 'whether cost-effectiveness is convincing': 20.5% in early stage (課題認識・情報収集), 18.9% in mid stage (要件定義～ベンダー比較), and 17.5% in late stage (ベンダー比較～発注決定). This remains the top factor across all stages.

In contrast, 'whether the price is cheaper than other companies' scores only 7.4% (early), 7.4% (mid), and 11.5% (late), showing final approvers have weaker attachment to absolute low price compared to other stakeholders.

Other notable early-stage priorities include product/service quality and performance matching the company (14.9%) and accurately grasping the company's challenges (11.5%). Quality superior to other vendors scores 8.7% early, 10.1% mid.

Final decision-makers' judgment criteria resemble those of budget supervisors: they evaluate based on 'whether the investment delivers commensurate value' rather than cheapest option, because they must later justify that 'this investment was correct.'

Salespeople who clearly demonstrate 'reasons why the investment is worthwhile' earn more trust. Recommended approaches include offering materials that organize expected company-specific outcomes or providing quantified post-implementation effects with supporting numbers.

Example sales phrasing: 'Shall I prepare materials organizing what results can be expected for your company from this investment?' or 'I will bring a numerical summary of the anticipated XX effects after introduction.'
The key to understanding purchasing (buying) behavior in B2B sales is the combination of a '5-stage process' and '6 types of stakeholders' (関係者).

When dealing with the final decision-maker (最終決裁者), the most effective approach is to clearly provide 'reasons that make the investment worthwhile' rather than competing primarily on discounts or price reductions. Focusing effort on explaining return on investment (投資対効果) builds greater trust with the final approver.
A single individual can simultaneously hold multiple roles among the 6 types of stakeholders (for example, being both a field/end user and an internal champion/promoter).
To identify which of the 6 stakeholder roles the person currently speaking with you occupies, use targeted diagnostic questions rather than assuming their position.

Direct questions to confirm overall role and decision structure: 'In this current evaluation, what position/role does Mr./Ms. XX play?' and 'Including Mr./Ms. XX, what does the review/consideration team structure look like this time?'

Questions to determine if the person is (or represents) a field/end user: 'After introduction, will the members of Mr./Ms. XX's team be the ones using it on a daily basis?' and 'When you imagine the actual scenes of use in the field, are there any points of concern?'

Questions to determine if the person is an internal champion/promoter (社内推進者): 'Did Mr./Ms. XX originate/propose this evaluation and are you the one driving it internally?' and 'Are the explanations and coordination with other internal stakeholders mainly being handled by Mr./Ms. XX?'
Once you confirm the counterpart's role(s), the complex 'maze' of the internal buying process becomes much easier to navigate because that person can become a powerful internal guide and ally.

In B2B sales conversations, systematically probe the counterpart's role using targeted questions to map organizational decision-making structure, covering purchaser, budget supervisor, influencer, final decision-maker, and multi-role possibilities.

To identify if the person is the ordering/purchasing contact (発注担当者): Ask 'お見積もりの取得や契約手続きなど、実務的なやり取りは○○さんが窓口になられますか？' (Will you serve as the contact for practical matters such as obtaining quotes and contract procedures?) and '今回のお見積もりは、社内のご予算計画用でしょうか、それとも具体的なベンダー選定の段階でのものでしょうか？' (Is this quote for internal budget planning or for the actual vendor selection stage?).

To identify if the person is the budget supervisor (予算の監督者): Ask '御社においてご予算の管理や財務的観点の検討は、○○さんのご担当でいらっしゃいますか？' (Are you responsible for budget management and financial considerations at your company?) and 'こういったケースでいつも金額の妥当性を最終的にチェックされるのは、○○さんでしょうか？' (In cases like this, are you the one who ultimately checks the validity of the amount?).

To identify if the person is an influencer on the decision-maker (決裁者への影響者): Ask '最終的にご判断をされる方とのディスカッションを定期的にされていらっしゃるような感じでしょうか？' (Do you regularly hold discussions with the person who makes the final judgment?) and 'いつもこういった局面で、決裁者の方から相談が○○さんのもとに来られるのですか？' (Does the decision-maker usually come to you for consultation in these situations?).

To identify if the person is the final decision-maker (最終決裁者): Ask '○○さんが『これで行こう』とお決めになったあと、社内でさらなる検討プロセスはあるのでしょうか？' (After you decide 'let's go with this,' is there a further internal review process?) and '○○さんの下された結論が、社内の議論でさらに変わる可能性はございますか？' (Is there a possibility that the conclusion you reached will still change through internal discussions?).

To explore whether one person holds multiple roles: Ask '○○さんは、ご自身でもお使いになりつつ、社内のご推進もされている、という感じでしょうか？' (Do you both use it yourself and also drive it internally?) and '今回は○○さんが実務の窓口も、社内の取りまとめもされていらっしゃるのですか？　かなりご負担が大きいのではないでしょうか' (Are you handling both the practical contact point and internal coordination this time? That must be quite a burden.).
After securing the current contact as an ally, shift to questions that uncover the existence, roles, and opinions of still-unmet stakeholders in order to plan subsequent approaches.
The key to understanding purchasing (buying) behavior is the combination of a '5-stage process' and '6 types of stakeholders'.

Sales professionals must systematically uncover stakeholders they have not yet met by asking targeted questions across six categories: overall stakeholder mapping, approval/decision routes, hidden influencers, opinions and sentiment of unmet parties, creating contact opportunities, and proactively addressing objections.
To grasp the overall picture of stakeholders, ask: 'Who else is involved in this consideration?' and 'Has an internal team or meeting been formed for this evaluation?'

To map the approval (決裁) route, ask: 'Who will make the final decision?', 'Will this be escalated from you, and if so to whom will you explain it?', and 'How many approval stages are typically required in the ringi (稟議) process?'

To identify hidden influencers, ask: 'Is there anyone whose opinion the final decision-maker consults?' and 'Is there anyone the president or management typically consults when judging investments of this type?'

To probe the opinions and 'temperature' (sentiment) of unmet stakeholders, ask about others' reactions so far, whether anyone holds cautious views, what the budget owner thinks, and what the actual end-users feel about the proposed introduction.

To create contact with unmet stakeholders, offer to include field users in the next meeting, provide a direct ROI explanation to the budget manager, prepare internal presentation materials that the current contact can easily use, or supply a one-page summary if a direct meeting is difficult.

To anticipate and neutralize opposing opinions or concerns, ask about past similar implementations and the internal reactions they generated, then proactively offer to prepare explanation materials the contact can use when presenting to higher-ups.
This chapter explained concepts along two axes: the 5-stage purchasing process (5段階の購買プロセス) and the 6 types of stakeholders/involved parties (6種類の関係者).

The three 'torches' (松明) for escaping the '4 mazes' (4つの迷路) introduced in Chapter 1 are: (1) identifying which stage of the customer's purchasing process you are currently in, (2) understanding what role the person you are currently meeting plays, and (3) determining how to proceed going forward so that the customer decides to place an order with your company.

By this point in the book, the reader has deepened their understanding of points (1) and (2); the subsequent content will provide detailed, specific approaches for point (3) applied to each of the four mazes.

Part I of the book covers preparatory understanding of the customer's 5-stage purchasing process and 6 types of stakeholders, which illuminates the hidden structural dynamics occurring behind corporate (B2B) sales activities, likened to lighting a torch in a dark maze.

Part II focuses on four common 'mazes' (obstacles) frequently encountered in corporate sales, providing case-specific countermeasures to escape them and convert to orders; these are described as 'defensive winning patterns' (守りの勝ちパターン).

The four mazes in corporate sales are: ① Unable to meet the key person (キーパーソンに会えない), ② Unable to make contact (連絡がつながらない), ③ Consideration/evaluation process does not advance (検討が進まない), and ④ Budget does not increase (予算が増えない).

On the surface, these four mazes all appear as a single problem of 'stagnation in proposal activities,' but when structurally decomposed, each maze has distinct root causes and therefore requires different countermeasures.

Effective escape from sales mazes requires correctly diagnosing 'which maze you are currently in and what is causing the blockage,' rather than blindly repeating actions such as making another phone call or persisting longer.
The overall strategy emphasized is to avoid falling into mazes in the first place and instead build winning patterns through defensive (守り) strategies in corporate sales.

When a contact person promises to introduce their superior (a presumed key person) but schedule coordination stalls for weeks despite follow-ups, the delay often signals an unidentified true decision-maker rather than simple indecision or busyness.

A useful diagnostic question to uncover hidden stakeholders is: 'By the way, is this consideration something that can be completed entirely within your department?' This casually probes whether other departments or individuals hold veto power or strong opinions.

In the case study, the HR section chief (A-san) was attempting to involve their own boss (HR director), but progress halted because the corporate planning department's B-bucho held strong personal views on the topic; the HR director could not easily proceed without B-bucho's approval.

The apparent 'key person' being introduced by a gatekeeper is not always the real influencer; true key persons frequently exist outside the contact's immediate department and must be identified through targeted questioning.

Faced with stalled introductions, the binary choice of 'urge the contact' (increasing their burden) versus 'wait passively' (risking the deal disappearing) is usually incorrect; the better approach is to diagnose the underlying organizational dynamics causing the delay.

In B2B sales, a deal can stall indefinitely at the 'internal coordination' (社内調整中) stage not from lack of interest but because the internal contact (A-san) faces a high psychological barrier to approaching a key person (B-bucho) in a different department.

A practical diagnostic question to unblock access: ask the contact 'What theme is the key person particularly concerned about right now?' In the case study this revealed 'resolving operational personalization / knowledge silos' (業務の属人化解消).

Instead of chasing or waiting, create a short, targeted case-study report on the key person's known pain point and give it to the contact with the request 'Please pass this to someone close to the key person if you think it will interest them.'

The indirect route worked: the contact forwarded the report to a subordinate of the key person, the subordinate mentioned it, and the key person himself requested a meeting. A deal frozen for three weeks moved in three days.
Core principle: merely prompting or waiting would have killed the opportunity; the breakthrough came from diagnosing the true structural cause of the stall rather than treating the symptom.

This chapter structurally decomposes the 'cannot meet the key person' maze into nine distinct pitfalls and supplies an overall diagnostic map so the seller can identify exactly which blockage is active at any moment.

When salespeople feel they cannot meet the key person, they often repeat the same approaches such as calling again or following up more carefully, but repeating identical tactics does not change the situation.
The reason the situation does not improve is that the salesperson cannot see exactly where they are stuck.
Being inside a maze causes confusion because the exit is not visible, but an overview of the whole allows identification of dead ends and viable shortcuts.
The 'Pitfall Map' (落とし穴のマップ) presented in the chapter functions as a guide map that provides an overview of the entire situation in stalled B2B sales processes.
Falling into a pitfall makes escape difficult, whereas proceeding without falling into one enables reaching the exit.
Even when proposal activities stall due to inability to meet the key person, identifying the current specific situation enables planning of appropriate countermeasures.
Acting without first identifying the current state leads to repeatedly applying misguided or ineffective tactics.

In the chapter's opening episode, recognizing that 'Mr. A feels psychological burden in taking the topic to a key person in another department' enabled the precise action of delivering information around Director B in a manner that reduced Mr. A's burden.
The ability to accurately identify the current situation serves as a key weapon for navigating the maze of corporate (B2B) sales.

The 'Unable to Meet the Key Person' maze is a strategic framework (Chapter 3, Defensive Strategy II) for diagnosing and navigating barriers in sales or business negotiations when access to the decision-maker is blocked.

The overall map of this maze (Figure 3-1) begins with a single diagnostic question: 'Does the person in front of you know who the key person is?' This question then branches into three primary paths that further subdivide into a total of nine pitfalls.

The three main branches of the maze are: (1) the contact knows the key person but does not attempt to make an introduction, (2) the contact knows and attempted an introduction but the key person themselves refused the appointment, and (3) the contact does not know who the key person is.
There are exactly nine pitfalls (traps) in the maze that practitioners must avoid falling into when trying to reach the key person.
Identifying 'who the key person is' is itself a non-trivial question and not as simple as it first appears; earlier chapters establish that the key person equals the final decision-maker.

Nine specific reasons or pitfalls that prevent connection to the key person include: the method for confirming the identity of the key person is not visible or clear to the contact; the person in front cannot understand the value of the proposal; multiple candidate individuals exist as possible connection targets, causing hesitation; the contact cannot spare the time required to take connecting actions; the contact wants to avoid communications that would skip or bypass them; the contact does not want to invest time in meeting coordination or preparation; the contact fears receiving a negative evaluation as a result of making the introduction; the key person themselves cannot understand the value of the proposal; and the contact prefers to concentrate on other issues or priorities.
In B2B sales, the 'key person' (キーパーソン) is not always the formal decision-maker (決裁者). It can instead be an internal promoter/advocate or an influencer who effectively sways the decision-maker.

The identity of the key person can shift depending on the stage of the customer's purchasing process. During the issue-recognition stage, field-level users may be the key persons; during vendor comparison, budget supervisors or overseers may become the key persons.

A primary sales pitfall is failing to identify who the key person actually is. Salespeople often assume the current contact knows, but the contact frequently does not—especially in push-generated opportunities or when the contact has only been tasked with gathering information.

In Japanese companies it is common for there to be no internal consensus on who holds real influence. Formal authority (the person with official sign-off power) and actual decision-making influence frequently reside in different people.
Salespeople should deliberately distinguish the language '最終的に' (ultimately / finally) from '実質的に' (substantially / in practice) when discussing who will decide.

Diagnostic question to test whether you have fallen into the 'unknown key-person' pitfall: '今回のご検討にあたって、会社としてのご判断に影響力をお持ちの方は、どなたになりますか？' (Regarding this evaluation, who in the company has influence over the organization's decision?). If you have no idea, you are in the pitfall.
Section 3.3 of the source material is titled '落とし穴①キーパーソンを知らない' (Pitfall ①: Not knowing the key person).

In B2B sales, instead of leaving stakeholder identification entirely to the customer, the salesperson must bring a structured organizational framework and collaboratively think through the buying process together with the customer.

Apply the six types of stakeholders (from the prior chapter) by asking diagnostic questions such as 'Is there someone internally promoting this theme?' and 'Who is responsible for budget management?' to jointly surface influential people.

The essential practice is to verbalize the 'chain of influence' with the customer during the meeting: map how the evaluation process should proceed, which influencers must be reached, and the sequence in which people should be involved.

A typical influence-chain map includes roles such as final decision-maker (e.g., Business Division Head), influencer to the decision-maker (Development Department Manager), budget supervisor (Purchasing Department Manager), order placer (Purchasing Section Chief), field users (Production Technology Room Head), and internal champion/promoter (Product Development Room Chief, often the key person).

Distinguish NG routes (dead-end paths that fail to reach real influence) from OK routes (paths that respect field-level priorities, leverage trusted subordinates, and systematically introduce the salesperson to the right development-department contacts).

A frequent failure pattern is ending the meeting after the customer says 'I'll check internally who should join next time'; because identifying key persons feels bothersome, the process simply stalls.

Therefore the influence-chain mapping must be completed live in the sales conversation rather than postponed; for example, immediately co-create the next-step sequence starting from the current contact's position in the organization.

To identify key persons (キーパーソン) inside a company, collaboratively ask questions such as “Who in the company is involved in this?” and “What are that person’s thoughts on this matter?” so that influential stakeholders can be uncovered together.
When the contact does not know the key person, simply taking the confirmation steps together is sufficient; subsequent communication then becomes relatively straightforward.

Two additional, more difficult patterns must be distinguished: (1) the contact knows the key person exists but will not attempt to connect you, and (2) the contact tried to connect you but the key person personally refused. Separating these situations is the key to escaping the “maze.”

Pitfall ② occurs when the person sitting in front of you cannot understand the value of the proposal. A diagnostic check question is: “If you were to explain this proposal to others inside your company, how would you convey it?” Hesitation or inability to answer indicates the value has not been internalized.
Asking someone to introduce you implicitly signals “I believe this proposal has value.” Therefore a person who has not yet accepted the value will naturally refuse to make the introduction.

It is essential to keep in mind the specific role the person in front of you is playing. In the early stages of consideration, an internal champion (社内推進者) primarily cares whether the problem is being correctly understood, while the person who will actually place the order focuses on different criteria.

Decision-makers and executives tend to prioritize whether a solution's capabilities match their needs, while frontline users prioritize whether daily operations will change immediately; the same 'value' message resonates at completely different points depending on the counterpart's role.

The focus of the message to convey shifts by purchasing-process stage: in the information-gathering stage the upstream argument ('why we must address this issue') is critical; in the vendor-comparison stage the differentiation argument ('why us rather than others') becomes critical.
From the customer's viewpoint, introducing a salesperson to an internal key person requires courage because a poor performance by that salesperson can damage the introducer's own internal evaluation.

A 2022 survey of 10 000 customers showed that not only proposal content but also the salesperson's personal impression and perceived expertise determine whether an introduction occurs; customers must feel 'this salesperson is safe to introduce internally' for the introduction to happen.

Even when the value of a proposal is understood, connecting actions may still fail because they constitute extra work (writing internal chat messages, checking a boss's calendar, preparing briefing materials) that busy staff treat as low-priority non-core tasks.

Typical sequence: a contact person agrees 'I'll talk to the manager next week,' yet the following week reports that other work piled up and the conversation never occurred; the proposal itself is not rejected, only deprioritized.
Diagnostic check question: 'When you discuss this internally, will any extra tasks land on your plate?' If the answer is yes and those tasks look heavy, the 'no time to connect' pitfall is active.
After a business meeting (商談), the most effective follow-up is to send a memo as soon as possible that the customer can forward internally within their company as-is.
The follow-up memo should concisely include: a summary of the conversation, next steps, and specific points on which a decision is requested.
Two critical success factors for the memo: (1) send organized content quickly, and (2) format it so that it can withstand being forwarded internally (社内転送に耐える体裁).
Timing is essential because the customer's memory fades and their motivation to 'connect' cools with each passing day; ideally send the same day, at latest the next day.

Example email opening prioritizes speed and politeness: thank the recipient for the call, note that the memo is being sent quickly for reference (with apology for any typos or clumsy phrasing), then use clear section headers.

Structure the memo with labeled sections such as 【本日お伺いしたことの要点】 (key points heard today) that list the client's stated challenges (e.g., young members take time to ramp up; guidance from superiors is overly personalized and lacks reproducibility).

Further client-issue details captured in the example: post-ride-along feedback tends to be 'sensory/gut-feel'; role-plays fail to produce on-the-job behavior change; yet members have high potential and managers have a strong desire to develop them properly.

Company-side insight section 【当社からお話ししたポイント】: the root cause of unsuccessful development is not 'the content of what they are having people do' but that 'what to observe and how to give feedback' has never been verbalized.
Additional discussion point in the example: how far to decompose the thinking and judgment process of high-performing salespeople.
The book explicitly notes that conversation summary and next-step information should also be included in the memo.
In designing sales training or team development programs, the critical dividing line is deciding the appropriate level of information sharing with members.
A customer's busyness can cause a project's priority to drop, and this is closely tied to the current stage of their purchasing process.
If the customer is still in the problem-recognition stage, they often feel it is not yet time for serious action, which naturally lowers priority.

When the process advances to the vendor-comparison stage, urgency increases because the customer feels they must soon seek approval from superiors; this raises the required quality of materials and can stall work at the contact-person level.
Pitfall ④ occurs when the contact person fears being bypassed and left out of the conversation once a key person (キーパーソン) is introduced.
A typical signal of this fear is a sudden change in expression (expression clouds) followed by a request such as 'Please let me handle it at this stage' when a meeting with a manager is suggested.

Sales professionals should watch for complex emotional reactions when asking whether the contact person and the key person have already been communicating on the matter, as this often indicates the contact person wants to remain the central conduit.

When a contact refuses to introduce or involve a key person (キーパーソン), it is typically not a denial of the proposal or an attempt to hide the manager's existence. Instead, it stems from the psychology of disliking situations where discussions progress without their knowledge: 「自分の知らないところで話が進んでしまうのが嫌だ」.

If communication between the key person and the current contact is not already established, the current contact cannot predict how events will unfold after the introduction, increasing their resistance.

Anxieties differ by role: An internal promoter (社内推進者) fears losing initiative or control (主導権を失いたくない). A procurement or ordering officer (発注担当者) dislikes decisions being made over their head (頭越しにいろいろと決まるのは困る).

The essential principle is to maximally respect the position of the person in front of you and demonstrate through concrete actions that you will never engage in communications that bypass them: 「あなたを飛ばしたやり取りは絶対にしません」.

Effective tactic for an internal promoter: Involve them as a partner in strategy by asking, 「○○様のご意見を社内にもきちんと理解してもらうために、どう進めるのがよろしいでしょうか」 (How should we proceed so that your opinion is properly understood internally?).

Effective tactic for a procurement officer: Promise information sharing and let them choose the method of involvement, e.g., 「必ず情報共有します。メールのCC の入れ方はどのようにするのがよいですか」 (I will definitely share information. How should I include CC in emails?).
Iron rule (鉄則): When unsure whose side to take, always stand with the person immediately in front of you first.
The 'minus' of being bypassed that the current contact feels can be categorized into three main patterns.

Pattern 1: Simply wanting to avoid unknown developments after connecting to the key person. Countermeasure is straightforward: Explicitly state 「ご安心ください。必ず情報共有します」 (Please rest assured. I will definitely share information) and let the contact choose how they are included (e.g., email addressing and wording patterns) to reduce resistance by explicitly involving them.
Pattern 2: Anxiety that their own opinions may conflict with those of the key person (text cuts off, but this is identified as a distinct source of resistance).

When a key person is facing a different direction, aligning with that instead of the person in front of you is not a pleasant experience for the current contact. Add a preface such as 'I want to properly understand your thoughts, Mr./Ms. XX...' before digging deeper. First understand the thoughts of the person in front of you and stand on the same side, then consider together how you can help from an external position regarding differences of opinion with the key person.

Pattern 3: The person in front wants to retain initiative. This is similar to disliking unknown developments, but here the psychology of wanting to hold the initiative is stronger rather than mere lack of information. Thoroughly hear what the contact is thinking, carefully scoop up their intentions and priorities, then jointly create a scenario in which the person in front takes the lead. This builds a route to reach the key person.
Anxiety about being bypassed in communications has multiple types, and it is important to design the involvement method according to each type.

Pitfall ⑤: Not wanting to receive a negative evaluation by making the connection. Check question: What themes or issues is the key person particularly interested in right now? (This is a pitfall if that content differs from the current proposal.) This is the anxiety that connecting might lower one's internal evaluation. If you make the key person spend time on a matter different from their interests, they will naturally feel displeased, and the connecting person will suffer as a result.

Requesting a key person (decision-maker) to attend a meeting for the salesperson's convenience can lower the evaluation of the connecting staff member. The key person may interpret it as the field team being unable to make independent judgments, weakening the connector's internal standing.

Example of a poorly received request: A salesperson saying 'We'll bring our superior, so please bring yours too' leads the key person to think 'Can't they handle this at the operational level?' Similarly, framing it as a 'milestone greeting' often elicits 'I have no time for greetings,' creating unnecessary friction for the connector.

The justification for involving a key person must be tied to the key person's own interests and concerns, not the salesperson's agenda. Offering useful information on a topic the key person is already researching makes them more likely to agree to a meeting ('If there's information not in the materials, I'll meet').

The most powerful trigger for a key person to attend is a request from someone they trust. A key person's core concern is ensuring their trusted 'right-hand' members can work comfortably and effectively. Information or a request rising from a close, trusted subordinate (e.g., 'There's this relevant case/example') makes the key person far more willing to act.

When a trusted member's work would be hindered, the key person is highly motivated to intervene immediately ('I'll go right now'). This contrasts with weaker reasons like ceremonial greetings or matching the other party's hierarchy.

Key person's psychology when asked to join (from Figure 3-3): Passive/negative reactions include viewing it as an unnecessary escalation ('Handle it in the field') or a time-waster. Active/positive reactions occur when it aligns with current information-gathering needs, trusted recommendations, or solutions to company issues ('Let's hear it first').

The 'bead-stringing' (数珠つなぎ) concept is a key strategy: when you cannot connect directly to a key person, first ally with an influential person who is closer/in front, then use that connection to reach the target.

Pitfall ⑥: Multiple candidate people exist to connect with, and the customer is confused about whom to connect to. This differs from pitfall ① (no idea who to connect to at all); here, candidates are known but the customer cannot decide the sequence or procedure.

Example of pitfall ⑥: When asked who to connect with, the contact lists several people (e.g., business unit director who should be informed, managing director of admin HQ who has budget authority, technical department director with strong opinions) and cannot decide who to speak to first, causing paralysis.

Effective tactic for multiple candidates: Actually simulate each possible path. Lay out Scenario A (approach via business unit director, leading to this development...), Scenario B (approach via admin HQ, leading to that development...), etc., on the table so the customer who knows internal circumstances can choose the better route.

It is important to consider the stage of the purchasing process when deciding contact order: In the requirements definition stage, prioritize meeting field users and internal promoters. In the vendor comparison stage, urgently approach the budget supervisor and final decision-maker.
Design 'which stage, which role of person, in which order to contact' as a structured plan.
When the person in front of you has tried to connect you to the key person but the key person themselves is refusing (and this fact is not shared with the salesperson), a 're-challenge' is necessary.

The key person has already reacted with comments like 'Handle it at the field level' or 'I'm busy now, do it later,' so you must prepare an excuse or conditions to meet again and have the person in front of you re-challenge.

Re-challenge tactics include: changing 'who says it' inside the company by having a different person put in a good word, or preparing materials that will resonate with the key person so the person in front can bring them internally (sometimes supporting the creation of internal materials yourself).
Another re-challenge tactic is creating an excuse, such as 'I consulted others but I still want to ask you (the key person),' to make it easier for the person in front to take action.

Pitfall ⑦: The key person cannot understand the value of the proposal. Check question: What kind of materials are needed to make a busy key person think 'I should look at this'? (This pitfall applies if existing materials don't meet this.)
When unable to meet a key person (キーパーソン) directly, value must be conveyed indirectly through materials, assuming no face-to-face meeting.

Common scenario: An internal contact presents a proposal to the key person who dismisses it as 'not relevant to us'; the contact then tells the salesperson that upper management shows little interest. Salespeople often wrongly blame poor proposal quality, when the real issue is that the value was not delivered in a form that resonates with the key person.

The key person's role determines what message resonates: Final decision-makers respond to managerial impact—how the investment connects to the company's future. Budget supervisors respond to cost-effectiveness and adoption records from similarly sized companies. Influencers on the decision-maker want concrete evidence that the offering fits their specific company.

The stage of the buying process also shifts emphasis: At the issue-recognition stage, provide materials that help the internal team organize and clarify problems. At the vendor-comparison stage, clearly demonstrate why the company should be chosen over alternatives.
Do not rely on a single message; design materials to cover multiple angles so different stakeholders can find relevant value.

Survey of 10,303 customers on what is needed to feel comfortable meeting a salesperson: The top two factors are 'match with our company's issues' and 'cost-effectiveness.' The next cluster (roughly equal) includes salesperson knowledge/skills, trust from transaction track record, salesperson personality/behavior, and contribution to operations. What resonates varies by individual.

For a sales appointment to be granted, the two most important factors are how well the proposed product matches the company's challenges (score: 8,188) and the cost-effectiveness of the proposed product (score: 7,240).

Other highly ranked factors for granting a meeting include: the salesperson's knowledge and skills being excellent (5,477), existing transaction history and trust with the company (5,262), the salesperson's personality and demeanor being proper (5,210), and the feeling that introducing the product would be useful for one's own work (5,146).

Scoring method for the survey ranking: 1st place = +3 points, 2nd place = +2 points, 3rd place = +1 point. Survey conducted by TORiX Corporation using Macromill panel internet survey (May 2022, n=10,303), among people who have purchased something with company budget.

Salesperson personality and demeanor are difficult to express in documents, but other factors should be aligned with the front-line contact person on how to incorporate them into materials, which increases the success rate of obtaining appointments.
An effective tactic is to prepare a simple one-page document tailored to the key person's area of interest and have it delivered via the contact person.

The key point is to use an angle that makes the key person feel 'this is a story that relates to me.' Example: an case study report tailored to Director B's interest theme (resolving personalization/dependency on individuals) became the breakthrough.
Pitfall ⑧: The key person does not want to spend time on meeting coordination or preparation. Even if they agree with the content itself, they may be concerned about the labor involved in discussion.
For a key person who recognizes the necessity but simply finds the effort of preparation and coordination bothersome, the key is to design a process that does not take their time before the meeting.

A common case is when a contact person says something like 'To take this to the department head, we need to organize the information a bit more...' — you need countermeasures so they do not shut you out just because it is a hassle.

Three things to prepare in advance: (1) Demonstrate through the materials that you understand the key person's context — convey that you grasp the company/business situation and the themes the key person is currently focusing on, so they feel this salesperson is unlikely to make off-target remarks.

(2) Clearly state what you want from the key person — organize in advance the purpose, discussion points, and expected decisions. The biggest barrier is the anxiety of 'I don't know what they will talk about,' so stating 'On the day I would like your opinion on these two points: XX and XX' greatly lowers the hurdle.

(3) Present many candidate dates so that it becomes a state of 'it proceeds as soon as they reply.' If scheduling back-and-forth takes 3 or 4 rounds, that alone feels bothersome. Offer 5–6 or more candidate slots and say 'just pick one convenient time,' reducing the burden of arrangements.
The ideal state is: 'We will handle all the preparation and agenda, so you just need to show up.'
Pitfall ⑨: Key person wants to focus on other issues. Check question: Does it feel like the key person's mind is currently full with other themes? (If yes, this is the pitfall.)
When a key person explicitly states they are fully occupied with another issue, avoid making unreasonable requests. They are not rejecting the proposal but simply lack capacity for new themes.

Example case: A contact reports that the department head said, 'We are currently concentrating on formulating the mid-term management plan, so wait until that settles down.' This is not a rejection but a matter of current priorities and limited bandwidth.

Do not pressure with fear-based statements such as 'If we don't move quickly, competitors will get ahead of us.' This increases the key person's psychological burden and leads them to view you as a troublesome salesperson.
Effective stance shift: Instead of forcing a decision, say 'No judgment is needed right now, but I would like to share the information in advance.'
If the key person perceives it as a potential waste of time or thin content, limit the request to 'Just the first 10 minutes, please' to create a low-burden face-to-face opportunity.

Practical method: Request to appear for just 10 minutes in an already scheduled regular internal meeting between the contact and the key person (for in-person meetings, connect online via the contact's PC). This avoids setting up a new meeting.

When using short time slots, always prepare highly impactful materials in advance because the available time is limited. The goal is to create an initial 'just a little' opening and then draw the key person in once you meet.
For hard-to-meet key persons, prepare talking points, information, and suggestions in advance as a last-resort breakthrough tactic.
Present specific topics in advance so the meeting does not feel thin or unclear; greater visibility of what will be discussed lowers the counterpart's psychological barrier.

Show how the proposal relates to the issues the key person is currently focused on as the connection point (e.g., 'I have data that may be useful when you formulate the mid-term management plan—may I deliver it?').
The customer's position in the 5-stage buying process determines which of the 9 pitfalls they are most likely to fall into.

In the issue-recognition to information-gathering stage, internal identification of the key person is often still unclear, making pitfall ① (no visible method to confirm the key person) common; the stakeholder map is vague, so verbalizing the chain of influence is especially important; purchasing priority is still low, so pitfall ③ (no time for connecting actions) is also frequent because the contact feels it is not yet time to act seriously.

In the requirements-definition stage, multiple departments become involved as discussions concretize, making pitfall ⑥ (multiple candidate contacts causing indecision) and pitfall ④ (desire to avoid being skipped) more likely; internal champions also begin asserting project leadership at this point.
66.8 % of deals stall in the three upstream stages that precede requirements definition.

In B2B purchasing processes, deals are substantially decided by the requirements definition stage, so establishing contact with key persons before that point largely determines overall success or failure of the opportunity.

During the vendor comparison to order-decision stage, involvement of budget supervisors and final approvers increases, making specific pitfalls more likely: ⑤ (fear of receiving a negative evaluation) and ⑦–⑨ (the key person themselves is refusing contact).

At the comparison/decision stage, key persons usually have clear, identifiable reasons for refusing meetings; success requires correctly diagnosing those reasons and designing a precise re-challenge rather than generic follow-up.
Speed is critical once vendor comparison begins because competitors are also being evaluated; missing a re-challenge window risks losing the deal to another vendor.
Consciously mapping the current stage of the buying process allows salespeople to predict which of the nine common pitfalls are most likely and to take preemptive action.

Point 1 for escaping the 'cannot meet the key person' maze: treat contacts as a 'bead-string' (数珠つなぎ) rather than aiming in a straight line at a single person. There are six types of stakeholders; the final decision-maker is not the only person worth meeting.

Assuming 'key person = final approver' narrows perspective and often causes failure. The decisive factor is whether one starts from the premise that other stakeholders besides the final decision-maker must also be met.

Illustrative case: an opportunity that remained stalled when approached solely through person A suddenly progressed once an alternative route (another stakeholder chain) was opened, demonstrating the power of the bead-string approach.
The bead-string (multi-stakeholder chaining) tactic becomes even more important as the buying process advances and the number of involved parties increases.

When unable to meet a key person, shift from trying to 'go meet them' to creating an internal 'support group' (応援団) within the customer's company. This is a broader perspective on winning over the person in front of you as an ally.

Creating supporters is not merely about becoming friendly. Each stakeholder has their own rationality and motivations: the internal project promoter seeks 'project success'; the budget supervisor seeks 'evidence that can prove the validity of the investment'; field users seek 'reduction of operational burden'.
The essence of building a support group is designing messages that specifically resonate with what each individual stakeholder is seeking.

It is critical to also examine the relationships among the support group members themselves. If the internal promoter and budget supervisor already have a good relationship, it becomes easier for the promoter to communicate with the supervisor on your behalf. If their relationship is strained, an alternative path may need to be considered.
Deeply understanding the human relationships inside the customer's organization increases the precision of designing the support group.
A common situation (beyond certain specific pitfalls) is that customers 'understand the value but still cannot take action.' Showing value alone (the accelerator) is insufficient.

An often-overlooked complementary action is reducing the customer's psychological burden (releasing the brake). Concrete tactics include: quickly sending easily forwardable memos, always including the person in charge in the information-sharing loop, and presenting many candidate dates so the other party only needs to reply for progress to occur.

Value appeal (accelerator) and reduction of psychological burden (brake release) function as two complementary wheels. Only when both are in place does it become easy for the customer to move forward.

When a case or project is not progressing, begin by expanding the overall map and specifically identifying your current position ('自分はいまどこにいるのか'). Knowing the present state enables effective countermeasures; acting without this awareness leads to repeatedly applying misguided or off-target actions.
A maze (metaphor for a complex project or sales case) is not frightening if an overall map exists. Every maze has an exit.

Three essential elements create an illuminated path (like a torch lighting the way): (1) grasping the purchasing process (購買プロセスの把握), (2) grasping the stakeholders/related parties (関係者の把握), and (3) a map of pitfalls (落とし穴のマップ). With these aligned, proceed one step at a time while continuously confirming your position.
Confirmation process for identifying which of 9 pitfalls (落とし穴) you are stuck in when unable to meet the key person (キーパーソン): sequentially self-question to pinpoint the current trap.
Step 1: Does the frontline contact have any idea who the key person is? If no idea → Pitfall ①. If they have an idea → proceed to Step 2.
Step 2: Is the contact trying to connect you to the key person? If not trying at all → go to Step 3. If they tried but the key person appears to have refused → go to Step 4.

Step 3 reasons the contact will not connect you: Proposal value not yet sufficiently understood → Pitfall ②; Value understood but no bandwidth for internal coordination → Pitfall ③; Anxiety that things will proceed without their knowledge → Pitfall ④; Anxiety that making the introduction will lower their own evaluation → Pitfall ⑤; Multiple candidates exist and they are unsure whom to introduce → Pitfall ⑥.

Step 4 reasons the key person refused: Proposal value was not communicated → Pitfall ⑦; Meeting preparation and coordination feels troublesome → Pitfall ⑧; They want to focus on other issues right now → Pitfall ⑨.
Multiple pitfalls can exist simultaneously; in such cases address the more fundamental (lower-numbered) pitfall first for greater effectiveness.

This framework is presented as an appendix checklist titled '落とし穴の見分け方チェックリスト' (Checklist for Distinguishing the Pitfalls) within the chapter on defensive strategy for the 'maze of being unable to meet the key person'.

A sales case study from the author's 30s: After a highly positive initial meeting with C-san (HR contact at a mid-sized manufacturer), who took notes throughout and said they wanted to proceed positively and would contact next, there was complete silence for weeks despite a follow-up email with thanks and extra information.
The salesperson experienced growing anxiety and self-doubt, repeatedly reviewing their own actions and wondering if they had said something wrong or if the proposal was off-target.

After three weeks, a phone call revealed the client was actually very interested in the proposal. However, just as C-san was about to escalate it to their superior, a sudden large internal project launched, consuming their time and causing the reply to be postponed.
C-san admitted a psychological barrier: they found it burdensome to figure out how to explain the delay, having started and abandoned email drafts about three times.
Key realization: '連絡が返ってこない＝興味がない' ではない (No reply does not equal lack of interest). Customer silence ('音信不通') often has reasons unrelated to the salesperson or proposal quality.
Section 4.1 introduces '「連絡がつながらない」迷路' (the maze of being unable to get in touch), framing why customers become unresponsive as a common sales challenge to analyze rather than take personally.
Even if a client (such as C-san) is positively inclined toward a proposal, internal company circumstances can prevent them from replying to emails.

The reasons customers cannot reply to emails are frequently completely different from what the salesperson imagines. Salespeople often doubt their own proposal content, but actual causes can include a new internal matter arising that consumes available time, plus the cognitive burden of composing a reply itself.

When encountering a 'cannot get in contact' situation, habitually decompose the customer's circumstances structurally. Correctly estimating 'what is happening' on the client side completely changes the next action that should be taken.

A common B2B sales experience is a meeting that ends calmly with a phrase like 'I'll contact you later,' after which follow-up emails receive no replies despite the reaction not having been particularly negative; this creates the sensation of being lost in a maze.
The chapter frames unresponsive follow-up as the 'maze of not being able to get in contact' and presents an overall map of that maze (section 4.2) as part of defensive strategy II.

Many sales representatives tend to blame themselves when emails go unanswered, thinking they said something wrong or that their proposal was poor, but in reality, customer-side circumstances often prevent replies.
The reasons why contact cannot be established are not singular; the appropriate action differs completely depending on the customer's situation.
To escape the 'maze' of unanswered communications, situations should be specifically broken down using a diagnostic map.
The overall map for the 'cannot make contact' maze starts with the question: Is the customer reading the communication from us?
If not reading: Possible reasons include (1) they haven't noticed it at all, or (2) there is too much information causing thinking to stop.
If reading but no intention to respond: Possible reasons include (3) they have a bad impression of salespeople, or (4) the value of the proposal is not being conveyed.

If reading and intending to respond but there is a bottleneck: Possible reasons include (5) they don't have time available for the series of responses, (6) previous interactions have actually faded from memory, (7) they can write a reply but need internal confirmation so cannot reply now, (8) the customer lacks sufficient verbalization skills, or (9) they want to avoid a troublesome situation after replying.
When contact cannot be established with a customer, hypothesize the cause based on prior history and their reactions, then send a tailored email followed by a phone call to confirm the situation.
The first major decision branch for hypothesizing why contact has been lost is whether the customer has actually read the outgoing communications.

Email tactics and tone must be adapted according to the six types of stakeholders (internal champion/promoter, budget overseer, end-user/field practitioner, etc.), because the information to include and the appropriate expression style differ by role.
Always identify which of the six stakeholder roles the unresponsive person occupies before choosing wording or content.
Pitfall ①: the recipient simply has not noticed the message at all.
Self-check question for this pitfall: 'Is this customer the type of person who would normally reply if they had not overlooked the mail?' If yes, treat it as an oversight case.
When the customer is known to reply unless they miss something, the most probable cause is that the email was buried in a high volume of incoming mail and never seen.
If the message has not been read, a simple resend is unlikely to be perceived as bothersome.
Do not open with an urging tone such as 'How about it?' or 'Please reply promptly to the earlier matter,' because that creates a negative impression even when the original mail was unread.
The chapter supplies ready-to-adapt email draft templates for each scenario so that practitioners can customize rather than invent wording from scratch.

Sending a simple reminder or follow-up email (e.g., just asking 'How about it?') after a sales meeting often backfires: customers who never read the original email only retain the impression of being pressured or rushed, which can destroy the positive rapport built during the meeting.
Recommended alternative: Send a completely separate 'helpful/value-adding email' that is threaded to the previous conversation but contains zero hint of a reminder or follow-up pressure.

Structure the email by referencing the customer's previously mentioned challenges, then introduce relevant helpful content (such as a seminar) and explicitly list 3 company-specific points of relevance that you have already summarized for them.

Example opening: Instead of asking 'How about it?', write 'Regarding the issues you mentioned previously, I thought this seminar might be helpful, so I am contacting you.' Then add 'The 3 points I believe are most relevant to your company are:' followed by tailored bullets.

Sample email template (threaded to prior conversation): Greeting + reference to previously discussed challenges + introduction of a seminar that may help + 3 specific relevant points (e.g., (1) effective systematization techniques for individual variation, (2) immediate results even with an understaffed planning team, (3) case studies matching the company's size and growth stage) + seminar overview and URL + polite close.

Critical rule: Never make the email a mere announcement or invitation. Casually reference the original topic without reminding or pressuring. Embed the actual selling/appeal points inside the value-adding content. Removing pressure also makes it psychologically easier for the customer to reply about the original matter later.

In sales follow-up emails, avoid pushy 'push' tactics or repeating requests like 'how about it?', 'please reply', or 'I'm in trouble without a response'. Instead, summarize tailored points based on the recipient's situation to make them feel the salesperson is reliable and demonstrate expertise with phrases like 'I thought I could help from this perspective.'

Avoiding pressure in follow-ups has two key advantages: it is easier and less painful for the sender to dispatch (as 'pure contribution' rather than a reminder), and it makes it psychologically easier for the recipient to casually reply about the original unanswered matter.

When pressured with reminders, recipients often feel anxious about how to respond. Contacting about a separate topic creates natural openings such as 'by the way, about last time...', allowing customers to raise topics at their own pace and thereby increasing overall reply rates.
Link new emails to the previous thread so that modern thread-display email clients help the recipient immediately recall the full context and history.

Customize the angle of 'helpful information' according to the recipient's role: for internal champions/promoters, share competitor industry trends; for budget overseers, share successful case studies; for end users/field staff, share voices from counterparts at companies that have already implemented the solution. Matching the cut to their specific interests significantly improves open and reply rates.

Customers still in the problem-recognition or information-gathering stages of the buying process treat sales emails as just one of many low-priority messages. In these early stages, providing new value is far more effective than sending reminders or follow-ups.
A common communication pitfall occurs when too much information is sent, causing the recipient to experience 'thinking stop' (思考停止) where they have read the email but do not know how to reply.
Self-check question for this pitfall: Ask yourself whether the customer has been able to fully digest the information you sent. If the answer is no, this pitfall applies.

Busy recipients often receive huge volumes of email and spend significant time just checking messages; a long email then triggers hesitation ('do I really have to write a reply?') and results in the message remaining read but unanswered.
This is not a lack of intention to reply but a lack of mental organization; the recipient is drowning in an information sea and cannot structure a response.
Recommended opening phrase to reduce burden: Begin with a statement such as 'I contacted you because I thought I could reduce your burden' (ご負担を減らせないかと思いご連絡しました).
Follow the opening with a polite preface ('誠に恐れ入りますが、現状としてはどれに近いでしょうか') and then present a small set of numbered options so the recipient can reply with only a number.
The explicit goal of offering numbered choices is to lower the response load to the absolute minimum.
Always insert a cushion phrase that frames the entire message as an effort to reduce the other party's burden rather than to extract information.

Pitfalls ②–④ as a group describe situations in which the recipient has read the message but currently has no intention of taking action; the techniques above are designed to convert that state into an easy reply.

When following up with unresponsive customers (連絡がつながらない), send a multiple-choice email listing four situations and ask them to reply with only a number: (1) they have intent to introduce but are occupied with other matters; (2) they have concerns or issues but still want to consider proceeding; (3) they honestly feel it does not currently fit their company; (4) other. This lowers the reply burden to a single number.
Add the phrase 'Based on this answer I will propose a less burdensome way forward' so the request is not merely for information but clearly leads to a next, considerate proposal.

The two aims of this approach are (a) to reduce the customer's reply load and (b) to elicit at least a minimal reaction even if the customer is in a 'thinking-stopped' state, thereby creating an opening for the sender's next action.
A caution: an overly dry tone can backfire. Always insert a cushion such as 'this is to reduce your burden' so the customer understands the design is for their benefit.

Tailor the follow-up material to the customer's specific role, because 'what needs to be organized to unlock thinking-stop' differs by role: for a procurement/order person attach a one-page function-comparison summary; for an internal champion prepare a three-point slide of introduction benefits for internal explanation; for a budget supervisor send a one-page cost-effectiveness summary only.
Softly wording option (3) as 'honestly it may not fit yet' lets the customer decline without guilt, increasing the chance of any reply at all.

A common sales pitfall for receiving no customer replies is that the customer has a poor impression of the salesperson personally (self-check: during the meeting, can you be confident the customer holds a favorable impression of you? If no, this is the issue).
A negative impression is usually directed at the individual salesperson rather than the company or the proposal content itself, so recovery actions remain possible.

Small accumulated mistakes (e.g., giving vague answers to customer questions or delaying promised materials) can lead the customer to conclude 'there is no point in replying to this person,' even if they do not reject the proposal.
Recommended recovery tactic: have a superior or team leader send a follow-up email instead of the original salesperson.
