Sample superior email structure: introduce yourself as the team leader of the original salesperson, thank the customer for prior interactions, explicitly reference a specific customer pain point previously shared (example: 'we want to work on sales talent development but lack internal resources'), treat that comment as highly important, state that it was discussed internally, and begin outlining a solution to the resource-gap challenge.

In sales recovery situations involving poor impressions or unresponsive contacts, involve a superior by having them send a follow-up email that acknowledges prior customer comments as important, states that they were discussed internally, and attaches summarized materials.

Structure the attached summary around approximately three professional key points to demonstrate expertise; example points include: (1) tips for effective systematization to address individual variations, (2) immediate effectiveness even with an understaffed planning team, and (3) case studies matching the client's company scale and growth stage.

Introduce the superior naturally (e.g., 'I serve as the person in charge of the team') and use phrasing such as 'We took the comments we previously received as important and discussed them internally' to show the customer's input is not being treated lightly and to avoid the impression of an abrupt unsolicited email.

This approach operates on two axes to generate positive counter-materials against a negative sales impression: (1) changing the person involved (introducing a higher-level contact) and (2) appealing the company's overall expertise through organized, professional summaries.
From the customer's perspective, the appearance of a superior creates the expectation that 'higher-ups at this company will get involved and things will move quickly.'

Timing relative to the customer's purchasing process is critical: in early stages such as information gathering or requirements definition (before full competitor comparison), a single well-crafted email can still recover the impression; once the process reaches vendor comparison, impressions shift rapidly in relative evaluations, requiring faster, committed responses with visible executive involvement.
A common sales pitfall is that the value of a proposal is not being communicated to the customer, even if they have read the materials.
Self-check question: Is there any point about this proposal that the customer might be stuck on? If something comes to mind, this is likely the issue.
If a customer reads a proposal but has no intention of responding, they likely do not feel its value or do not understand how it benefits them personally.
A frequent cause is packing lots of information into proposal materials without explicitly linking it to the customer's specific challenges.
Salespeople may assume that sending comprehensive materials is enough for the message to get through, but customers often think 'so what does this actually do for us?'
When resending, clearly state the reason, such as 'I thought this would make internal discussions easier, so I'm sending additional materials.'
Highlight around 3 points from a specialist perspective to make the reason for sending convincing; this is a re-appeal that reinforces how value is communicated.

An effective technique is to show material contents directly in the email by embedding slides or document excerpts as images in HTML emails, which lowers the barrier of opening attachments by making content immediately visible.

When previous contact attempts have not connected, send a follow-up that summarizes the key points of previously presented materials. This makes it easier for the recipient to initiate internal discussions at their company.

Structure the follow-up around three specific points: (1) practical tips for creating effective systematization that reduces variation between individuals, (2) methods that deliver immediate results even when the planning team is understaffed, and (3) case studies from companies of similar size and growth stage to the recipient’s organization.

Embed or attach only the most relevant slides and add concise comments explaining why they matter. For example, highlight a case from Company X whose sales-team structure and situation closely match the recipient’s, especially their innovative internal-communication practices.
Close by proposing a short discussion meeting and offering to send candidate dates if the recipient is interested.

The psychological hurdle of opening email attachments is high for busy prospects who have not yet grasped the proposal’s value. Downloading a file feels like extra work, and the intended “I’ll look at it later” almost never happens. Therefore design the email so that the most important information is immediately visible in the body text itself.
HTML emails allow images (such as key slides) to be pasted directly into the message, further lowering the barrier to consumption.

Prepare six distinct value-reiteration angles, one for each type of stakeholder. If the recipient is an internal champion, emphasize how the material makes it easier for them to promote the idea inside their own organization.
Always explicitly state the reason for sending the follow-up (“改めて送る意味を伝える”) so the recipient understands why they are receiving the message again.

Tailor proposal messaging to the specific recipient's role and concerns rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach: an order/procurement officer responds best to a concrete correspondence table showing how the offering fits the company's requirements; a frontline user is drawn to case examples of how daily work will change after introduction; a budget supervisor notices ROI payback-period simulations and performance data from similarly sized companies; an influencer to the decision-maker needs evidence that the product fits the company's situation; the final decision-maker requires a management-level message on how the investment contributes to the company's mid-to-long-term strategy.
Redesigning 'who to address and from which angle to convey value' can produce a large change in response even when the underlying proposal remains the same.
When follow-up emails receive no reply, combine a concise summary that demonstrates expertise with a design that reduces the recipient's burden.

A common situation is that the customer is actually reading the emails and intends to reply, yet some bottleneck prevents them from doing so; this case has a relatively high chance of producing a response if the correct action is taken, but misidentifying the bottleneck can lead to an off-target approach that worsens the situation.

One frequent bottleneck (pitfall ⑤) is simply that the person in charge is extremely busy and has no spare time for the series of actions required to reply; a self-check question is: 'Apart from the customer's busyness, is there any other reason the reply is stalling? If not, this is the pitfall.'

Most customers juggle multiple tasks in parallel, so replies to salespeople tend to have low priority among must-do work. Replies are especially likely to be postponed during fiscal year-end, the start of a new fiscal year, or busy periods of large projects.
Even when a customer (C-san) was positively inclined toward a proposal, internal other projects could keep them too busy to respond, matching the author's own experience.
A defensive strategy for unreturned contact is to anticipate the customer's next internal action and proactively reduce their burden.

Example follow-up email structure: thank the customer for the meeting, acknowledge they are busy, state the intent to lighten the load of internal review, infer the likely next steps they will take (discuss based on materials, compile 'problem awareness and root-cause analysis' plus 'proposed measures and evaluation'), then attach a personally prepared slide deck summarizing prior discussions.

Offer the attached material as something the customer can freely edit and add to, and invite specific requests for wording changes or additional source materials, thereby providing help without being pushy.
Send non-PDF materials so the customer can easily process and adapt them.
Key tactics annotated in the example: (1) anticipate the customer's next action, (2) offer help in a non-imposing way, (3) send easily editable source materials.

When contacting a busy customer, first acknowledge their busyness in writing (e.g., 'I understand you are busy'), then clearly show a posture of 'if you don't have time, we can take action on our side.'
Provide a draft/template document based on previous exchanges as raw material, simultaneously demonstrating commitment and your own capability.
Add language such as 'I imagine there may be points your company would like to supplement, so please add as needed and make use of it' to invite their input.

Send materials in editable formats (PowerPoint, Word, Excel) rather than PDF, because customers often need to create their own internal review documents and want to customize them to their own context; designing for ease of revision is the greatest consideration for busy customers.
Offer flexibility by stating you will accommodate wording adjustments or additional specifications as much as possible if they contact you.
The key tactic is to proactively provide easily processable materials.

Tailor the draft content to the recipient's role for greater effect: for internal champions, provide a 'story draft for internal approval explanations' to directly support their main job of internal persuasion; for purchasing staff, send a 'vendor comparison table draft' to greatly reduce comparison workload; for budget supervisors, provide an editable 'ROI calculation sheet' to smooth the budget approval process.

Customers in the requirements-definition or vendor-comparison stage of the purchasing process have intensified internal review work and thus greater busyness; for them, minimize the burden of 'replying to sales' and instead provide 'materials directly usable for internal review,' so that interaction with sales is positioned as part of their actual work.
Pitfall ⑥: Previous interactions have faded from the customer's memory (self-check: Has too much time passed since the last meeting? If so, this is the trap).
This is a realistic scenario: the customer has read the email and intends to reply, but their memory of the details has faded.

The customer may be positively inclined but has forgotten the content and does not know how to respond. Customers handle multiple vendors and internal projects in parallel daily, making it unrealistic to remember every detail of each deal.

Especially for customers still in the problem-awareness or information-gathering stage who have not yet reached full-scale consideration, memories of individual deals fade more easily. For them, it may have been just 'a casual conversation.'

Effective approach: Reorganize and present the key points yourself. Recap the challenges previously discussed, the past discussions, and the next expected steps in a concise summary. Past email excerpts can be attached if available.

Then propose a short call: 'I apologize for the inconvenience given how busy you are, but if possible, could we speak for about 10 minutes?' Offer relevant materials that could be useful for their internal proposals or discussions.

Clarify the value that 'a phone call will resolve things quickly.' Because the customer is positively inclined, one phone call is often enough to revive the deal. Email requires recalling details, composing a reply, and sending it, whereas a call allows the conversation to restart immediately with 'Ah, that's right.'

Follow-up email template after a meeting with a busy client: Start with greeting and thanks for previous discussion time, acknowledge their busyness, then provide a structured recap of [situation heard], [discussion content], and [next expected steps], followed by a request for 10 minutes of phone time this week or next, while offering useful materials for their internal proposals or discussions.

To make recap emails more effective, do not just summarize previous points; add recent industry movements or new information that occurred afterward. Use phrasing such as: '前回は○○というお話でしたが、最近△△という動きがありましたので、御社にとってのインパクトを整理してみました' (Last time we discussed ○○, but recently there was a △△ development, so I organized the impact for your company). This transforms a mere reminder into an email that delivers new value.

Customize the added 'new information' according to the recipient's role to match their interests: field users receive details on recently released new features; internal promoters/champions receive latest competitor introduction case studies from the same industry; budget supervisors receive latest relevant cases or examples.
Additional technique for follow-ups: Reorganize the previous discussion points clearly and explicitly appeal that a phone conversation would allow faster and more efficient discussion than email.

One common reason a prospect does not reply is situation ⑦: they can draft a response but require internal confirmation before sending anything externally. This is frequently driven by company culture that is cautious about information leaving the organization.

Typical internal blockers include: ongoing discussions that have not yet produced a definitive position for the vendor, required approvals from a supervisor or related departments, an unconfirmed budget, or internally divided opinions.
Self-check question for the salesperson: “Is it possible that this company’s culture treats external information carefully?” If yes, treat the silence as this pitfall rather than disinterest.
Effective defensive tactic: send material that other clients found useful precisely when internal opinions were split, thereby helping the prospect’s own discussion move forward.

Sample follow-up email structure: thank them for the previous meeting; hypothesize that internal discussion is underway; attach or offer a resource that previously “made internal debate smoother”; list three concrete, relevant points (e.g., (1) a systematization tip that reduces person-to-person variation, (2) an immediately usable method even when the planning team is understaffed, (3) case studies of companies at a similar size and growth stage); offer additional materials once more internal context is shared; and politely request a brief check-in this week or next.
Core persuasive move inside the email: explicitly appeal to the benefit the prospect gains by sharing their internal situation (they receive more targeted support).
Check-question reminder for the salesperson: “Appeal the merit of the client communicating their internal situation.”
Customers often withhold replies because they feel it would be impolite or incomplete to communicate something half-finished; they are not necessarily uninterested.

An effective follow-up is to send materials framed as: 'When opinions were divided at other companies, this kind of information made internal discussions smoother.' This lowers the psychological barrier to responding.
The six-stakeholder framework is especially useful here: if you can estimate which parties inside the customer's organization are in disagreement, you can tailor the angle of the materials you send.
If the budget overseer is resisting on cost grounds, send cost-effectiveness simulation materials.
If front-line users worry about post-implementation workload, send a phased rollout plan or operational case studies from other companies.
If an influencer to the decision-maker questions 'Does this really fit us?', send same-industry, same-scale implementation examples.
If the final decision-maker is hesitating on the investment, send materials that visualize impact on management KPIs.
Always add the line 'If I understood your internal situation a little better, I have additional materials I could send' to reopen a short phone conversation.

The reason to insist on a phone call is that email creates a written record; customers therefore hesitate to put anything in writing while matters are still undecided. A phone call allows candid, off-the-record discussion.
Explicitly state: 'If you share the internal situation, I can provide more appropriate support.' The real goal is to obtain agreement that 'deep conversations should happen by phone.'

Once you know what internal debates are occurring, the precision of your next actions rises dramatically. This particular stall typically occurs between the requirements-definition stage and the vendor-comparison stage of the buying process.

In B2B sales follow-up, the psychology of 'wanting to wait until everyone's consensus is obtained' (全員の合意が取れるまで待ちたい) occurs especially easily during the internal consideration/comparison stage (較の段階), because more internal stakeholders become involved and their individual judgment criteria come into alignment.

Pitfall ⑧ for non-response: The customer's verbalization skills (言語化スキル) are insufficient. Self-check question: Is the customer the type who finds it easier to write or to speak? If speaking is easier, this pitfall applies.

Some customers have the intention to reply but struggle with verbalization in writing. A certain number of people cannot summarize thoughts into written text; the more complex the theme, the more they feel that composing an email is troublesome.

Even customers who can speak fluently in a rambling style ('あれがこうで、これがああで') require a completely different skill to structure the same content as email text. When multiple arguments are intertwined, the act of summarizing into writing itself imposes a high cognitive load.

Follow-up tactic for this pitfall: Contact them with the phrasing 'ご負担を減らせないかと思いご連絡しました' (I contacted you thinking I could reduce your burden) and present selectable situation options so they can reply easily without composing a full explanation.

Sample follow-up email structure: Thank them for the previous meeting, acknowledge they are busy, state the intent to reduce their internal discussion burden, then offer multiple-choice status options such as (1) they became very busy with other work (situation change) or (2) they need to organize information before communicating with internal colleagues.
Key implementation point: The way the multiple-choice options (選択肢) are constructed is critical to making a low-effort reply possible; this is highlighted as a check-question focus.
When a person is thinking but finds it difficult to put thoughts into words (unlike the 'thinking stop' case), prepare pre-written options that somewhat verbalize the situation for them.
Provide numbered choices (e.g., 1-5) so the recipient can simply reply with a number, lowering the barrier to response.
Follow up by offering to send phone appointment candidates after a one-word reply, as phone calls are often easier for people who struggle with written language.
Email content that takes 30 minutes to write can often be handled in 5 minutes by phone; identify the communication channel with the lowest hurdle for the customer.

This approach relates to the 6 types of stakeholders framework: e.g., on-site users may have high technical expertise but be unaccustomed to writing business documents; internal promoters may think strategically but struggle to organize multiple points in email.
Identify the other party's preferred communication method and propose a matching channel to elicit replies.
People who are poor at verbalization find phone calls easier than writing.

One common reason prospects fail to reply to sales follow-ups is the fear that responding will trigger unwanted next steps such as a heavy sales pitch, an estimate, or a request to schedule a detailed meeting they are not yet ready for.

The act of replying is psychologically interpreted by the customer as committing to further action; therefore they choose inaction to avoid that commitment, especially among personality types that are highly cautious about hassle.
Salespeople can neutralize this fear by proactively inserting a low-pressure statement such as 'It may not be a situation in which we need to rush to a conclusion at this point.'

Such a statement signals that the salesperson understands the customer’s current situation, lowers the customer’s guard, and paradoxically makes a reply more likely because the customer no longer feels they will be rushed.

An illustrative follow-up email begins by thanking the prospect for a prior meeting and then recaps three specific value points (mechanisms to reduce individual variation, immediate impact even with a short-staffed planning team, and case studies from companies of similar size and growth stage) before posing a check question.
When a prospect may not yet feel urgency, propose a short 10-minute phone call focused only on 'estimate/pricing points' so they have something easy to reference later for internal discussion.
Frame the pricing-only call with a rationale: monetary details are better conveyed while still fresh in memory.
Even at the information-gathering stage, customers typically want a sense of cost; appeal to that desire.

Position the offer so that knowing a price range later makes it easier to consult when needed and gives the customer more options—i.e., 'You don't have to decide now, but having the information is advantageous.'

Tailor the 'reassuring message' to the recipient's role: for the purchasing contact, emphasize that this is only information-sharing and next steps can match internal temperature; for an internal champion, offer data they can use as material while still in the planning stage; for a budget overseer, provide a rough cost sense as input for investment judgment and note that a formal quote can wait until consideration progresses.
Imagine what each stakeholder fears and proactively neutralize that fear; doing so is key to eliciting a reply.
This pitfall (and the need for such careful framing) is especially common with customers who are still in the problem-recognition or information-collection phase.
A preventive line can be drawn from the seller's side rather than waiting for the buyer to raise objections.

For customers whose company has not yet internally decided to 'seriously consider' a purchase, they tend to avoid deepening interactions with salespeople. An effective approach is to explicitly communicate that 'there is no need to decide right now' and then gradually provide information that 'even just holding onto it as material for future judgment is a plus.'
The 5-stage customer purchasing process and 9 pitfalls are interrelated: the stage of the buying process determines which pitfalls customers are most likely to fall into.

In the problem recognition to information gathering stage, the customer's internal team often has not yet decided which vendor proposals to seriously consider. Common pitfalls include ① (not reading the salesperson's contact), ④ (value not being conveyed), ⑥ (memory fading), and ⑨ (wanting to avoid troublesome developments after replying). At this stage, a salesperson's contact is merely 'one of many emails' to the customer, so approaches that provide new value (rather than mere follow-up or urging) are especially important.

In the requirements definition stage, as consideration becomes more concrete, the number of internal stakeholders increases and judgment criteria become clearer. Common pitfalls include ② (information overload causing thinking to stop), ⑤ (no time), ⑦ (need for internal confirmation preventing a reply), and ⑧ (issues with verbalization skills). Customers are often in a state of wanting internal agreement but not yet having things solidified, and they hesitate to provide incomplete or half-baked information to the salesperson.

In the vendor comparison to order decision stage, proposals from multiple vendors have been gathered and internal comparison/evaluation becomes full-scale. Common pitfalls include ③ (poor impression of the salesperson) and ⑤ (no time). The risk of falling into ④ (value not being conveyed) also increases due to more complex stakeholders. Customers at this stage are simultaneously handling contacts from other companies, so salespeople who combine both speed and expertise are prioritized.

Key framework: Purchasing process 5 stages × likely pitfalls (section 4.6). The five stages referenced are: problem recognition, information gathering, requirements definition, vendor comparison, and order decision.

In the vendor comparison stage of B2B purchasing, the top three customer concerns typically originate from 'ズレ' (misalignments or discrepancies between seller and buyer). If contact cannot be established at this stage, other vendors may have already advanced, so prompt response is required.

Purchasing process stages have characteristic pitfalls (はまりやすい落とし穴) with specific background circumstances: (1) Challenge recognition ~ information gathering: unread messages, value not conveyed, fading memory, desire to avoid troublesome next steps; background is that the deal is not yet in serious consideration so sales outreach has low priority. (2) Requirements definition: thinking stoppage, lack of time, need for internal confirmation, difficulty verbalizing needs; background is more internal stakeholders requiring time-consuming consensus. (3) Vendor comparison ~ order decision: poor impression, value not conveyed, lack of time; background is parallel evaluation of multiple vendors where selection occurs on speed and perceived expertise.

Consciously mapping a deal to its current purchasing-process stage makes it easier to anticipate the most probable communication pitfalls (use only as a thinking starting point; avoid rigid assumptions).

All nine identified follow-up pitfalls share a common principle: the seller must demonstrate expertise that the customer actually feels as value. Generic chase emails such as 'How is it going?' or 'I look forward to your reply' are frequently perceived as pressure even when no pressure is intended.
Three distilled action points emerge from the nine pitfalls; the first is '専門性を感じさせる価値提供をする' (provide value that makes the customer feel the seller’s expertise).

When contact cannot be established, replace generic check-ins such as “how's it going?” with information the customer perceives as personally valuable; customers respond to demonstrated professional expertise rather than routine follow-up language.
A concrete alternative is to send “I have organized three points related to your company’s situation” as a professional; this single change completely alters how the message is received.

The three points must be tailored to the recipient’s role: internal champions receive information that helps them advocate internally; budget overseers receive data that substantiates cost-effectiveness; end-users receive a concrete image of post-implementation operational improvement.
Six distinct stakeholder types exist, each resonating with different value points; merely recognizing this variation changes how an email lands.

In the opening case, a three-week wait followed by a call that supplied new, issue-relevant information produced an engaged response (“I was just thinking about that”) and restarted the opportunity; a generic “any update?” would likely have elicited only an awkward apology.
Customer research on actions that raise order probability ranked highest: speed of response, a stepwise deepening approach, assistance with actual work, and provision of useful information.

The same research ranked lowest: frequent contact and the application of “healthy pressure.” Reminder messages of the form “we need a reply by this date or it becomes a problem” are therefore poorly received by most customers.

A common salesperson trap is the seemingly natural impulse “no reply, so I will chase.” From the customer’s side such messages read as “this salesperson is acting for their own convenience,” which damages rather than advances the relationship.
Point 2 in sales follow-up: Thoroughly lower the customer's 'reply hurdle'. The common issue in pitfalls 5-9 is that customers want to reply but are unable to do so.

Three concrete techniques to lower the reply hurdle: (1) Prepare reply options that can be answered with just a number, converting the burden of writing a long email into a one-line reply. (2) Shift from email to a short phone call, which lowers the barrier for people who struggle to verbalize thoughts or who need internal confirmation that is hard to put in writing. (3) Proactively provide editable materials such as templates or draft documents that the customer can use for internal discussions, thereby converting the burden of 'replying to the salesperson' into 'internal review work'.
All three techniques share the same underlying mindset: stand in the customer's shoes, imagine what is specifically blocking their reply, and remove that obstacle.
Point 3: Form hypotheses and discover winning patterns. The correct action depends on the situation and cannot be known without testing, but one should not act blindly.

Always form a personal hypothesis about 'what is happening right now' based on clues from the previous meeting (whether the customer took notes, asked questions, or mentioned internal circumstances) and then test actions aligned with that hypothesis.

Repeating the hypothesize-and-test cycle will not make every customer reply immediately, but if 2–3 out of 10 companies respond, an effective method (winning pattern) becomes visible and constitutes personal learning.
This hypothesis-verification approach itself is a valuable individual sales skill.

Sharing successful response patterns within a sales team significantly increases organizational capability to handle the 'no-contact maze' (連絡がつながらない迷路). Examples include: sending editable materials to customers facing 'pitfall ⑤ (no time)' which elicited a reply, and sending an email explicitly stating 'you don't have to decide right now' to customers facing 'pitfall ⑨ (want to avoid troublesome developments)' which proved effective.
Do not immediately conclude that 'no reply = no interest/pulse.' Customer reasons for failing to respond are highly diverse; applying the right countermeasure frequently restarts stalled cases.

The 'no-contact maze' appears to be a dead-end dark struggle, but structurally decomposing the customer's situation and following the appropriate path for each identified pattern reliably leads to an exit.

Case study: After three weeks of silence with client C, the author called to grasp the situation, empathized with C's busyness, and proactively sent a draft document that C could use internally. C used the draft as the basis for a report to their superior, after which the process moved forward smoothly and the deal was won.

Key lesson: The choice is not binary ('wait' versus 'urge'). Instead, correctly infer the customer's actual situation and execute a third, situation-specific action. When lost in the maze, stop, unfold the map, and confirm your current position—this is the shortest route out.
A sequential diagnostic checklist (付録1：落とし穴の見分け方チェックリスト) can identify which follow-up pitfall a non-responsive prospect has fallen into after a sales interaction.

Step 1 checks whether the prospect may simply not have noticed the message. If the person is not typically someone who ignores emails, Pitfall ① (読んでいない / has not read it) is most likely; send new useful information rather than a reminder.
If the prospect could have read the message but still taken no action, proceed to Step 2.

Step 2 evaluates the reaction during the previous sales meeting. A thin reaction, few questions, or any sense of discomfort points to Pitfall ③ (営業への印象がよくない / poor impression of the salesperson) or Pitfall ④ (提案の価値が伝わっていない / value of the proposal not conveyed); consider a follow-up from a superior or a change in value-proposition angle.
A positive meeting reaction (taking notes, asking questions) leads to Step 3.
Step 3 isolates the remaining bottleneck when the meeting was positive yet no reply arrived.

Large volume of proposal materials or multiple options presented indicates Pitfall ② (情報が多すぎて思考停止 / information overload causing decision paralysis); reduce choices so the prospect can reply with a simple number.
Remarks such as “busy” or “hectic” indicate Pitfall ⑤ (時間がない / no time); send an editable draft (たたき台) to lower the reply burden.
Comments about consulting internally (“来週社内で相談します”) indicate Pitfall ⑦ (社内確認が必要 / internal confirmation required); supply materials useful for internal review and propose a phone call.
If none of the above apply, the remaining possibilities are Pitfall ⑥ (記憶が薄れている / memory fading) or Pitfall ⑧.

When a contact cannot be reached, it may indicate pitfall ⑧ (difficulty verbalizing a reply) or pitfall ⑨ (desire to avoid troublesome developments). In such cases, reorganize the key points and either propose a phone call or send a message stating that there is no rush.

Step 4 of the process: Execute the chosen action based on the hypothesis and observe the customer's reaction. If there is still no reaction, reconsider and try a different pattern. Combining multiple approaches can be effective, but sending many emails in a short period can be counterproductive, so space them out with intervals.

Pitfall ①: Email not read (customer has not noticed the email). Effective approach: Attach new useful information to the existing email thread without any scent of a follow-up. Avoid: Completely sales-driven follow-up emails.

Pitfall ②: Thinking stopped (too much information, cannot organize a reply). Effective approach: Present about three options so the customer can reply with just a number. Avoid: Sending even more materials.

Pitfall ③: Poor impression (distrust of the individual salesperson). Effective approach: Switch contact to a supervisor or responsible person to overwrite the impression with expertise. Avoid: Repeated contacts from the same person.

Pitfall ④: Value not conveyed (unclear how the proposal relates to the customer). Effective approach: Re-appeal using an angle tailored to the customer's role and embed images of materials in the email body. Avoid: Resending the same materials or repeating generic explanations.

Pitfall ⑤: No time (too busy to handle the matter). Effective approach: Proactively provide an editable draft or easy-to-process materials. Avoid: Deadline-based follow-ups or phrases like 'please reply soon'.

Pitfall ⑥: Memory fading (forgetting the content and unsure how to reply). Effective approach: Reorganize and attach the key points, then propose a 10-minute phone call. Avoid: Short emails that only say 'about the previous matter'.

Pitfall ⑦: Internal confirmation needed (holding the reply until internal agreement is reached). Effective approach: Provide materials usable for internal discussions and have them share the internal situation privately by phone. Avoid: Pressuring questions like 'when can we expect your conclusion?'.

Pitfall ⑧: Poor at verbalizing (high burden to write a reply). Effective approach: Prepare pre-written options and propose switching to a phone channel. Avoid: Emails that demand long written answers.

Pitfall ⑨: Want to avoid trouble (fear of being sold to if they reply). Effective approach: Explicitly state first that there is no rush, then propose a 10-minute information-only phone call. Avoid: Closing-style tone or requests to schedule a meeting.

When email contact cannot be established, the content and tone must change substantially based on the recipient's specific role among six types of stakeholders, in order to increase the chance the message is read and receives a reply.
Field users (現場の利用者) primarily care about how their own daily work will actually change after adoption, whether the tool is easy to use, and whether it will increase their operational burden.
Emails targeting field users should include real voices from field staff at companies that already adopted the product, plus before-and-after comparisons of actual work flows.
Visual proof such as screenshots of the interface, photos or video links showing real usage scenes is highly effective for field users.
Proactively address common field-user anxieties in a concise list covering implementation workload, learning cost, and integration with existing systems.

Effective phrasing for field users includes statements like 'We have received comments such as 〇〇 from frontline staff at companies that introduced the system' and 'We have summarized the rollout steps designed to minimize impact on daily operations.'
Avoid sending field users only abstract management-level benefits such as ROI or long-term strategy; their core question is 'What is it actually like to use this in practice?'

Internal champions / project promoters (社内推進者) focus on ensuring project success, obtaining concrete materials they can use to persuade colleagues internally, and collecting results that demonstrate their own ability to drive initiatives.
Chapter 4 of '迷路' (Labyrinth) titled '守りの戦略Ⅱ' (Defensive Strategy II) covers email strategies for internal advocates and purchasing personnel.

For internal advocates (社内推進者): Include a 1-page summary or storyline draft usable for internal explanations; competitor case studies (e.g., 'Company A with similar challenges achieved XX results'); preemptive answers to likely opposing opinions; data showing risks of leaving the issue unaddressed.

Effective phrases for internal advocates: 'I've summarized the key points into 3 pages for easy internal explanation'; 'Please don't hesitate to let me know if there's anything I can help with as you move this forward.'
Avoid bypassing the internal advocate to approach upper management directly; respect their initiative and design information flow through them.
For purchasing/order personnel (発注担当者): They prioritize smooth internal coordination, matching of performance to requirements, and unhindered procedures.

Email elements for purchasing personnel: A correspondence table matching their requirements to your proposal (e.g., 'Your Requirement A → Our corresponding measure is XX'); a vendor comparison format that's easy to use against other companies; answers to FAQs on quotes and contract terms; a schedule proposal and overall implementation flow.

Effective phrases for purchasing personnel: 'I've created a correspondence table matching your requirements for use in your internal review'; 'Please feel free to contact us anytime if you have questions about the quote.'

When emailing procurement/ordering officers (発注担当者), avoid asking them to make judgments. They often act as balancers and become wary if you try to steer them toward a specific direction. Instead, provide decision-making materials and involve them as a partner who can connect you to the company's true internal decision-maker.
Budget supervisors (予算の監督者) prioritize cost-effectiveness, the ability to internally justify the validity of an investment, and a sense of security derived from precedents and proven track records.

Emails to budget supervisors should include: an investment recovery period simulation with specific numbers; introduction results and effect data from companies of similar size and industry; a phased introduction plan that reduces initial investment; and visualization of the 'cost of not introducing' such as opportunity losses and increased personnel costs.

Effective phrases for budget supervisors include: 'At company A of similar scale, investment recovery was completed in X months after introduction' and 'We have prepared a phased introduction plan that is easy to incorporate into your budget plan.'
Avoid appealing only to functional superiority when emailing budget supervisors. They have little interest in features and instead seek reassurance that approving the investment is safe.
Influencers to decision-makers (決裁者への影響者) focus on whether a solution fits their company's specific situation and need convincing evidence that 'it suits us.'

Emails to influencers should include customized proposals tailored to industry characteristics and current organizational realities (e.g., 'In your industry, this challenge is common, so this usage is most effective'), specific introduction stories from similar companies, and objective information such as third-party evaluations or analyst reports.

For communications targeting influencers (影響者), avoid generic product introductions because they evaluate based on whether a solution specifically fits their own company; explanations that could apply to any company do not resonate.

Effective phrases when addressing influencers include: 'Customers in industries like yours particularly value this point' and 'I am also sending an evaluation report from a third-party organization for your reference.'
Final decision-makers (最終決裁者) primarily care about whether an investment is worthwhile, how it connects to the company's future, and whether they can later justify that the decision was correct.

Emails to final decision-makers should include: quantified impact on management indicators (sales growth, cost reduction, productivity gains); explicit linkage to the company's mid-to-long-term strategy; risks of not investing (widening competitor gaps or delayed response to market changes); and a concise one-page executive summary.

Effective phrases for final decision-makers include: 'I have organized how this investment contributes to the [specific initiative] outlined in your mid-term management plan' and 'As material for your judgment, I have summarized an executive summary on one page for your review.'

Avoid listing detailed features or technical specifications in emails to final decision-makers, as they seek the overall picture and investment rationale rather than implementation details (which they delegate). Also avoid competing solely on discounts, since they judge based on investment value rather than price alone.

When a sales proposal receives strong initial enthusiasm from a contact person (e.g., 'This is perfect for us, we want to introduce it'), the phrase 'We'll review it internally' or 'Please give us some time' often conceals internal organizational barriers rather than genuine progress.

A real-world case: A mid-30s consultant proposing training services to a manufacturing client encountered a highly motivated contact (D-san) who later revealed three internal walls blocking approval after one month of delay.

First internal barrier: The business unit director (D-san's superior) prioritized post-M&A organizational integration and stated there was no bandwidth for new training initiatives that fiscal period.
Second internal barrier: The corporate planning budget officer insisted that the proposal could not proceed without cost-effectiveness / ROI data.
Third internal barrier: One on-site department head opposed the idea due to a previous similar training program that had failed.
Key insight: Even when the primary contact strongly agrees with the proposal, they may not yet have successfully involved or aligned other internal stakeholders, causing the review process to stall.

Effective response strategy: Collaborate with the internal champion to create targeted materials that address each stakeholder's specific concerns—e.g., linking the training to post-M&A integration priorities for the director, and preparing other-company investment-recovery simulations for the budget officer.

When internal review of a sales proposal stalls ('検討が進まない'), it is typically a structural/organizational problem inside the customer's company rather than a lack of the customer's personal intent or motivation.

Even a highly motivated internal champion (e.g., D-san) cannot advance a deal if they lack the right 'weapons' (supporting materials, data, simulations) and 'procedures' (step-by-step process) to navigate internal politics and decision-making.

Effective sales intervention: instead of waiting passively for the customer to progress the review, jointly diagnose and remove specific bottlenecks. In the D-san case this included organizing simulations and facilitating a discussion with the department head to analyze why a previous training initiative failed and how the new proposal differs.
Result of collaborative bottleneck removal: the stalled case received formal approval three months later.

Core lesson for salespeople: understand the customer's internal decision-making structure and actively help the champion overcome organizational walls; the salesperson's role is to co-create a path through the internal maze rather than merely deliver a proposal and wait.

This content belongs to Chapter 5 ('守りの戦略 Ⅱ' / Defensive Strategy II) of a framework that maps the '迷路' (maze) of stalled internal reviews, specifically section 5.2 which presents the overall map of that maze.

After making a proposal to a customer, salespeople often encounter a situation where the customer says they will 'consider it internally' and then time passes with little progress. Follow-up contact yields replies like 'still considering' or 'hasn't progressed yet.'

This 'maze' is difficult because contact with the customer is still possible (unlike cases where contact is lost), yet it is hard to strongly urge action since they claim to be considering it. Simply waiting often leads to the deal disappearing.
To escape this maze, break down the situation specifically: first distinguish between 'individual problems' and 'organizational problems.'
For individual problems, identify 'which person it is stuck with.' For organizational problems, identify 'what the bottleneck is.'

This distinction is crucial because applying organizational-level measures to an individual problem (or vice versa) will miss the mark. The correct countermeasure requires first determining the nature of the problem.

Customers do not always accurately explain why things are not progressing; often they themselves do not fully grasp the reason. Behind 'we're considering it internally' might be a specific manager opposing it, or other projects taking priority that month. Customers rarely volunteer such details unprompted.

In organizational settings where a proposal or initiative is stuck in a 'consideration not progressing' (検討が進まない) state, it is essential to first diagnose the precise bottleneck; otherwise any countermeasures will be misaligned.
A diagnostic map (Figure 5-1) organizes ten common pitfalls that trap an issue in this maze, grouped by whether the blockage is an individual-level problem or an organizational-level problem.

Key diagnostic questions to locate the blockage: (a) Is the issue an individual problem or an organizational problem? (b) What exactly is the bottleneck? (c) At which specific person has the process stopped?
Pitfalls ①–⑤ are classified as individual problems (the process is stuck with a particular person).

Pitfall ①: The 'ball' (responsibility) has not been passed to the person who is supposed to carry out the practical work of consideration. Check question: 'Is there anyone other than the person immediately in front of you who can take the lead on this consideration inside the company?' (A 'yes' indicates this pitfall.)
Pitfall ②: The person who is supposed to carry out the practical consideration does not actually support or agree with the initiative.
Pitfall ③: The person assigned to carry out the practical consideration lacks the necessary skills.
Pitfall ④: A specific opponent is deliberately obstructing the consideration process.
Pitfall ⑤: The person who holds decision-making authority is withholding judgment.
Pitfalls ⑥–⑩ are classified as organizational problems.
Pitfall ⑥: The organization has other issues that it must prioritize over the current consideration.
Pitfall ⑦: The set of relevant stakeholders has not even been clearly identified.
Pitfall ⑧: Each stakeholder is too busy to convene a meeting.
Pitfall ⑨: Stakeholders are discussing the matter, but the decision criteria remain ambiguous.
Pitfall ⑩: Stakeholders are discussing the matter, but there is no mechanism for reconciling differences of opinion.
The framework (section 5.3) supplies targeted check questions that allow a practitioner to test which of the ten pitfalls is active and therefore to choose an appropriately focused intervention.
A common pitfall in advancing business considerations (検討実務) is that the person who received the proposal does not actually hold the 'ball' to move the internal review process forward.

The initial contact or proposal recipient is not necessarily the person responsible for driving internal consideration; they may only serve as a window/contact point while someone else handles the actual advancement.

From the six types of stakeholders (outlined in Chapter 2): the contact person may be the 発注担当者 (ordering/purchasing coordinator who handles vendor interactions), but the actual internal driver is often the 社内推進者 (internal champion who proposes, leads, and involves stakeholders for introduction/implementation).
Example: The 発注担当者 acts as the vendor-facing window, while their superior serves as the 社内推進者 who involves relevant parties and advances the consideration process.
If the person in front of you does not handle the practical consideration work, simply waiting provides no guarantee that the process will move forward.

There are four main methods for the person advancing the consideration work to create opportunities for discussion, plotted on a 2x2 matrix with axes of 'ease of discussion arising' (議論の起こりやすさ: high at top, low at bottom) and 'setup hurdle' (設定のハードル: low on left, high on right).
Method A (high discussion ease, low setup hurdle): Incorporate the topic into the agenda of an existing regular meeting (定例会議の議題に組み込む).
Method B (high discussion ease, high setup hurdle): Convene the necessary members specifically for a discussion (必要なメンバーを招集して議論).
Method C (low discussion ease, low setup hurdle): Conduct individual consultations (個別の相談).
Method D (low discussion ease, high setup hurdle): Make individual approval requests (個別の承認依頼).

A 2x2 framework classifies venues for advancing internal consideration (検討) by two axes: likelihood that discussion will occur, and the hurdle of setting up the venue. Practitioners who actually move consideration forward always select one of the four types and take concrete action to create that venue.

Type A (discussion likely × low setup hurdle): Slip the topic into an existing regular meeting agenda. Example: add “vendor-proposal review” as an item on the weekly Monday departmental meeting. Setting the venue is easy and discussion tends to arise naturally.

Type B (discussion likely × high setup hurdle): Convene a dedicated meeting solely for the topic with the necessary members. Discussion can go deep and a single session can produce large forward movement, but calendar coordination and securing attendance raise the setup cost.

Type C (discussion unlikely × low setup hurdle): Hold informal one-on-one consultations with anyone who seems approachable. Easy to start, yet organizational momentum is hard to generate. Useful as 根回し (groundwork/nemawashi) that later makes formal discussion smoother.

Type D (discussion unlikely × high setup hurdle): Submit a formal approval request to someone with decision authority. The interaction is more “please decide” than open discussion; the hurdle is high, but if materials are complete a decision can be obtained on the spot.

When the person you are speaking with is not the one actually driving the internal process, direct questions such as “How will this be decided internally?” or “What materials do you need?” typically produce only vague replies.

A more effective questioning tactic is to set the current case aside and inquire about customary practice and past precedents: “How do other investment decisions normally proceed?”, “What is the usual flow when an external proposal is received?”, or “For a similar monetary scale, what process is typically followed?”

When assessing a prospect's evaluation process, inquire about their 'usual way' of proceeding rather than focusing only on the current deal, because someone experienced in advancing practical evaluations (検討実務) will typically have a ready answer based on prior practices.
If a contact cannot envision any usual process or venue for evaluations, they are likely not the person responsible for advancing practical consideration, or this is their first time in such a role.

Useful follow-up questions to surface the right discussion venue include: whether incorporating the topic into regular meetings would make discussion easier, who should participate to enable progress, what documents are needed, and whether starting with unofficial one-on-one consultations would be more effective.

In the early stages of the buying process (problem recognition and information gathering), the internal person who will advance practical evaluations is often not yet identified, so the 'ball' has no clear owner and time can pass without progress; this pitfall is especially common before a formal evaluation project exists.
By the requirements-definition stage, an evaluation structure is usually more established, making it comparatively easier to identify who holds responsibility for moving the process forward.

A second common pitfall is that the person tasked with advancing practical consideration does not personally support or agree with the proposal, resulting in a state where 'the ball has been passed but nothing moves.'
Diagnostic check question for this pitfall: 'How do you feel about this proposal?' A non-positive answer indicates the person advancing the work is not bought in.

For the evaluation owner to actually take action, they themselves must be convinced; they need to be able to explain the proposal in their own words (for example, answering a superior who asks 'Why does this fit us?').
Lack of personal conviction or perceived internal hurdles (political, process, or risk-related) are the typical reasons the evaluation owner fails to advance the opportunity.
Simply forwarding received materials internally is insufficient and raises doubts about genuine endorsement of the proposal.

Promoting new internal initiatives typically generates opposing opinions and extra coordination work, creating a major brake due to fears of significantly increased personal workload for the person handling practical review.
The personal agreement and buy-in of the individual advancing the consideration work serves as a critical accelerator to move stalled situations forward.

Stakeholder motivations and fears vary by role among the six types of related parties: an internal promoter in this position is driven by desire for project success but fears evaluation damage from failure; a procurement/ordering person is motivated by smooth procedures but worries about added adjustments.
Recognizing how different roles perceive hurdles differently makes it easier to increase the agreement level of the person advancing the practical consideration.

To create a state where the customer feels they 'should do it,' three perspectives are essential: bird's-eye view (alignment with company policy and direction, as misalignment makes internal advocacy frightening), insect's-eye view (on-the-ground specifics and credibility, e.g., 'this exact issue occurs in the field with X troubles per month'), and fish's-eye view (consistency with industry trends and competitor movements, e.g., 'peers are adopting this' or 'industry-wide change is happening' to support 'now is the time').
The 'three eyes' framework (鳥の目・虫の目・魚の目) is used to prepare materials that provide reassurance from multiple stakeholder perspectives when advancing internal corporate considerations or proposals.
Bird's-eye view (鳥の目) corresponds to management's perspective: cite the vision and policies that executives constantly communicate and demonstrate how the proposal aligns with them.

Insect's-eye view (虫の目) corresponds to the frontline/field perspective: express the concrete issues that on-site members face using both quantitative and qualitative information, and show that the proposal leads to solving those issues.
Fish's-eye view (魚の目) corresponds to the external-environment perspective: verbalize how societal trends and industry currents are moving and demonstrate that the proposal rides those waves.

When materials exist that satisfy all three viewpoints (management, field, and external environment), they serve as a strong push for the person responsible for advancing the practical internal review.
A common pitfall is that the person tasked with advancing internal consideration lacks the required skills, even if they personally support the idea.

In large organizations, advancing a review generates a high volume of internal interactions that require sequential execution of actions such as considering, discussing, coordinating, reaching agreement, organizing, explaining, and reporting.

The person advancing the work must be able to produce circulation-ready documents, implement thorough risk countermeasures, handle complex administrative procedures, and perform similar organizational tasks that are often invisible from the sales side.

A diagnostic check question for this pitfall is: 'What specific tasks will arise for [the named person] in advancing the internal consideration?' If a clear answer is not forthcoming, the skills gap is present.

In B2B sales processes involving internal consideration (検 討), simply assigning tasks to the contact person with a request like 'please proceed' is often insufficient and will stall progress; salespeople must provide ongoing '側面支援' (lateral/side support) including helping with internal stakeholder involvement.
Effective side support requires skills in involving internal sales teams and crafting internal communications that match the client's company culture and tone & manner (トンマナ).

Figure 5-4 outlines four checkpoints for side support, structured as a Yes/No decision tree: (1) Does the contact person personally resonate with our proposal? (2) What is their skill level at involving others internally—can they handle it with our support or independently? (3) Is all decision-related information gathered (approver type: individual or committee, schedule, required materials, anticipated approval/rejection reasons)? (4) Always secure an appointment (even by phone) with relevant parties, including decision-makers when possible; if not feasible, revert to a prior process.

If any checkpoint is No, insert targeted support at that stage (e.g., create compelling materials/emails to attract the contact if they are not resonating; provide copy-paste-ready emails for internal involvement; obtain low-pressure 'homework' assignments that will not cause issues if unanswered to prevent stalling). If support fails, return to and rebuild an earlier process.

When the customer cannot independently drive internal processes, sales must provide continuous, close accompaniment ('つかず離れず') aligned with the decision timing, using phone or meeting appointments as needed.

The first and foundational checkpoint is confirming the contact personally resonates with the proposal (corresponding to a known pitfall); without this, internal advocacy cannot begin, so the immediate action is creating attractive materials and emails focused on the individual in front of you.

In sales or internal advocacy processes, begin by building trust with a single contact through labor provision (assisting with the customer's actual work), empathy, information sharing, and refining proposals. Postpone any internal company-wide rollout and focus exclusively on moving that one person's mindset first.

Evaluate whether the contact has the skill to involve colleagues even with external support. If not, the salesperson must create ready-to-use assets such as email drafts, chat messages, and approval documents. These must be written in the customer's internal tone and style so they appear authored by the contact, never revealing they were produced by the salesperson. The goal is a copy-paste-ready state that lets the contact act immediately.

If the contact cannot independently drive internal involvement, provide continuous side support rather than one-off materials. Maintain small, ongoing rallies timed to the contact's internal actions. Always obtain a low-burden 'homework' item that the contact will not be blamed for ignoring, such as offering to send extra information the following week. This keeps the relationship active without imposing pressure that could cause communication to drop.

Confirm whether all decision-related information is complete: whether approval is by a single superior or a committee, the expected timeline, required materials, internal reasons that would produce a yes, and typical reasons for a no. If any of these are missing, conduct additional targeted hearings.

Once decision information is assembled, deliver precisely timed support: materials, issue summaries, internal-facing documents, and short phone calls or appointments inserted at the exact moments of internal decision-making. The combination enables the person handling the evaluation to move the process forward efficiently.

In the final phase of a sales process, even after creating a state where the customer can proceed without hesitation, support remains necessary. This includes preparing materials to present to decision-makers and reorganizing information when internal opposition arises. Phone-based support can sometimes be sufficient.

In the requirements definition stage of the purchasing process, skill shortages among those handling the evaluation become more apparent. This is because as the evaluation becomes more concrete, more internal stakeholders need to be involved and more types of documents need to be prepared.

A gap exists between the problem-recognition stage (where simply listening to a pitch is enough) and the requirements-definition stage (which requires circulating comparison materials internally and explaining the background to superiors). The salesperson's ability to support the evaluation practitioner through this gap is a decisive factor.
A specific type of pitfall is when a particular opponent is intentionally obstructing the evaluation. This can be identified by asking: 'Is there anyone in your internal evaluation who has concerns?'

Possible backgrounds for someone applying the brakes to an internal evaluation process include: promoting a competitor, not wanting to approve a project they are not leading, or becoming cautious after a past similar project failed.
When dealing with opponents, the response must be differentiated based on whether they have a counter-proposal or not.
If an opponent has no counter-proposal, special attention is needed because vague, unspecified opposition ('somehow against it') will prevent progress.

When facing someone who is vaguely opposing a proposal, do not immediately present your own proposal and try to persuade them with logical arguments. Doing so makes the person feel their opinion has been denied, which hardens their attitude further.

The first step is to carefully listen to what the opposing person is actually thinking. Convey that you want to hear in detail about the thoughts and feelings of this person who holds an important internal role regarding how they approach their work. Making the other party feel 'valued' is the essential first step.

A concrete opening phrase is: 'Let's set our company's proposal aside for now. Could you please share in detail the thoughts of Mr./Ms. XX, who plays an important role in the company, about how you approach your work?' This approach makes the opponent feel that their own opinion is being treated as important.

When the opponent already has a counter-proposal (for example, preferring another vendor, believing it should be handled internally, or thinking a completely different approach is needed), first listen thoroughly to that alternative idea.

After listening, the key is to reach a state where you can say 'Actually, our proposal can properly align with that way of thinking as well.' If there are currently insufficient points, ask to receive 'homework' by requesting time to reorganize the proposal according to their views.
Example request for homework: 'I would like to re-summarize our proposal in a form that aligns with your thinking, so could you spare some time to organize your requests?'

Once homework is successfully obtained, engage in high-speed back-and-forth (高速ラリー). Even if a reversal based on content is difficult, there is room to reverse the situation through speed, because many customers find speed attractive.

The method of handling an opponent also changes depending on which of the six types of stakeholders they represent. If field users are the ones opposing, the issue typically concerns the operational burden after implementation.

In stalled B2B sales processes ('検討が進まない' maze), opposition often stems from specific anxieties: for those fearing increased workload, present concrete images of improved business process flows; for budget supervisors, the issue is typically invisible cost-effectiveness, so use other companies' performance data or investment recovery (ROI) simulations; for influencers of the decision-maker, political fear that a wrong recommendation will lower their evaluation, so provide industry adoption records or third-party evaluations as reassurance.

Pitfall ⑤: The person with final decision-making authority is postponing judgment (not actively opposing, but unable to decide). Check question: 'Is the person who will make the final decision the type who decides immediately once materials are ready? (If No, this is the pitfall).'

The situation of 'not opposed but won't decide' is extremely frustrating for salespeople and occurs more frequently than expected; the proposal itself may have no issues and no opponents exist, yet no conclusion is reached.

Company survey of 10,303 people with purchasing experience (split between decision-makers and staff): Decision-makers more frequently receive proposals without fully established judgment criteria. Among decision-makers (n=5,153), 41.7% experienced this 3 or more times, and over 70% experienced it at least once (including 1-2 times).

In the same survey, 37.0% of decision-makers reported that priority dropped midway, resulting in not purchasing, and this happened 3 or more times. Decision-makers themselves often hesitate when criteria are undecided, and it is common for priorities to drop and the process to stall.
This content is from Chapter 5 on 'Defensive Strategy II' (守りの戦略Ⅱ), focusing on navigating the maze of stalled considerations in sales.
The assumption that decision-makers (決裁者) will always judge reasonably and quickly is not necessarily correct; they also hesitate, put matters on hold, or deprioritize them.
Five common patterns explain why decision-makers put decisions on hold, each requiring tailored countermeasures.

Pattern 1: Absence of a committed executor. Decision-makers fear investing when no one will seriously drive the initiative. Solution: Identify and ally with a person who can credibly raise their hand and commit when asked 'Who will actually do this?'

Pattern 2: Anxiety about whether the broader organization will truly support the initiative. Solution: Have a person with real authority or influence publicly declare their willingness to back the matter, thereby strengthening the support base.

Pattern 3: Consideration for opponents. Decision-makers often do not want to embarrass or override dissenters. Solution: Do not ignore opposing views; instead, understand their background and motives and design a process that produces a conclusion opponents can accept.

Pattern 4: Organizational consideration (even without outright opposition). When a specific department will bear extra burden, formal agreement is insufficient. Decision-makers need genuine buy-in in which that department's leaders and members see the initiative as beneficial to themselves.

Pattern 5: Information overload or lack of structure that prevents judgment. Decision-makers cannot decide without clear organization of: (a) accurate grasp of the problem, (b) analysis of structure and root causes, (c) candidate options, and (d) evaluation against explicit judgment criteria. Providing this as a well-prepared 'draft' (たたき台) from the proposing side often lifts the hold.

When a sales deal is on hold, the reason frequently depends on which of the 6 types of stakeholders holds decision-making authority. If the final approver (最終決裁者) has authority, the hold often stems from balancing risk versus return as a management judgment. If the budget supervisor (予算の監督者) has authority, the hold is commonly due to insufficient numerical justification of investment versus effect (ROI).
Estimating the specific reason for a hold by mapping it to the counterpart's organizational role increases the precision and effectiveness of subsequent sales actions (打ち手).
For stalls caused by organizational (rather than individual) problems, diagnose the structural bottleneck rather than focusing on a particular person.

Pitfall ⑥: The customer organization has other higher-priority issues that must be considered first. Diagnostic check question: 'Is there currently a theme or issue with the highest priority inside your company?' (Yes indicates this pitfall).

A vendor's proposal is always top priority to the salesperson, but to the customer it is merely one item among many competing considerations. Typical higher-priority examples include post-M&A integration work, company-wide allocation of resources to a core-system replacement, or an urgent HR-system reform.

First identify exactly what the competing high-priority issues are. Then evaluate whether the vendor's proposal can be discussed in the same conversation or positioned as an accompanying/subordinate theme.

A common ineffective sales tactic is attempting to forcibly elevate the priority of one's own proposal. This usually fails because the customer has no inherent reason to raise the ranking of a vendor-initiated idea over internal strategic priorities.

When customers acknowledge a proposal but insist other issues take priority, avoid insisting on the original idea; instead adopt the mindset of attaching the proposal to the customer's existing higher-level policies or priorities.
If a customer states that another challenge is currently most important, first deeply investigate and thoroughly understand that top-priority issue before proceeding.

Demonstrate a cooperative, helpful attitude toward the customer's stated key challenge even if it does not immediately benefit your company. Example: After proposing 'sales systematization' and hearing that hiring is the priority, respond by offering to discuss hiring (e.g., 'We may not be able to help directly with sales hiring, but if it's okay, could we hear more about it within appropriate bounds?').
Taking proactive, customer-aligned actions first (even without direct self-benefit) aligns your 'vector' or direction with the customer's, building rapport and openness.

After aligning, pivot by showing that the original proposal is not unrelated but actually synergistic with the customer's top issue. Example: Frame 'sales systematization' and 'sales hiring' together as an integrated 'sales organization project' that multiplies effectiveness.
Request dedicated discussion time specifically to explore how to generate those synergistic effects between the customer's priority and your proposal.

If directly linking the proposal to the current top issue proves difficult, at minimum secure a clear 'consider next' status (e.g., 'It's difficult now, but we'd like to revisit after [issue] settles') so the conversation can resume smoothly when timing improves.

The 'approach and attach' tactic must be adapted to the counterpart's role: For internal champions/promoters, position the proposal as complementary material that raises the success probability of their top-priority project. For budget overseers, emphasize that integrating multiple initiatives improves overall investment efficiency. For final decision-makers, frame it as considering everything holistically as part of broader management policy.

A common reason discussions or considerations fail to progress in B2B contexts is that the relevant stakeholders have not been identified or confirmed at all. Without knowing who the stakeholders are, it is impossible to determine who should be involved, causing the process to stall.

Corporate purchasing processes typically involve far more people than expected. Knowing only the 'window contact person' and their immediate supervisor is insufficient to understand the full decision-making process.

There are six distinct stakeholder roles to identify: 現場の利用者 (field/end users), 社内推進者 (internal promoters or champions), 発注担当者 (ordering or procurement staff), 予算の監督者 (budget supervisors/overseers), 決裁者への影響者 (influencers on the decision-maker), and 最終決裁者 (final decision-maker).

To map stakeholders, present these six roles and systematically confirm, one by one, whether the names of the corresponding individuals are known. The immediate counterpart may not know all of them, so role-by-role questioning is effective.
Example questions for identification: 'Who in your company makes the final judgment on this topic?' and 'How is the person who manages the budget involved in this project?'

This pitfall is especially common in the early purchasing process stages of problem recognition and information gathering, when even the customer's internal team has not yet determined who will be involved.

By the requirements definition stage, the stakeholder lineup typically becomes somewhat clearer, but this is also often the first time it becomes apparent that more people are involved than initially thought.
The key preventive practice is to consciously check the six roles from the earliest stages to avoid later surprises such as discovering unexpected additional stakeholders.
Pitfall 8: Stakeholders are too busy to gather together. Even if stakeholders have been identified, they may be too busy to all assemble at once.
The ideal situation is for the appropriate members to gather, discuss, and reach a conclusion, but this is often not easily achieved in reality.
If attempting to gather everyone at once does not work, it is necessary to design alternatives such as splitting meetings or gathering people in stages.
The key is how many alternative approaches can be proposed based on the 4 patterns of how the person advancing the practical examination can actually create venues (referencing Figure 5-2).

Figure 5-5: Sequencing of communication toward decision-making. It plots 'ease of discussion occurring' (high to low, vertical axis) against 'hurdle of setting up the venue' (low to high, horizontal axis).

The four types of communication venues are: A - Incorporate into the agenda of a regular meeting; B - Convene necessary members for discussion; C - Individual consultations; D - Individual approval requests.

Decision-making patterns include: Decided in one shot (A	o decision, or B	o decision); Decided through a series of continuous interactions (C	o C	o C	o decision, or D	o D	o decision); Decided after the type of venue changes (B	o A	o A	o decision, or D	o C	o B	o decision).
Check question: How frequently are meetings held where all relevant parties gather together? (If they cannot be held consistently, this is this pitfall.)

Decision-making patterns include simultaneous ones like A (incorporate into regular meetings) → decision or B (convene necessary members for discussion) → decision; sequential ones like C (individual consultations) → C → C → decision or D (individual approval requests) → D → decision; and mixed patterns that switch settings mid-process, such as B → A → A → decision or D → C → B → decision, which can create breakthroughs.

When stakeholders are busy, proactively suggest changing the 'setting of the venue' (ba no settei) rather than waiting; clients often lack this idea, so sales should propose alternatives based on the four patterns.

Customize approaches by role: For internal promoters, suggest unofficial individual consultations (C) for groundwork before adding to regular meeting agendas (A); for procurement staff, offer to set individual 15-minute online meetings to reduce scheduling burden.
The key to escaping the 'discussions not progressing' pitfall is not waiting due to busy stakeholders but designing different venues/settings to create openings.

Pitfall ⑨: Stakeholders are discussing but judgment criteria are vague. Check question: 'In your internal discussions, have the judgment criteria items already been agreed upon?' (If no, this is the pitfall).

Even when people gather, materials are distributed, and discussions occur, progress stalls if judgment criteria remain undefined, often ending with 'let's continue considering'—a common 'spinning wheels' meeting phenomenon.

Judgment criteria in internal meetings often become vague because meeting topics are constructed ambiguously, such as saying 'I've prepared the materials, please give your opinions.' This type of open-ended question provides no clear standard for judgment, causing participants to comment freely from their own positions and making the discussion diverge.
To prevent this, collaboratively design the discussion (議論の設計) together with the person responsible for advancing the practical examination work.
Discussions are fundamentally based on '選択肢' (options/choices) and '判断軸' (judgment axes/criteria).

When immediately presenting options (for example, comparing vendor proposals) would stir up controversy (波風が立つ), first carefully organize the issues and align on problem recognition. Ask something like: 'I've organized the issues this way; please share your opinions on whether there are any missing points or differences in understanding.'

Alternatively, first advance information gathering and present candidate companies, then ask: 'If we were to issue a request for proposal, what requirements should we use? Please share your opinions.' After these preparatory steps, presenting the actual proposals makes the subsequent discussion much more organized.

When it is acceptable to present options immediately, avoid vague questions such as 'What do you think about this proposal?' and instead convert them into specific questions that focus the discussion.

Effective specific question examples include: 'This initiative shows expected ROI (投資対効果), but if there are any anticipated risks or issues, please share your opinions.'; 'There are Plan A and Plan B; which do you think is more desirable? Please share your thoughts.'; and 'We basically want to proceed, but I've proposed a plan for the schedule and organization; please share any points you notice.'
Specific problem statements must be raised by the people actually advancing the review/practical examination work.

Discussions ultimately develop into judgment axes (判断軸) for choosing among options. Example axes include 'introduction impact', 'price', 'quality', 'delivery system', and 'support service'; each vendor proposal is then evaluated against these axes.
稟議 (internal approval process) means reducing the decision to the structure of 'options × judgment axes'.
The purpose of side/lateral support is therefore to shape the situation into a form that can be dropped into judgment criteria.
When the client has not yet organized their own judgment criteria, presenting a draft (たたき台) of those criteria is effective and is usually welcomed.
