Example additional proposals in a new-employee training (新人研修) context include: applying assessment tools previously used as HR evaluation material at listed companies with tens of thousands of employees, designed from scratch alongside a 1–3 year young-employee development system; designing the final graduation exam as a full simulation exercise covering 'appointment acquisition through follow-up' with assessor training on checkpoints; visualizing every participant's performance so the final exam must be cleared individually (with proven visualization methods from other companies); creating an Excel that lists the flow 'required on-the-job behaviors → necessary knowledge/skills/mindset → objective diagnostic exercises for those situations'; holding regular meetings that minimize client burden while aligning vendor expertise with client wishes on materials and operations; leveraging experience designing talent-development systems for 30+ prime-market listed companies to also support existing-employee development; applying on-site production experience from 20+ large-scale (300–1,300 person) new-hire programs; using 100% customized, 100% repeat-rate exercise-creation capability; embedding individual counseling sessions to address common mental/physical health issues in one-month programs; and balancing the severity of a graduation-style exam with group-learning formats and atmosphere-care measures (e.g., assigning leader roles) to maintain peer cohesion.

Supporting keywords/themes extracted from the example include: high-precision assessment, pace for clearing a fixed standard (graduation), embodying field severity, program standardization, tandem (二人三脚) design with the client, application to existing employees, large-scale training countermeasures, exercise-design quality, long-term training countermeasures, and balancing severity with peer-group awareness.

Additional proposals work because they present points the customer themselves had not noticed, creating the impression that 'this company is not merely returning what was asked.' Sales trust deepens not only through the ability to answer asked questions but through the ability to anticipate unasked ones.

At the order-decision stage, voluntary additional information is especially effective, as shown by a survey of 2,676 people (referenced from Chapter 2). Constructive additional proposals from the salesperson, even when not requested by the customer, can serve as the final push.
Proposal materials become far more readable when the correspondence between the customer's requirements and the proposed solution is shown visually (ビジュアル化).

Figure 11-4 example: explicitly map training outcomes to customer requirements using numbered elements (①研修成果物の持ち帰り, ②タテヨコのシナジー, ③会社の風土やテーマへの合致, ④若手のリテンション, ⑤講師の経験やスタイル, ⑥中期視点での施策連携, ⑦貴社の状況に沿った柔軟な対応) and employee segments (1–2年目社員, 3–5年目社員, 管理職未満の若手社員, 係長・課長).

Expected outcomes by segment in the visualization: 1–2 year employees become able to use free thinking to improve methods without being bound by rigid ideas; 3–5 year employees shift focus from their own work to junior development and team impact; young employees below management raise their perspective and support organizational development; section chiefs/managers prioritize tasks, delegate, and draw out junior initiative while transitioning from playing-manager roles.

Horizontal connections (ヨコのつながり) among trainees and vertical synergies are highlighted as ways training results are taken back into the organization, including mid-term policy linkage and flexible adaptation to the client's specific situation and culture.
Explicitly showing correspondence (対応関係の明示) between a customer's needs/requirements and the elements of a proposal is highly effective in sales, for two main reasons.

Reason 1: When a customer receives proposals from multiple companies, the volume of information they must process is enormous. It is often difficult to discern from the proposal documents alone exactly how each one matches their specific needs. Materials that explicitly map correspondences therefore become a scoring plus (加点要素) by themselves.

Reason 2: After receiving a proposal, the customer typically needs to explain it internally to other stakeholders. When correspondences are already explicit, they can directly say 'For this requirement of ours, this company responds in this way.' The proposal thus functions as ready-made internal presentation material that is convenient, easy to recommend, and easy to share—especially valuable when many people are involved in the decision.
Materials that are easy to explain and easy to share become powerful weapons in multi-stakeholder buying situations.

The same technique of explicit correspondence is particularly powerful in replacement (リプレイス) deals where the goal is to displace an incumbent competitor. Clearly showing 'what is different' makes it easier for the customer to evaluate a vendor switch.

A common mistake in replacement proposals is using a negation frame such as 'last year's vendor was not good.' This is risky because the person who originally selected that vendor may be sitting across the table; it implies their previous judgment was wrong and can create emotional resistance.

The winning structure for a replacement proposal is: first affirm that 'the good points from last year can be similarly realized by us,' then add an overlay—'if there are points that could be improved, we can address them to this extent.' Presenting both the inherited elements and the improvements side-by-side with explicit correspondences makes the decision easy for the customer.

Concrete example (adapted from Figure 11-5): Take last year's training program (the incumbent's previous proposal) and place 'points to inherit/continue' (踏襲する点) in parallel with 'points to improve' (改善する点), mapping each directly to the customer's original requirements.
In replacement proposals (リプレイス提案), explicitly show the correspondence (対応関係) between the new proposal and competing or previous plans to demonstrate continuity and improvements.

Proposal structure based on prior training should follow two key points: (1) inherit the purpose/intent of last year's training, and (2) address the improvement points identified from last year's training.

Example mapping from last year's training to new proposal: Last year focused on learning basics of questioning and negotiation methods; new version shifts to experiencing 'tough situations' assumed in actual sales talks via simulation exercises.

Example mapping: Last year used role-plays after assembling stories according to the counterpart's type; new version adds methods for countering negative responses such as customer doubts, concerns, and objections, incorporated into lectures and exercises.

Example mapping: Last year involved video-recording one's own sales scenes to objectively grasp personal habits; new version expands this to more systematic reviews using an enhanced framework, moving beyond habit-level analysis.

Concrete implementation measures (打ち手) include: incorporating questioning/negotiation methods into lecture portions and confirming via comprehensive exercises; conducting story-creation and role-play exercises tailored to counterpart types; adding video recording and review of sales scenes to the agenda; running simulation exercises for tough situations; adding counter-methods for negative customer responses; and expanding the self-review framework for sales scenes.

When it is not possible to fulfill all client requests exactly as specified, create a sense of specialness (特別感) by focusing on the background and underlying structure of the issues rather than just surface requirements. This is the 'create specialness through cause analysis' (原因の分析で特別感を出す) approach.

The value lies not only in the analysis results themselves but in explicitly showing the analysis process and content. Presenting only a conclusion such as 'This is optimal for your company' leaves the client wondering why that conclusion was reached.

By revealing the analysis process, the client perceives that the salesperson has thought deeply about their specific situation before arriving at the proposal, thereby generating a feeling of being specially considered.
Section 11.3 introduces three organized methods for customization that create specialness through cause analysis (though the specific methods begin after this introductory page).

In last-minute customization strategy just before an order decision, one way to add specialness to problem-cause analysis is to explicitly show the analysis process and its content so the customer understands why this specific proposal was chosen.

Verbalize comments and insights gathered from pre-proposal hearings with frontline staff or executives; presenting them as 'hearings revealed this situation' before the actual proposal instantly converts a mere sales pitch into a grounded, evidence-based recommendation.

Supplying a concise summary of hearing results also helps the customer's internal champion explain to superiors why this vendor should be selected, thereby supporting the customer's own decision-making process.

When stating problems, never write bluntly 'your company is weak here' or 'this is poorly done'; such wording can offend executives, especially if the root cause falls under a particular officer's responsibility and triggers emotional resistance ('are you criticizing my area?').

A practical phrasing technique is first to list positive 'driving factors that have supported growth so far' together with supporting comments, then recast the real issues as 'challenges toward the next stage' using forward-looking language.

When identifying challenges from an organization's strengths, do not merely rephrase the strength as a weakness. Instead, clearly reveal the underlying structure: the challenge arises as the flip side of the strength itself. Framing it as 'because this strength exists, this particular wall appears at the next stage' turns the observation into valuable analysis rather than simple criticism.

Concrete example of strength-to-challenge structure: A company's strength is that the president's personality and leadership have created unity and sustained growth. The structural flip side is that development of other leadership layers has not kept pace. Presenting this causal structure allows the client to receive the issue as 'preparation for the next stage' rather than as an attack.

Core consulting practice for creating a sense of analysis: always pair facts with a message. Facts alone leave the audience asking 'so what?'; a message alone leaves them asking 'what's the evidence?'. Delivering both together produces conviction and the feeling that genuine analysis has occurred.

A second technique for making cause analysis distinctive is to visualize the problem structure with arrow diagrams. This clarifies 'what is actually happening' far more effectively than evaluative statements such as 'this is weak' or 'this is bad'.

Evaluative language ('weak', 'bad') triggers defensiveness and invites rebuttal because it is judgment, not structure. Showing the causal mechanism itself allows the client to stay calm and think 'I see how this system produces the problem.'

A practical visualization method is to place a typical vicious-cycle diagram next to a virtuous-cycle diagram. Clients frequently recognize their own situation immediately ('ours is clearly the left-hand side') and begin describing the problem in their own words. Once that happens, the consultant and client share the same vantage point and can proceed without further persuasion.

In sales proposals, present hypotheses about what is occurring in 'management PDCA' as circular structures (vicious cycle on the left, virtuous cycle on the right). This visual approach, though requiring analytical thinking, clearly shows causes, effects, and outcomes at a glance and has strong power to engage customers.

Example of vicious cycle in a struggling sales team: abstract communication about members' sales processes leads to inability to verify action results, making improvement and PDCA difficult to cycle; sales numbers fail to rise, increasing the number of tasks; members do not know specifically what to do and simply try hard individually.

Example of virtuous cycle in a successful sales team: specific communication about members' sales processes makes it easy to verify action results, allowing improvement and PDCA to cycle well; numbers gradually rise and tasks become more focused; members understand and practice specific actions needed to produce results.
To add a special feel to root-cause analysis, apply the customer's current situation to a framework, organize it, and derive implications for the proposal.

After conducting hearings and analysis, presenting a framework that depicts the overall picture dramatically speeds customer understanding because frameworks function as a map that lets the customer grasp 'where they currently stand within the whole.'
A framework such as '5-stage purchasing process and 6 types of stakeholders' makes it easy to discuss 'where we are now' in the process.

A sales organization evolution-stage framework can be used in proposals to map each branch or office (e.g., A, B, C) onto a hypothesized current phase, creating a shared discussion foundation with the client.
An overall map converts scattered facts and impressions into a visible 'structure,' from which the next concrete actions become apparent.
Frameworks must be customized to the client's industry characteristics and organizational state rather than applied generically; otherwise the client perceives a one-size-fits-all pitch.

Four illustrative phases of sales-organization evolution are: 探る (exploring / discovering winning patterns), 回す (operating / executing the established pattern), 手放す (empowering / letting go), and a later stage marked by a sense of stagnation or the need to raise standards.
Corresponding leadership styles are 戦略思考型 (strategic-thinking), 指示統制型 (command-and-control), 権限移譲型 (empowerment), and 率先垂範型 (leading-by-example).

Success keys aligned with the phases include calculated trial-and-error (Safe Fail), rigorous execution of the 'kata' (Operation Excellence), willingness to delegate even at the risk of failure (Empowerment), and raising the bar while taking calculated risks (Revolution).

Typical risks at each stage are: being driven too hard by excessively high standards, excessive complexity from proliferating tasks, people doing only what they are told, and unnoticed erosion of performance standards.

Analysis thinking itself can be turned into a source of value. Three methods to create a special feeling through cause analysis are: (1) explicitly showing the analysis process and content, (2) visualizing causal relationships, and (3) utilizing frameworks. These share the common point of using analytical thinking as a source of value.

Explicitly showing the analysis process and content creates a sense of conviction about 'why this proposal'. Visualizing causal relationships clarifies problem recognition. Applying frameworks organizes information and derives insights.

When it is difficult to respond directly to a customer's request, delving into the background and structure of the problem allows creating a special feeling from 'cause analysis'. This creates a structure where the customer purchases 'analytical ability = high added value'.

This also expands 'what sales sells'. Not only the company's products or services are for sale, but 'the ability to structurally understand the customer's issues and derive the optimal solution' itself becomes value for the customer.

Three approaches to creating a special feeling through the proposal message: (1) Killing two birds with one stone: explicitly showing that other benefits can be obtained simultaneously; (2) Long-term scope: mentioning not only 'this time' but also 'the future'; (3) Specific impact: expressing Before → After in detail.

一石二鳥 (killing two birds with one stone) is the first technique for adding specialness to a proposal message: explicitly state that the proposal delivers unexpected additional benefits in other areas beyond the client's original request or challenge.
From the client's perspective, this framing means one investment yields advantages across multiple seemingly different domains.

Example: A client requests sales training. A basic response is simply to deliver skill-building training. An enhanced 一石二鳥 version adds: implementing the training will also systematize sales skills and produce a company-specific skill map that can be used for hiring and personnel evaluation, thereby extending impact from 'development' into 'recruitment and evaluation'.
The core action is to surface and communicate hidden benefits or added value that exist beyond the requested content itself.
The guiding mindset is: 'This proposal not only meets the original need but also produces positive spillover effects in surrounding areas.'

Practical self-questions to discover these effects: 'In what other situations can the deliverable of this proposal be used?' and 'What secondary capabilities or assets will grow through the process of executing this proposal?' Assuming a deliverable has only one use prevents noticing ripple effects.
長期スコープ (long-term scope) is the second technique: while fully covering the immediate requested scope, also explicitly indicate that future-stage support is possible after the current engagement.
Typical phrasing: 'We can of course handle the current scope. On top of that, for the next stage we can provide this kind of support.'
This long-term framing can become a selection reason for clients who evaluate proposals with a future-oriented perspective.

In B2B (corporate) sales, customers frequently evaluate whether a vendor can serve as a medium-to-long-term partner rather than completing only a one-time transaction; companies that demonstrate ongoing value over time are more likely to be selected.

To increase proposal attractiveness, include explicit sections such as 'immediate key themes' and 'key themes for the next 3 years,' and state upfront that the current proposal has been designed with a 3-year horizon in mind.

In addition to describing immediate deliverables, outline the kinds of future support that can be provided; this differentiates the proposal from vendors who present only short-term offerings and makes the overall package appear more appealing.

When describing a long-term scope, avoid overly grandiose or unrealistic future visions, because they tend to generate distrust ('Can they really do this?'). Instead, present an 'achievable future' together with concrete milestones.

A third technique for giving a proposal message a sense of specialness is to express specific impact in fine-grained detail using a Before → After format that shows exactly how the customer’s situation will change.

A quantitative survey of 2,676 respondents asked what constitutes the 'final push' when deciding the winning vendor; the most frequently chosen answer was 'return on investment (ROI) or concrete merits/benefits.'

Survey of 2,676 people on the 'final push' factors when deciding a vendor: the top-ranked element is '投資対効果や具体的メリット' (ROI or concrete benefits) at 22.1% for 1st place, followed by alignment with management policy/strategy (15.2%), comparison with other companies' products (13.5%), past transaction history/trust (11.5%), strong recommendation from field users (10.8%), reputation from other internal/group projects (10.4%), purchaser's own enthusiasm (8.2%), comments from other departments (5.0%), a single remark by the salesperson in the presentation (3.9%), and advice from an external expert different from the salesperson (3.8%). Rankings for 2nd and 3rd places are also shown in stacked bars.

Key sales principle: Concrete images of change ('いまこうなっているものが、こう変わる') are easy to visualize in the mind. Stating 'the work that currently takes 3 hours will become 30 minutes' delivers far more impact than a generic claim such as 'productivity will increase'.
To create that concrete impact it is highly effective to first grasp the client's current state (Before) in detail.

For tangible products such as SaaS, insert an extra process called a '逆デモ' (reverse demo) before showing your own demo: ask the client to show how they currently manage sales (actual screen flows) or allow you to observe a sales meeting.
After the reverse demo, organize the key points of the client's existing approach so that the subsequent demonstration can be framed as a precise Before-to-After transformation.

In last-minute sales closing, structure the demo by first summarizing noticed issues ('I've summarized the points I noticed') and showing a concrete image of how the product changes the situation, then entering the demo aligned to those points. This sequence makes issues explicit before closing and creates a stronger Before → After contrast because the customer's resolution of the current 'Before' state is higher.

A reverse demo (逆デモ) is highly effective because it forces the customer to re-recognize the hidden inconveniences and inefficiencies in their current 'this is just how it is' business processes. Once that awareness is created, the subsequent product demo makes a dramatically stronger impression.

Customization strategy to raise win rates at the order-decision stage has three angles. The first is creating a special feeling through request handling: start with high-quality requirement organization covering completeness (網羅性), concretization (具体化), and prioritization (優先順位). Add extras such as exhaustively capturing all needs, inserting additional proposals, and explicitly showing correspondence between needs and solutions. This produces the impression 'they understand us this thoroughly' and 'they prepared this much.' Differentiation comes from the quality of organization, not merely fulfilling requests as stated.

The second angle is creating a special feeling through cause analysis. Even when it is difficult to give individual responses exactly as requested, recapturing the background and underlying structure of the issues increases the persuasiveness of the proposal. Practical methods include explicitly showing the analysis process and content, visualizing causal relationships, and applying frameworks. Regular accumulation of information raises both the precision and speed of analysis, enabling highly reproducible creation of '納得感' (a sense of conviction) in the proposal.

The third method for creating a sense of specialness (特別感) in a proposal is through the design of the proposal message itself. Even in situations where there is insufficient time for detailed analysis, a well-designed message can still create a winning path (勝ち筋).
Key elements for designing an effective proposal message are: achieving two goals with one action (一石二鳥), adopting a long-term scope (長期スコープ), and demonstrating concrete, specific impact (具体的なインパクト).

The customization strategy (カスタマイズ戦略) builds a proposal's specialness across three layers: (1) precision in organizing requirements (要件整理の精度), (2) the manner of presenting root-cause analysis (原因分析の見せ方), and (3) the design of the proposal message (提案メッセージの設計).

While it is preferable to resolve issues cleanly at the upstream stage without complications, even if a competitive situation remains messy until the final stage, the created 'specialness' can still provide the customer with a compelling reason to select the proposal.
To create a special feeling (特別感) at the order-decision stage, confirm the degree of customization across three layers: A) responding to requests, B) analyzing causes, and C) proposal messaging.

Layer A (要望への対応で特別感を出す): Checklist for creating special feeling via request response includes: listing customer requests/issues as keywords (requirements organization); ensuring important requests are comprehensively covered without omissions (comprehensiveness check); specifying each request down to 'what is the problem and what must be satisfied to be OK'; clarifying priorities; including additional unspoken proposals; and explicitly showing the correspondence between requirements and proposals at a glance.

Layer B (原因の分析で特別感を出す): Checklist for creating special feeling via cause analysis includes: explicitly showing the analysis process and content in the proposal (to create conviction about 'why this proposal'); visualizing issue causes and structure with diagrams (causal relationship visualization); applying the customer's situation to a framework for organization; customizing the framework to the customer's industry/organization; expressing issue identification not as criticism but as a stepping stone to the next stage; and presenting facts paired with messages/implications.

Layer C (提案メッセージで特別感を出す): Checklist for creating special feeling via proposal messages includes: 'killing two birds with one stone' by showing spillover benefits beyond the original purpose; long-term scope by indicating possibilities for future support beyond the current range; and specific impact by visualizing Before → After in detail.
This forms an appendix checklist (付録：カスタマイズ提案チェックリスト) for customized proposals in offensive strategy, aimed at securing last-minute victory just before the order decision.

Customers decide on vendors earlier than salespeople typically imagine: in a 5-stage purchasing process, 66.8% of deals are already decided by the 3rd stage ('requirements definition'). More than two-thirds of cases are settled before vendors even submit formal proposals.

This early decision-making holds even for first-time purchases: among buyers who have never purchased the product/service before and are starting from scratch with comparison and decision-making (n=362), 61.3% still decide by the requirements definition stage. Meetings that appear to be mere information-gathering can actually be critical for winning the deal.

Purchasing initiative (leadership/control) is dispersed and fluid rather than concentrated. When all stakeholders are asked who has substantial influence over purchasing, only 16.7% name the 'final decision-maker'. Even the final decision-makers themselves report that 53.6% feel someone else is actually influencing the decision.

Every role in the buying process (not just the final approver) claims 30-50% of the time that they personally have the substantial influence over vendor selection. Consequently, a single deal typically has multiple key persons who continue to change over time.

Salespeople must recognize that key persons are distributed, ambiguous, and constantly shifting. The corporate buying process becomes a 'maze' because of the many stakeholders; sales teams should therefore navigate it while carrying a 'torch' (a guiding framework or insight provided by the book).

In B2B/corporate sales (法人営業), four common 'mazes' (迷路) or pitfalls that can stall deals are: the 'unable to meet the key person maze' (キーパーソンに会えない迷路), the 'unable to make contact maze' (連絡がつながらない迷路), the 'consideration not progressing maze' (検討が進まない迷路), and the 'budget not increasing maze' (予算が増えない迷路).

When at risk of falling into one of these mazes, form hypotheses (based on content from chapters 3–6) about: (1) which stage of the customer's purchasing process (購買プロセス) you are currently in, (2) what role the person you are currently meeting plays, and (3) how to proceed going forward so the customer decides to place an order with your company. These hypotheses act as a 'torch' (松明) that illuminates the maze and constitute the 'defensive strategy' (守りの戦略) as a winning pattern in corporate sales.

Before becoming lost in a maze, 'offensive strategies' (攻めの戦略) exist that map specific approaches to specific purchasing stages, of the form 'if the customer is in this purchasing stage, use this approach.'

Five winning-pattern strategies (from chapters 7–11) mapped to purchasing stages: Issue-recognition/challenge-awareness stage (課題認識段階) → Engagement Strategy (エンゲージメント戦略); Information-gathering stage (情報収集段階) → Expert Strategy (エキスパート戦略); Requirements-definition stage (要件定義段階) → Discussion Strategy (ディスカッション戦略); Vendor-comparison stage (ベンダー比較段階) → Guide Strategy (ガイド戦略); Order-decision stage (発注決定段階) → Customization Strategy (カスタマイズ戦略). These should be implemented in a manner suited to one's own sales organization.
Concentrating resources on a specific purchasing stage makes the corresponding offensive strategy visible and actionable.

The book '法人営業 勝ちパターン大全' presents an overall framework for B2B sales winning patterns centered on a 5-stage customer purchasing process where outcomes are often decided in ways different from what salespeople imagine.

The 5-stage purchasing process consists of: (1) 課題認識 (issue/problem recognition), where prospects struggle even before recognizing a formal issue; (2) 情報収集 (information gathering), where they tend to drown in a sea of information; (3) 要件定義 (requirements definition), by which stage 66.8% of deals are already decided; (4) ベンダー比較 (vendor comparison), a relative evaluation stage; (5) 発注決定 (order/purchase decision), where they cannot decide cleanly.

Three overarching perspectives that run through the entire approach: (1) identifying which stage of the purchasing process the deal is in, (2) identifying the role of the person being met, and (3) how to accompany/support them toward decision-making.
Busyness (忙しさ) is identified as the biggest bottleneck in the process.
Defensive strategies focus on escaping '4つの迷路' (4 mazes), covered in chapters 3-6.

Maze 1: Unable to meet the key person. Reasons categorized as A (not grasped: confirmation method is not visible), B (not trying to connect: do not understand the proposal's value, no time for connecting actions, do not want to be bypassed/skipped, do not want to receive negative evaluation, hesitation due to multiple candidates), C (key person themselves refuse: cannot understand the value, do not want to spend time on preparation/adjustment, want to focus on other issues).

Maze 2: Unable to establish contact. Reasons categorized as A (not reading emails: unaware/not noticing), B (deliberately not responding: information overload causing thinking shutdown, poor impression of the salesperson, proposal value not being conveyed), C (bottleneck preventing reply: no time available, faded memory of prior interactions, need for internal confirmation causing hold, lack of language/verbalization skills, desire to avoid troublesome developments).
Offensive strategies consist of 5 strategies to take the initiative, covered in chapters 7-11.
Engagement strategy: Take the lead at the issue recognition stage by warming relationships through outbound contact to avoid competition.
Expert strategy: Build trust at the information gathering stage by establishing a position as a consultable expert using specialized knowledge.
Discussion strategy: Enter at the requirements definition stage and build barriers against competitor entry through bidirectional co-creation.
In B2B purchasing processes, there are six types of stakeholders, and purchasing initiative (leadership/decision-making power) is distributed and fluid rather than concentrated.
The final decision-maker's actual influence is only 16.7%.

The six stakeholder types and their primary concerns are: (1) Field users who want things 'faster and cheaper'; (2) Internal promoters who ask 'Are we correctly grasping the issues?'; (3) Order/procurement staff who check 'Does the performance match?'; (4) Budget supervisors who focus on 'cost-effectiveness and peace of mind'; (5) Influencers on the decision-maker who ask 'Does it match our company?'; (6) Final decision-makers who evaluate 'Is it worth the investment?'.
Guide Strategy: Stand out during the vendor comparison stage by differentiating in the proposal process and leading the judgment criteria/axis.
Customize Strategy: Achieve a last-minute victory in the order-decision stage by creating a special feeling of 'they are going this far for us'.

Maze 3 (Consideration does not progress) - Personal problems: (1) The ball has not been passed to the person who actually advances the practical work; (2) The person immediately involved does not agree; (3) Insufficient skills; (4) Opponents are obstructing; (5) The authority holder is postponing judgment.

Maze 3 (Consideration does not progress) - Organizational problems: (6) There are other higher-priority issues; (7) Stakeholders have not been confirmed/identified; (8) Stakeholders are too busy to gather; (9) Judgment criteria are ambiguous; (10) There is no means to resolve differences of opinion.

Maze 4 (Budget does not increase) - Personal problems: (1) The business-side authority holder does not approve; (2) The management-side authority holder does not approve; (3) Inter-departmental coordination stakeholders do not approve.

Maze 4 (Budget does not increase) - Procedural problems: (4) Stopped before even entering the formal procedure; (5) The procedure itself is cumbersome; (6) The person in charge is busy with other work.
Maze 4 (Budget does not increase) - Cultural problems: (7) Preference for in-house/internal development; (8) Culture of starting small; (9) Culture that is strictly focused on ROI.

The Japanese proverb '勝ちに不思議の勝ちあり、負けに不思議の負けなし' (There are mysterious wins, but no mysterious losses) originated with Edo-period daimyo Matsura Seizan (Matsura Kiyoshi) and was frequently cited by baseball manager Nomura Katsuya.
Applied to sales, lost deals (失注) always have identifiable root causes that can and should be uncovered, whereas the factors behind won deals (受注) often appear elusive and mysterious.
The author's core question after supporting more than 40,000 salespeople is how to give sales-team 'wins' true reproducibility rather than treating them as unexplainable luck.

In B2B (corporate) sales the real decision process occurs off-stage: customers hold internal discussions, meetings, create documents, and reach a collective corporate decision; capturing this 'behind-the-scenes' activity is hypothesized to be the key to consistent results.
The author founded a company at age 25 with zero sales experience and no mentor, so the only teachers available were customers themselves.

A concrete feedback technique: after an unsuccessful presentation a customer invited the author to lunch and, while memory was fresh, marked every page of the proposal in the upper-right corner with ○ (resonated), △ (neutral), or × (did not resonate), thereby revealing exactly what had worked and what had not.

A major discovery was that parts of a proposal the author rated as 'good' (◯) were seen as 'bad' (×) by the customer, while parts the author considered 'so-so' (△) were rated 'good' (◯) by the customer.
When the author asked why the evaluations differed, it became vividly clear how greatly the opinions of people other than the main contact person influence decisions.
A key point for achieving results in sales is to thoroughly understand how customers make decisions in ways that are not visible from the salesperson's perspective.

The saying 'there are mysterious wins' should not be attributed merely to luck or uncontrollable external factors; instead, one should make every possible effort to unravel and understand that 'mystery' to the limit.

The author describes himself as not particularly competitive in self-awareness, and as quiet and mild-mannered in private life (he even runs a bookstore named 'Kapibara Shoten' after his personality, and customers note the contrast with his speaking persona).

Observing his then-3-year-old son, the author sees a glimpse of his own 'persistence' or 'obsession': the son's catchphrase is 'I'll do it myself!' and he keeps challenging himself until he can do something he previously couldn't.

Until age 2, the parents dressed the son and put on his socks; after a certain point, any attempt to help with dressing or putting on socks is met with 'I'll do it myself!' and he persists indefinitely.

If the parents accidentally try to help, the son cries intensely out of frustration; dressing takes a very long time (e.g., fastening a single button routinely takes over 5 minutes, putting on one sock takes several minutes), yet he continues until he succeeds at each step.
